Hence, if $c_{N} /\left(c_{0} / \mu\right)<49$, then the incremental backup is better than the cumulative one.# 9.3 Optimum Full Backup Level for Cumulative Backup In this section, we derive an optimum full backup level for the cumulative backup. Suppose that we do the full backup when the total files have exceeded a managerial level $K(0 \leq K \leq \infty)$ or when the recovery is completed if the database fails, whichever occurs first. The cumulative backup is done at each update between the full backups. Underlying the same assumptions as those of Section 9.2, the probability that the full backup is done when the total files have exceeded $K$ is $$ \sum_{j=0}^{\infty}\left[G^{(j)}(K)-G^{(j+1)}(K)\right] \int_{0}^{\infty} \bar{D}(t) \mathrm{d} F^{(j+1)}(t) $$ and the probability that it is done when the database fails is $$ \sum_{j=0}^{\infty} G^{(j)}(K) \int_{0}^{\infty}\left[F^{(j)}(t)-F^{(j+1)}(t)\right] \mathrm{d} D(t) $$ where $(9.40)+(9.41)=1$. Furthermore, the mean time to the full backup is $$ \begin{aligned} & \sum_{j=0}^{\infty}\left[G^{(j)}(K)-G^{(j+1)}(K)\right] \int_{0}^{\infty} t \bar{D}(t) \mathrm{d} F^{(j+1)}(t) \\ & \quad+\sum_{j=0}^{\infty} G^{(j)}(K) \int_{0}^{\infty} t\left[F^{(j)}(t)-F^{(j+1)}(t)\right] \mathrm{d} D(t) \\ & =\sum_{j=0}^{\infty} G^{(j)}(K) \int_{0}^{\infty}\left[F^{(j)}(t)-F^{(j+1)}(t)\right] \bar{D}(t) \mathrm{d} t \end{aligned} $$ and the expected number of backups before the full backup is $$ \begin{aligned} & \sum_{j=1}^{\infty} j\left[G^{(j)}(K)-G^{(j+1)}(K)\right] \int_{0}^{\infty} \bar{D}(t) \mathrm{d} F^{(j+1)}(t) \\ & \quad+\sum_{j=1}^{\infty} j G^{(j)}(K) \int_{0}^{\infty}\left[F^{(j)}(t)-F^{(j+1)}(t)\right] \mathrm{d} D(t) \\ & =\sum_{j=1}^{\infty} G^{(j)}(K) \int_{0}^{\infty} \bar{D}(t) \mathrm{d} F^{(j)}(t) \end{aligned} $$ Let us introduce the following costs: Cost $c_{F}$ is incurred for the full backup, cost $c_{K}+c_{0}(x)$ is incurred for the cumulative backup when the total files are $x(0 \leq x \leq K)$, and cost $c_{R}+c_{0}(x)$ is incurred for the recovery when the database fails, where $c_{0}(0) \equiv 0$. Using the same arguments for obtaining (9.26), the total expected cost until the full backup is$$ \begin{aligned} c_{F} & +\sum_{j=0}^{\infty} \int_{0}^{\infty}\left[F^{(j)}(t)-F^{(j+1)}(t)\right] \mathrm{d} D(t) \\ & \times\left\{\sum_{i=1}^{j} \int_{0}^{K}\left[c_{K}+c_{0}(x)\right] \mathrm{d} G^{(i)}(x)+\int_{0}^{K}\left[c_{R}+c_{0}(x)\right] \mathrm{d} G^{(j)}(x)\right\} \\ = & c_{F}+\sum_{j=1}^{\infty} \int_{0}^{\infty} \bar{D}(t) \mathrm{d} F^{(j)}(t) \int_{0}^{K}\left[c_{K}+c_{0}(x)\right] \mathrm{d} G^{(j)}(x) \\ & +\sum_{j=0}^{\infty} \int_{0}^{\infty}\left[F^{(j)}(t)-F^{(j+1)}(t)\right] \mathrm{d} D(t) \int_{0}^{K}\left[c_{R}+c_{0}(x)\right] \mathrm{d} G^{(j)}(x) \end{aligned} $$ Therefore, the expected cost rate is, dividing (9.44) by (9.42), $$ \begin{gathered} c_{F}+\sum_{j=1}^{\infty} \int_{0}^{\infty} \bar{D}(t) \mathrm{d} F^{(j)}(t) \int_{0}^{K}\left[c_{K}+c_{0}(x)\right] \mathrm{d} G^{(j)}(x) \\ C_{C}(K)=\frac{+\sum_{j=0}^{\infty} \int_{0}^{\infty}\left[F^{(j)}(t)-F^{(j+1)}(t)\right] \mathrm{d} D(t) \int_{0}^{K}\left[c_{R}+c_{0}(x)\right] \mathrm{d} G^{(j)}(x)}{\sum_{j=0}^{\infty} G^{(j)}(K) \int_{0}^{\infty}\left[F^{(j)}(t)-F^{(j+1)}(t)\right] \bar{D}(t) \mathrm{d} t} \end{gathered} $$ In particular, when $K=0$, i.e., the full backup is done at the first update or at the failure of the database, whichever occurs first, the expected cost in (9.45) is $$ C_{C}(0)=\frac{c_{F}+c_{R} \int_{0}^{\infty} \bar{F}(t) \mathrm{d} D(t)}{\int_{0}^{\infty} \bar{F}(t) \bar{D}(t) \mathrm{d} t} $$ where $\bar{F}(t) \equiv 1-F^{(1)}(t)$. When $K=\infty$, i.e., the full backup is done only at the failure of the database, the expected cost in (9.45) is $$ \begin{aligned} \frac{C_{C}(\infty)}{\gamma}= & c_{F}+c_{R}+c_{K} \sum_{j=1}^{\infty} \int_{0}^{\infty} \bar{D}(t) \mathrm{d} M_{F}(t) \\ & +\sum_{j=1}^{\infty} \int_{0}^{\infty}\left[2 F^{(j)}(t)-F^{(j+1)}(t)\right] \mathrm{d} D(t) \int_{0}^{\infty} c_{0}(x) \mathrm{d} G^{(j)}(x) \end{aligned} $$ where $M_{F}(t) \equiv \sum_{j=1}^{\infty} F^{(j)}(t)$. Next, suppose that $c_{0}(x)=c_{0} x$ and a database is updated in a Poisson process with rate $\alpha \lambda$, i.e., $F^{(j)}(t)-F^{(j+1)}(t)=\left[(\alpha \lambda t)^{j} / j!\right] \mathrm{e}^{-\alpha \lambda t}(j=0,1,2, \cdots)$, $D(t)=1-\mathrm{e}^{-\beta \lambda t}$, and $\gamma=\beta \lambda$, where $0<\alpha<1$ and $\beta=1-\alpha$. In this case, the expected cost rate in (9.45) is rewritten as $$ \frac{C_{C}(K)}{\lambda}=\frac{c_{F}-c_{K}+(1+\beta) c_{0} \sum_{j=1}^{\infty} \alpha^{j} \int_{0}^{K} x \mathrm{~d} G^{(j)}(x)}{\sum_{j=0}^{\infty} \alpha^{j} G^{(j)}(K)}+c_{K}+\beta c_{R} $$ We find an optimum level $K^{*}$ that minimizes $C_{C}(K)$. Differentiating $C_{C}(K)$ with respect to $K$ and setting it equal to zero,$$ \sum_{j=0}^{\infty} \alpha^{j} \int_{0}^{K} G^{(j)}(x) \mathrm{d} x=\frac{c_{F}-c_{K}}{(1+\beta) c_{0}} $$ whose left-hand side is strictly increasing from 0 to $\infty$. Therefore, there exists an optimum $K^{*}\left(0<K^{*}<\infty\right)$ that satisfies (9.49), and the resulting cost rate is $$ \frac{C_{C}\left(K^{*}\right)}{\lambda}=(1+\beta) c_{0} K^{*}+c_{K}+\beta c_{R} $$

Example 9.3. Suppose that $G(x)=1-\mathrm{e}^{-\mu x}$, i.e., $G^{(j)}(x)=\sum_{i=j}^{\infty}\left[(\mu x)^{i} / i!\right] \mathrm{e}^{-\mu x}$ $(j=0,1,2, \cdots)$. Then, an optimum $K^{*}$ is given by a unique solution of the equation $$ K-\frac{\alpha}{\beta \mu}\left(1-\mathrm{e}^{-\beta \mu K}\right)=\frac{\beta}{1+\beta} \frac{c_{F}-c_{K}}{c_{0}} $$ Furthermore, an optimum $K^{*}$ is approximately $$ \widetilde{K}=\frac{1}{1+\beta} \frac{c_{F}-c_{K}}{c_{0}} $$ and $K^{*}<\widetilde{K}$ that approaches $\widetilde{K}$, as $\beta \rightarrow 0$. In the same values of Example $9.2, \mu K^{*}=6.09, \mu \widetilde{K}=23.53$, and $C_{C}\left(K^{*}\right) /\left(\lambda c_{0} / \mu\right)=48.21 \mathbf{I}$ Furthermore, when the full backup is done at time $T$ before the total files exceed $K$ or the database fails, and its full backup cost is $c_{F}$, the expected cost rate in (9.45) is easily extended as $$ \begin{gathered} c_{F}+\sum_{j=1}^{\infty} \int_{0}^{T} \bar{D}(t) \mathrm{d} F^{(j)}(t) \int_{0}^{K}\left[c_{K}+c_{0}(x)\right] \mathrm{d} G^{(j)}(x) \\ C_{C}(K, T)=\frac{+\sum_{j=0}^{\infty} \int_{0}^{T}\left[F^{(j)}(t)-F^{(j+1)}(t)\right] \mathrm{d} D(t) \int_{0}^{K}\left[c_{R}+c_{0}(x)\right] \mathrm{d} G^{(j)}(x)}{\sum_{j=0}^{\infty} G^{(j)}(K) \int_{0}^{T}\left[F^{(j)}(t)-F^{(j+1)}(t)\right] \bar{D}(t) \mathrm{d} t} \end{gathered} $$ When $c_{0}(x)=c_{0} x$ and $K=\infty$, this corresponds to the cumulative backup model in Section 9.2.# Other Related Stochastic Models The cumulative damage model is called the compound renewal process or the compound Poisson process in the theory of stochastic processes when shocks occur in a Poisson process. Examples to these processes of other practical fields are total claims on an insurance company, drifting of stones on river beds, model for Brownian motion, distribution of galaxies, number of customers or amount of materials in a queuing process or storage process $[11,238,239]$ and cancer epidemiology $[240,241]$. For example, we can apply the damage model to the simplest queuing process. A customer arrives at a counter with one server. If the server is free, the customer can be served immediately. Otherwise, if the server is busy with another customer, the customer has to wait for the service and forms a queue [61]. If the arrivals of customers are replaced with shocks and their total times of waiting and service with total damage, this corresponds to the cumulative damage model whose total damage decreases with time (Figure 10.1). In this process, we are mainly interested in the busy period that the server is working for arrival customers. We introduce briefly typical related models such as the downtime of repairable systems, shot noise, insurance, and stochastic duels. ### 10.1 Other Models ## (1) Downtime Distribution An operating unit is repaired when it fails, and after the completion of its repair, it begins to operate again. It is assumed that the failure time is a random variable $X_{j}$ having an identical distribution $F(t)$ with finite mean $1 / \lambda$ and the repair time is a random variable variable $W_{j}$ having an identical distribution $G(x)$ with finite mean $1 / \mu$, i.e., $F(t) \equiv \operatorname{Pr}\left\{X_{j} \leq t\right\}$ and $G(x) \equiv$ $\operatorname{Pr}\left\{W_{j} \leq x\right\}(j=1,2, \cdots)$. Then, the total downtime $D(t)$ during the interval $[0, t]$ is, replacing $t$ in (2.3) with $t-x$ (see (2) of Section 2.1.1 in [1]), Fig. 10.1. Process for the total waiting and service time $Z(t)$ of a queuing model $$ \operatorname{Pr}\{D(t) \leq x\}=\sum_{j=0}^{\infty} G^{(j)}(x)\left[F^{(j)}(t-x)-F^{(j+1)}(t-x)\right] $$ where $G^{(j)}(x)\left(F^{(j)}(t)\right)$ is the $j$-fold Stieltjes convolution of $G(x)(F(t))$ with itself. Thus, the distribution that the total downtime exceeds a specified level $K>0$ in time $t$ is $$ \operatorname{Pr}\{D(t)>K\}=\sum_{j=0}^{\infty}\left[G^{(j)}(K)-G^{(j+1)}(K)\right] F^{(j)}(t-K) \quad \text { for } t>K $$ The mean time that the total downtime first exceeds $K$ is $$ \int_{0}^{\infty} \operatorname{Pr}\{D(t) \leq K\} \mathrm{d} t=K+\frac{1}{\lambda}\left[\sum_{j=0}^{\infty} G^{(j)}(K)\right] $$ In particular, when $F(t)=1-\mathrm{e}^{-\lambda t}$ and $G(x)=1-\mathrm{e}^{-\mu x}$, from

Example 2.2 , $$ \begin{aligned} & \operatorname{Pr}\{D(t)>K\} \\ & =1-\mathrm{e}^{-\lambda(t-K)}\left[1+\sqrt{\lambda \mu(t-K)} \int_{0}^{K} \mathrm{e}^{-\mu u} u^{-1 / 2} I_{1}(2 \sqrt{\lambda \mu(t-K) u}) \mathrm{d} u\right] \\ & \text { for } t>K \end{aligned} $$$$ \int_{0}^{\infty} \operatorname{Pr}\{D(t) \leq K\} \mathrm{d} t=K+\frac{1}{\lambda}(1+\mu K) $$ Next, let $Y$ be the first time that one amount of downtime due to unit failures exceeds a fixed time $c>0$, that is called an allowed time. Then, the distribution of a random variable $Y$ and its mean time is, from (1.39) and (1.40) of [1], respectively, $$ \begin{aligned} \int_{0}^{\infty} \mathrm{e}^{-s t} \mathrm{~d} \operatorname{Pr}\{Y \leq t\} & =\frac{F^{*}(s) \mathrm{e}^{-s c} \bar{G}(c)}{1-F^{*}(s) \int_{0}^{c} \mathrm{e}^{-s t} \mathrm{~d} G(t)} \\ E\{Y\} & =\frac{1 / \lambda+\int_{0}^{c} \bar{G}(t) \mathrm{d} t}{\bar{G}(c)} \end{aligned} $$ where $\bar{G}(x) \equiv 1-G(x)$, and $F^{*}(s)$ is the Laplace-Stieltjes (LS) transform of $F(t)$. The mean time $E\{Y\}$ is easily given by solving the renewal equation $$ E\{Y\}=\int_{c}^{\infty}\left(\frac{1}{\lambda}+c\right) \mathrm{d} G(x)+\int_{0}^{c}\left(\frac{1}{\lambda}+x+E\{Y\}\right) \mathrm{d} G(x) $$ # (2) Shot Noise Suppose that a shot noise occurs at time interval $X_{j}$ and its amount is $W_{j}$. The total amount of shot noise is additive and falls into decay with time according to the rate function $h(\cdot)$. Then, the total amount of shot noise at time $t$ is $$ Z(t) \equiv \sum_{j=1}^{N(t)} W_{j} h\left(t-S_{j}\right) $$ where $S_{j} \equiv \sum_{i=1}^{j} X_{i}$ and $N(t) \equiv \max _{j}\left\{S_{j} \leq t\right\}$ [242, 243]. The stochastic behaviors of such shot noise were mathematically analyzed [244-248]. This can be also applied to riverflow [249], dams [250-253], and storage models [254256]. If $h(t)=\mathrm{e}^{-\alpha t}$, then this corresponds to the cumulative damage model with annealing in (3) of Section 2.5. Some failure distributions of reliability models were investigated by using the model of shot noise [126, 257]. ## (3) Insurance The cumulative process can be applied to insurance, replacing shock with claim and damage with claim size [258]. In this case, random variables $W_{j}$, $N(t)$, and $Z(t)$ defined in (2.1) represent a claim size, the number of claims up to time $t$, and the total claim amount up to time $t$, respectively. Furthermore, the risk reserve $R(t)$ at time $t$ is given by [259] (Figure 10.2) $$ R(t)=u+b t-\sum_{j=1}^{N(t)} W_{j}=u+b t-Z(t) $$ Fig. 10.2. Process for risk reserve $R(t)$ of an insurance model where $u$ is the initial risk reserve and $b>0$ is the premium rate. The probability of ultimate ruin is given by $$ \begin{aligned} \psi(u) & \equiv \operatorname{Pr}\{R(t)<0 \text { for some } t>0\} \\ & =\operatorname{Pr}\{Z(t)-b t>u \text { for some } t>0\} \end{aligned} $$ The properties of ruin probability $\psi(u)$ have been studied and summarized [258-261]. # 10.2 Stochastic Duels This section introduces a classical model of stochastic duels in which each firing delivers an amount of damage governed by a random variable and it requires a specified threshold level of damage to kill the opponent. The theory of stochastic duels was studied [74, 75, 262-266]. The optimum engagement problem of shooting strategy with incomplete damage information was considered [267]. The stochastic model in which each firing delivers the same amount of damage to the opponent and the kill requires a fixed number of hits was proposed, and the probability that a duelist wins against the opponent was obtained $[263,264]$. In addition, the weapon lifetimes that can be functions of time or number of rounds fired were considered [265], and the total damage resulting from firings was assumed to depend on both time and the number of rounds fired [75]. Recently, multiple damage functions to estimate theprobability that a single weapon detonation destroys a point target were discussed [266]. This section assumes that each firing delivers an amount of damage and it requires a prespecified threshold level of damage to the opponent, where each damage is additive. A duelist loses when the total damage exceeds a threshold level. This corresponds to the cumulative damage model by replacing rounds fired with shocks and threshold level with failure level. We consider five models of stochastic duels and derive analytically the probabilities of winning the duel with reference to Chapter 2. # (1) Standard Model Consider a stochastic duel with two contestants, say, A and B. Both contestants have unlimited ammunition and unlimited time to kill the opponent. Duelist A (B) begins simultaneously with a weapon and fires at time intervals according to an identical probability distribution $F_{A}(t)$ with finite mean $1 / \lambda_{A}\left(F_{B}(t)\right.$ with finite mean $\left.1 / \lambda_{B}\right)$, respectively, i.e., $F_{A}(t)$ and $F_{B}(t)$ are distribution functions of times between rounds fired. Each firing delivers an amount of damage with a general distribution $G_{A}(x)\left(G_{B}(x)\right)$, and requires a threshold level $K_{A}\left(K_{B}\right)$ of the total damage to kill the opponent. Duelist A (B) wins the duel if he or she delivers $K_{A}\left(K_{B}\right)$ to A (B), respectively. It is assumed that each damage is additive and does not deteriorate. Let $Z_{A}(t)\left(Z_{B}(t)\right)$ be the total damage up to time $t$ by $\mathrm{A}(\mathrm{B})$. Recalling that duelist A kills B when the total damage delivered by A exceeds a threshold level $K_{A}$, the probability that A kills B up to time $t$ is, from (2.9), $$ \Phi_{A}(t) \equiv \operatorname{Pr}\left\{Z_{A}(t)>K_{A}\right\}=\sum_{j=0}^{\infty}\left[G_{A}^{(j)}\left(K_{A}\right)-G_{A}^{(j+1)}\left(K_{A}\right)\right] F_{A}^{(j+1)}(t) $$ Taking the LS transform of (10.8), $$ \Phi_{A}^{*}(s) \equiv \int_{0}^{\infty} \mathrm{e}^{-s t} \mathrm{~d} \Phi_{A}(t)=\sum_{j=0}^{\infty}\left[G_{A}^{(j)}\left(K_{A}\right)-G_{A}^{(j+1)}\left(K_{A}\right)\right]\left[F_{A}^{*}(s)\right]^{j+1} $$ where $F_{A}^{*}(s)$ is the LS transform of $F_{A}(t)$. The mean time for A to kill B is $$ l_{A} \equiv \int_{0}^{\infty} t \mathrm{~d} \Phi_{A}(t)=\frac{1}{\lambda_{A}} \sum_{j=0}^{\infty} G_{A}^{(j)}\left(K_{A}\right) $$ In the same fashion, the probability $\Phi_{B}(t)$ that B kills A up to time $t$ can be obtained by exchanging from suffix $A$ into $B$. Therefore, the probability $P_{A}(t)$ that A wins the duel up to time $t$ is $$ P_{A}(t)=\int_{0}^{t}\left[1-\Phi_{B}(u)\right] \mathrm{d} \Phi_{A}(u) $$and conversely, the probability $P_{B}(t)$ that B wins the duel up to time $t$ is $$ P_{B}(t)=\int_{0}^{t}\left[1-\Phi_{A}(u)\right] \mathrm{d} \Phi_{B}(u) $$ # (2) Imperfect Hit It is assumed that A (B) hits the opponent B (A) with probability $p_{A}\left(p_{B}\right)$ and A (B) misses B (A) with $q_{A} \equiv 1-p_{A}\left(q_{B} \equiv 1-p_{B}\right)$, respectively. Then, the probability distribution of time for A to score one hit on B up to time $t$ is, from

Example 1.1, $$ F_{1}(t)=\left[1+q_{A} F_{A}(t)+q_{A} F_{A}(t) * q_{A} F_{A}(t)+\cdots\right] * p_{A} F_{A}(t) $$ Thus, replacing $F_{A}(t)$ in (10.8) with $F_{1}(t)$, we have $\Phi_{A}(t)$. The LS transform is $$ \Phi_{A}^{*}(s)=\sum_{j=0}^{\infty}\left[G_{A}^{(j)}\left(K_{A}\right)-G_{A}^{(j+1)}\left(K_{A}\right)\right]\left[\frac{p_{A} F_{A}^{*}(s)}{1-q_{A} F_{A}^{*}(s)}\right]^{j+1} $$ and the mean time for A to kill B is $$ l_{A}=\frac{1}{p_{A} \lambda_{A}} \sum_{j=0}^{\infty} G_{A}^{(j)}\left(K_{A}\right) $$ The other quantities can be obtained in a similar fashion. ## (3) Independent Damage It is assumed that the amount of damage is not additive and the amount is nullified immediately when it is less than $K_{A}\left(K_{B}\right)$. The other assumptions are the same as those of case (1) except that the total damage is additive. Then, the LS transform of the probability that A kills B up to time $t$ is, from Section 2.2, $$ \begin{aligned} \Phi_{A}^{*}(s) & =\sum_{j=0}^{\infty}\left\{\left[G_{A}\left(K_{A}\right)\right]^{j}-\left[G_{A}\left(K_{A}\right)\right]^{j+1}\right\}\left[F_{A}^{*}(s)\right]^{j+1} \\ & =\frac{\left[1-G_{A}\left(K_{A}\right)\right] F_{A}^{*}(s)}{1-G_{A}\left(K_{A}\right) F_{A}^{*}(s)} \end{aligned} $$ and the mean time for A to kill B is $$ l_{A}=\frac{1}{\lambda_{A}\left[1-G_{A}\left(K_{A}\right)\right]} $$# (4) Random Threshold Level It is assumed that a threshold level $K_{A}\left(K_{B}\right)$ is a random variable with a general distribution $L_{A}(x)\left(L_{B}(x)\right)$, respectively. Then, from (2) in Section 2.5, for case (1), $$ \Phi_{A}^{*}(s)=\sum_{j=0}^{\infty}\left[F_{A}^{*}(s)\right]^{j+1} \int_{0}^{\infty}\left[G_{A}^{(j)}(x)-G_{A}^{(j+1)}(x)\right] \mathrm{d} L_{A}(x) $$ for case (2), $$ \Phi_{A}^{*}(s)=\sum_{j=0}^{\infty}\left[\frac{p_{A} F_{A}^{*}(s)}{1-q_{A} F_{A}^{*}(s)}\right]^{j+1} \int_{0}^{\infty}\left[G_{A}^{(j)}(x)-G_{A}^{(j+1)}(x)\right] \mathrm{d} L_{A}(x) $$ and for case (3), $$ \Phi_{A}^{*}(s)=\sum_{j=0}^{\infty}\left[F_{A}^{*}(s)\right]^{j+1} \int_{0}^{\infty}\left\{\left[G_{A}(x)\right]^{j}-\left[G_{A}(x)\right]^{j+1}\right\} \mathrm{d} L_{A}(x) $$ The other quantities can be obtained in a similar fashion. ## (5) Lifetimes of Weapons Consider the lifetimes of A's (B's) weapon distributed with $R_{A}(t)\left(R_{B}(t)\right)$, respectively. It is assumed that the failed weapon of A (B) remains in the duel until A (B) is killed or B's (A's) weapon fails. Then, the probability that A wins in the duel up to time $t$ is $$ P_{A}(t)=\int_{0}^{t}\left[1-R_{A}(u)\right]\left\{1-\int_{0}^{u}\left[1-R_{B}(v)\right] \mathrm{d} \Phi_{B}(v)\right\} \mathrm{d} \Phi_{A}(u) $$ and the tie probability is $$ P_{A B}(t)=\int_{0}^{t}\left[1-\Phi_{A}(u)\right] \mathrm{d} R_{A}(u) \int_{0}^{t}\left[1-\Phi_{B}(u)\right] \mathrm{d} R_{B}(u) $$ that represents the probability that both A and B cannot kill the opponent because of failures of the weapons up to time $t$. Note that $P_{A}(\infty)+P_{B}(\infty)+$ $P_{A B}(\infty)=1$.

Example 10.2. Suppose in case (4) that all random variables are exponential, i.e., $F(t)=1-\mathrm{e}^{-\lambda t}, G(x)=1-\mathrm{e}^{-\mu x}$, and $L(x)=1-\mathrm{e}^{-\alpha x}$, where the suffixes of the three parameters are omitted. Then, from (10.18), $$ \Phi_{A}^{*}(s)=\frac{\alpha \lambda p}{(\alpha+\mu) s+\alpha \lambda p} $$ By inversion, $$ \Phi_{A}(t)=1-\mathrm{e}^{-\theta_{A} t} $$ where $\theta_{A} \equiv \alpha \lambda p /(\alpha+\mu)$. For duelist B, $$ \Phi_{B}(t)=1-\mathrm{e}^{-\theta_{B} t} $$ Thus, from (10.11), $$ \begin{aligned} & P_{A}(t)=\frac{\theta_{A}}{\theta_{A}+\theta_{B}}\left[1-\mathrm{e}^{-\left(\theta_{A}+\theta_{B}\right) t}\right] \\ & P_{B}(t)=\frac{\theta_{B}}{\theta_{A}+\theta_{B}}\left[1-\mathrm{e}^{-\left(\theta_{A}+\theta_{B}\right) t}\right] \end{aligned} $$ Furthermore, when the lifetimes of the weapons are assumed to be $R_{A}(t)=$ $1-\mathrm{e}^{-\gamma_{A} t}$ and $R_{B}(t)=1-\mathrm{e}^{-\gamma_{B}(t)}$, from case (5), $$ \begin{aligned} P_{A}(t)= & \frac{\theta_{A}}{\gamma_{B}+\theta_{B}}\left\{\frac{\gamma_{B}}{\gamma_{A}+\theta_{A}}\left[1-\mathrm{e}^{-\left(\gamma_{A}+\theta_{A}\right) t}\right]\right. \\ & \left.+\frac{\theta_{B}}{\gamma_{A}+\theta_{A}+\gamma_{B}+\theta_{B}}\left[1-\mathrm{e}^{-\left(\gamma_{A}+\theta_{A}+\gamma_{B}+\theta_{B}\right) t}\right]\right\} \\ P_{B}(t)= & \frac{\theta_{B}}{\gamma_{A}+\theta_{A}}\left\{\frac{\gamma_{A}}{\gamma_{B}+\theta_{B}}\left[1-\mathrm{e}^{-\left(\gamma_{B}+\theta_{B}\right) t}\right]\right. \\ & \left.+\frac{\theta_{A}}{\gamma_{A}+\theta_{A}+\gamma_{B}+\theta_{B}}\left[1-\mathrm{e}^{-\left(\gamma_{A}+\theta_{A}+\gamma_{B}+\theta_{B}\right) t}\right]\right\} \\ P_{A B}(t)= & \frac{\gamma_{A}}{\gamma_{A}+\theta_{A}} \frac{\gamma_{B}}{\gamma_{B}+\theta_{B}}\left[1-\mathrm{e}^{-\left(\gamma_{A}+\theta_{A}\right) t}\right]\left[1-\mathrm{e}^{-\left(\gamma_{B}+\theta_{B}\right) t}\right] \end{aligned} $$ where it is clearly seen that $P_{A}(\infty)+P_{B}(\infty)+P_{A B}(\infty)=1$.# References 1. Example 2.1 An electronics company purchases a component from two vendors, A and B. A supplies $30 \%$ and B supplies $70 \%$ of the total number of the components to this company. On average, the percentage of defective components supplied by A and B are known to be $3 \%$ and $4 \%$, respectively. What is the probability that a randomly selected component is defective? If a selected component is defective, what is the probability that it was supplied by vendor A or vendor B? # Solution: (i) The Bayes' formula indicates, $$ \begin{aligned} & \mathrm{P}(\text { defective })=P(\text { defective and from } A)+P(\text { defective and from } B) \\ & \quad=P(\text { from } A) P(\text { defective from } A)+P(\text { from } B) P(\text { defective } \mid \text { from } B) \\ & \quad=(0.3)(0.03)+(0.7)(0.04)=0.037 \end{aligned} $$ (ii) If the selected component is defective, it follows that, $$ \begin{aligned} & P(\text { from } A \mid \text { defective })=\frac{P(\text { from } A, \text { Defective })}{P(\text { defective })}=\frac{(0.3)(0.03)}{0.037}=0.243, \text { and } \\ & P(\text { from } B \mid \text { defective })=\frac{P(\text { from } B, \text { Defective })}{P(\text { defective })}=\frac{(0.7)(0.04)}{0.037}=0.757 \end{aligned} $$

Example 2.3 Suppose that 10 identical lots numbered from 0 to 9 are contained in a black box. We continue to draw the lots one by one until we draw the number 7 lot. If we return the lot into the box every time we draw one, what is the probability of finishing this game on the fourth draw? And what is the probability if we do not return the drawn lots? ## Solution: (i) If we return, the probability to select the number 7 lot at each draw is 0.1 . Thus, we get: $$ P(X=4)=(1-p)^{4-1} p=(0.9)^{3}(0.1)=0.0729 $$ (ii) If we do not return, the probability to select the number 7 lot changes at each draw: $$ \begin{array}{ll} P(\text { do not select } 7 \text { at } 1 \text { st draw })=\frac{9}{10} & P(\text { do not select } 7 \text { at } 2 \text { nd draw })=\frac{8}{9} \\ P(\text { do not select } 7 \text { at } 3 \text { rd draw })=\frac{7}{8} & P(\text { select } 7 \text { at } 4 \text { th draw })=\frac{1}{7} \end{array} $$ It follows that, $$ P(X=4)=\left\{\left(\frac{9}{10}\right)\left(\frac{8}{9}\right)\left(\frac{7}{8}\right)\right\}\left(\frac{1}{7}\right)=\frac{1}{10} $$ # Binomial Distribution A discrete random variable $X$ is said to have the binomial distribution when its probability density function is given by $$ f(x)= \begin{cases}n C\_{x} p^{x}(1-p)^{n-x} & x=0,1,2, \ldots, n, \& 0 \leq p \leq 1 \\ 0 & \text { otherwise }\end{cases} $$ Fig.2.2 (c) shows the pdf of a binomial distribution. It applies to the cases where we repeat the experiment $n$ times and random variable $X$ represents the number of successes in the $n$ experiments, given $p$ and $1-p$ as the probability of success and failure at each trial, respectively. That formula is derived from the equation that, $$ (a+b)^{n}=\sum*{x=0}^{n} C*{x} a^{x} b^{n-x} $$ If we replace $a$ and $b$ by $p$ and $1-p$, respectively, we would have $$ [p+(1-p)]^{n}=1=\sum*{x=0}^{n} C*{x} p^{x}(1-p)^{n-x} $$ Figure 2.2 Pdfs of some discrete probability distributionsThe binomial distribution is often denoted by $b(n, p)$, where the two parameters $n$ and $p$ represent the number of trials and the probability of success at one trial, respectively. The binomial distribution becomes an excellent mathematical model for experiments where the trials are repeated many times with identical conditions at each trial.

Example 2.4 Suppose that we toss a fair die seven times. Let $X$ be the number of ' 6 's appeared in this experiment. Then, $X$ is a binomial random variable whose density function is given by $$ P(X=x)= \begin{cases}c*{x} C*{x}\left(\frac{1}{6}\right)^{x}\left(\frac{5}{6}\right)^{7-x} & x=0,1,2,3, \ldots, 7 \\ 0 & \text { otherwise }\end{cases} $$ # Poisson Distribution We say that a random variable $X$ has the Poisson distribution with parameter $\lambda(\lambda>0)$ if its density function is given by $$ P(X=x)=\frac{\lambda^{x} e^{-\lambda}}{x!} \quad x=0,1,2,3, \ldots $$ Fig.2.2 (d) shows the pdf of a Poisson distribution. Poisson distribution is widely used to express the number of events occurring in a time period. Specifically, it is known that the Poisson distribution provides a good mathematical model for the pattern of the occurrence of failures in many systems and components. It can be also used as an approximation to the binomial distribution when the binomial parameter $n$ is large.

Example 2.6 Let $X_{1}$ and $X_{2}$ be two independent Poisson random variables with parameters $\lambda_{1}$ and $\lambda_{2}$, respectively. What is the distribution of $X_{1}+X_{2}$ ? ## Solution: $$ \begin{aligned} & P\left(X*{1}+X*{2}=n\right)=\sum*{k=0}^{n} P\left(X*{1}=k, X*{2}=n-k\right)=\sum*{k=0}^{n}\left[\frac{\lambda_{1}^{k} e^{-\lambda_{1}}}{k!}\right]\left[\frac{\lambda_{2}^{n-k} e^{-\lambda_{2}}}{n-k!}\right] \\ & \quad=\frac{e^{-\left(\lambda*{1}+\lambda*{2}\right)}}{n!} \sum*{k=0}^{n} \frac{n!}{k!(n-k)!} \lambda*{1}^{k} \lambda*{2}^{n-k}=\frac{e^{-\left(\lambda*{1}+\lambda*{2}\right)}}{n!}\left(\lambda*{1}+\lambda\_{2}\right)^{n} \end{aligned} $$ Therefore, $X_{1}+X_{2}$ has the Poisson distribution with the parameter $\lambda_{1}+\lambda_{2}$.# 2.3.2 Continuous Distributions Continuous distribution functions, including the Weibull distribution, are very important to describing the reliability of components over the life of a system or product. ## Continuous Uniform Distribution The uniform distribution can also be defined over a range $(a, b)$ instead of a set of points $\left\{x_{1}\right.$, $\left.x_{2}, x_{3}, \ldots, x_{n}\right\}$. The one defined over a range is called a continuous uniform distribution. The density function of a continuous uniformly distributed random variable X is given by $$ f(x)= \begin{cases}\frac{1}{b-a} & \text { if } a \leq x \leq b \& a<b \\ 0 & \text { otherwise }\end{cases} $$

Example 2.7 Suppose that a random variable $X$ is uniformly distributed between 0 and 2. What is the probability that $X$ is less than or equal to 1.5 ? Solution: Since the density function of $X$ is given by $$ f(x)=1 / 2 x \in[0,2] $$ the probability would be calculated as: $$ P(X \leq 1.5)=\int\_{0}^{1.5} \frac{1}{2} d x=0.75 $$ ## Normal Distribution We say that a random variable $X$ has normal (or Gaussian) distribution with parameters $\mu$ and $\sigma^{2}$ when the density function of $X$ is given by $$ f(x)=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2 \pi} \sigma} \exp \left[-\frac{1}{2}\left(\frac{x-\mu}{\sigma}\right)^{2}\right] \quad-\infty<x<\infty $$ The normal distribution is often denoted by $N\left(\mu, \sigma^{2}\right)$, where these two parameters represent the mean and variance of $X$, respectively. Fig. 2.3(a) shows the two density functions of normal distribution when $\mu=2, \sigma=1$ and $\mu=2, \sigma=2$. As shown in Figure 2.3a, the normal distribution is symmetric around the mean, and the standard deviation indicates the level of deviation from the mean. Due to the complexity of normal density function, it is not possible to derive a closed form expression for cdf by integration. However, if we define another random variable $Z$ as $$ Z=\frac{X-\mu}{\sigma} $$ Then, since $X=Z \sigma+\mu$, the density function of $Z$ will be obtained as $$ f(z)=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2 \pi}} \exp \left[\frac{-(z \mathrm{~s}+\mu-\mu)^{2}}{2 \sigma^{2}}\right]=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2 \pi}} \exp \left[\frac{-z^{2}}{2}\right] \quad-\infty<z<\infty $$ Therefore, we know that $Z$ has normal distribution with a mean of 0 and variance 1 (which is called the Standard Normal Distribution). We often denote the distribution function of the standard normal distribution by $\Phi($.$) . We can calculate the probability using the Normal$ Table for the standard normal distribution.

Example 2.8 Suppose that $X$ is a normal random variable with a mean $\mu$ and a variance $\sigma^{2}$. What is the probability that $X$ is less than or equal to $x$ ? Solution: Let $z=\frac{x-\mu}{\sigma}$. Then, we have, $$ P(X \leq x)=P\left(\frac{X-\mu}{\sigma} \leq \frac{x-\mu}{\sigma}\right)=P\left(Z \leq \frac{x-\mu}{\sigma}\right)=\Phi\left(\frac{x-\mu}{\sigma}\right) $$ The importance of the normal distribution is that many real-life phenomena can be approximated by the normal distribution, as the number of samples increases. We will dwell on this issue later in this section. Finally, it must be mentioned that the normally distributed random variables are defined over a range from $-\infty$ to $\infty$. Since we generally deal with positive values in probability assessment, this fact restricts the applicability of the normal distribution. However, we can control the distribution of the normal random variables apart from 0 when we have a relatively small variance. # Exponential Distribution We say that a random variable $X$ has an exponential distribution with parameter $\lambda$ if its density function is given by $$ f(x)= \begin{cases}\lambda \exp (-\lambda x) & \text { if } x \geq 0 \\ 0 & \text { if } x<0\end{cases} $$ The exponential distribution is often denoted by $\exp (\lambda)$. The parameter implies the rate of the occurrence in the event that the random variable $X$ represents. Fig. 2.3(b) shows the density functions of the exponential distribution when $\lambda=1$ and $\lambda=2$. The exponential distribution is widely applied in the analysis of the life of systems. Figure 2.3 Pdfs of Some Continuous Probability DistributionsExample 2.9 Suppose that a random variable $X$ represents the life of a component, and it is exponentially distributed with parameter $\lambda$. What is the probability that this component will survive at least $s$ hours more, given that it has already survived $t$ hours so far? Solution: Since $t+s>t$, we have, $$ P(X>t+s \mid X>t)=\frac{P(X>t+s)}{P(X>t)} $$ For any $t(t \geq 0)$, we have, $$ P(X>t)=1-P(X \leq t)=1-\int\_{0}^{t} \lambda e^{-\lambda x} d x=1-\left(1-e^{-\lambda t}\right)=e^{-\lambda t} $$ Thus, it follows that, $$ P(X>t+s \mid X>t)=\frac{e^{-\lambda(t+s)}}{e^{-\lambda t}}=e^{-\lambda s}=P(X>s) $$ This equation shows that the probability that the component survives at least $s$ additional hours, given that it has already survived $t$ hours, is the same as the probability that it survives at least s hours. The distribution of the remaining life of the component is independent of the time used, so it is 'memoryless'. Therefore, a random variable with this property is said to have a memoryless property. It was proven that the exponential distribution is the only distribution with this property (Ross 1993).

Example 2.10 Suppose that $X$ and $Y$ are independent and identically distributed exponential random variables with parameter. Then, what is the distribution of the sum of $X$ and $Y$ ? Solution: Let $Z$ be the sum of $X$ and $Y$. Then, for any positive real value $z$, we have, $$ \begin{aligned} & P(Z \leq z)=P(X+Y \leq z)=\int*{0}^{z} \int*{0}^{z-x} \lambda e^{-\lambda x} \lambda e^{-\lambda y} d x d y \\ & \quad=\int*{0}^{z} \lambda^{2} e^{-\lambda x}\left(\int*{0}^{z-x} e^{-\lambda y} d y\right) d x=\int\_{0}^{z} \lambda e^{-\lambda x}\left(1-e^{-\lambda(z-x)}\right) d x=1-(1+\lambda z) e^{-\lambda z} \end{aligned} $$ Thus, the density function of $Z=X+Y$ would be, $$ f(x)=\frac{d F(z)}{d z}=\lambda^{2} z e^{-\lambda z} $$ # Gamma Distribution We say that a random variable $X$ has a gamma distribution with parameters $\lambda$ and $k$ if its density function is given by $$ f(x)=\frac{\lambda(\lambda x)^{k-1} e^{-\lambda x}}{\Gamma(k)} x \geq 0 $$ where is the scale parameter, $k$ is the shape parameter, and $\Gamma(k)$ is the gamma function defined as $$ \Gamma(k)=\int\_{0}^{\infty} x^{k-1} e^{-x} d x $$ Fig. 2.3(c) shows the density functions of gamma distribution with different values of $k$. In the case where $k$ is an integer greater than 1 , $$ \Gamma(k)=(k-1)! $$ The gamma distribution is widely applied to model the duration of time needed to finish an activity. From the example $2-10$, we derived the density function of the sum of two identically distributed exponential random variables as $$ f(k)=\lambda^{2} x e^{-\lambda x} $$ This is the same as the density function of a random variable that has the gamma distribution with the parameters $\lambda$ and 2 . This result can be generalized by induction as that if $X_{1}, X_{2}$, $\ldots, X_{n}$ are independent and identically distributed exponential random variables with parameter $\lambda$, then $X_{1}+X_{2}+X_{3}+\ldots+X_{n}$ has a gamma distribution with parameters $\lambda$ and $n$. # Weibull Distribution We say that a random variable X has a Weibull distribution with a scale parameter $\mu$, and a shape parameter $\beta$, if its density function is given by $$ f(x)=\left\{\frac{\beta}{\mu} \left\|\frac{x}{\mu}\right\|^{\beta-1} \exp \left[-\left(\frac{x}{\mu}\right)^{\beta}\right]\right\} \quad x \geq 0 $$ If the Weibull random variable X shifts left or right from 0 , we can redefine the density function of the Weibull distribution with one more parameter $v$, the location parameter $(-\infty<v<\infty)$ as follows. $$ f(x)=\left\{\frac{\beta}{\mu} \left\|\frac{x-v}{\mu}\right\|^{\beta-1} \exp \left[-\left(\frac{x-v}{\mu}\right)^{\beta}\right]\right\} \quad x \geq v $$ The location parameter does not affect the variance. This modification is often referred to as the Three Parameter (3-P) Weibull Distribution or Modified Weibull Distribution. The cdf of the 3-P Weibull distribution is derived as $$ F(x)= \begin{cases}0 & \text { if } x<v \\ 1-\exp \left[-\left(\frac{x-v}{\mu}\right)^{\beta}\right] & \text { if } x \geq v\end{cases} $$ Fig. 2.3(d) shows some density functions of the Weibull distribution when $v=0$. As shown by the Figure, we can generate many different shapes by manipulating the values of the two parameters $\mu$ and $\beta$. Thus, the Weibull distribution provides us with convenience to fit experimental data. It can be shown easily when $\mu=\frac{1}{\lambda}, \beta=1$, and $v=0$, the density function would be $f(x)=\lambda e^{-\lambda x}$. This is the same as the density function of the exponential distribution. Therefore, we can say that the exponential distribution is a special case of the Weibull distribution. The reader should note that different authors use various notations for the parameters in the Weibull distribution.

Since simulation models generally include many events with different patterns of probability distribution other than uniform distribution, we need to know how to convert uniformly distributed random numbers into random variates in a general distribution. In order to do this, we need to design a process that consistently samples values in the random variable of interest that correspond to the uniform random numbers $[0,1]$ generated. For example, let's consider a discrete random variable $X$ whose density function is given by $$ \begin{array}{ll} P(X=1)=0.2, & P(X=2)=0.4, \quad P(X=3)=0.2 \\ P(X=4)=0.1, & P(X=5)=0.1 \end{array} $$ If the generated uniform random number value $U$ is 0.1534 , what is the corresponding random variate with this distribution? Since $P(X=1), P(X=2)$ and $P(X=3)$ are greater than $0.1534,1,2$ and 3 can be the candidate comparable to this random number. One easy approach to consistently match the value for a random number is to use the cumulative probability instead of the density function. In this context, the conversion mechanism can be designed as $$ X=\left\{\begin{array}{ll} 1 & \text { if } 0.0 \leq U<0.2 \\ 2 & \text { if } 0.2 \leq U<0.6 \\ 3 & \text { if } 0.6 \leq U<0.8 \\ 4 & \text { if } 0.8 \leq U<0.9 \\ 5 & \text { if } 0.9 \leq U<1.0 \end{array}\right. $$ There is no law in the order of the arrangement, as long as we keep the order consistent. This process can be applied to generate random variates with many other distributions. Fig. 2.7 summarizes the concept of this conversion process. Finally, we must consider uncertainty in the separate treatment of failure mechanisms in order to derive effective corrective action in design. # 3.4 System Reliability Prediction and System Models A system reliability model can be constructed from its components. For most engineering systems, a series model applies. In this case, the failure of a single component in the series will cause the system to fail. Some systems may be comprised of parallel arrangements of components. In this case, one of the components in the parallel arrangement may fail, without causing system failure. This can be a way of increasing reliability by adding redundancy of a critical component. In any case, we can generally construct a block diagram describing the interaction between the components of the design. ### 3.4.1 Series and Parallel Systems First, lets consider the simple series system. As we see Figure 3.7 the arrangement of components will result in system failure if a single component fails. We can describe the reliability of the series system at time $t$, as the probability of the event that each component will operate successfully to time $t$. Figure 3.7 A simple series system. The series system model describes many types of systems.Hence: $$ R*{s}(t)=\operatorname{Pr}\left(E*{1}\right) \cap \operatorname{Pr}\left(E*{2}\right) \cap \operatorname{Pr}\left(E*{3}\right) \cap \ldots \ldots \cap \operatorname{Pr}\left(E\_{n}\right) $$ where $R_{s}(t)$ is the system reliability and $E_{i}$ is the event of successful operation of component $i$ to time $t$. We quickly see that, for independent events: $$ R*{s}(t)=\operatorname{Pr}\left(E*{1}\right) \bullet \operatorname{Pr}\left(E*{2}\right) \bullet \operatorname{Pr}\left(E*{3}\right) \bullet \ldots . . \bullet \operatorname{Pr}\left(E\_{n}\right) $$ And for a total of $n$ components: $$ R*{s}(t)=\prod*{i=1}^{n} R\_{n}(t) $$ $R_{n}(t)$ is the reliability at time $t$, as described by the individual component reliabilities. If we apply the Exponential distribution to describe the failure distribution of the $n$ components, the system failure rate, $\lambda_{s}$, is the sum of the component failure rates and the system Mean Time Between Failures or MTBF is simply: $$ \begin{aligned} & \lambda*{s}=\sum*{i=1}^{n} \lambda*{n} \\ & \text { MTBF }=\frac{1}{\lambda*{s}} \end{aligned} $$ Applying the Exponential distribution to the series systems greatly simplifies the calculation, but it should be applied only as appropriate. Its application often leads to MTBF as a descriptor of system reliability. However, in complex systems there may be no reason to expect repeated failure patterns of the same components, particularly when overstress failures dominate. MTBF is therefore not a system property as is weight or size. As stated, the series model description fits most types of systems. The model tells us that individual component reliability must be very high to achieve reasonable probabilities of successful system operation.

Safety factors have been widely applied in many industries. The concept works when we have significant experience with the materials commonly used for components in our systems and when we can anticipate the worst case loading conditions. Common steel alloys for example are well characterized materials and their use includes a wide variety of application. The Safety Factor may be defined as the ratio of available component strength to the demanded load: $$ S F=\frac{S_{\text {Available }}}{L_{\text {Demand }}} $$ In general, we would anticipate the worst case conditions and compare our safety factor to our desirable design margin. An acceptable margin or value for SF is of course based upon experience with the product and components under consideration. During component design, a fixed level of the safety factor is used to reduce the allowable stress developed in a component, which effectively increases the component strength. The safety factor, SF , is then applied as: $$ \sigma_{\text {Allowable }}=\frac{\sigma}{S F} $$ where $\sigma$ is the material strength, such as yield strength for a metal component or ultimate strength for a ceramic material, and $\sigma_{\text {Allowable }}$ is the allowable stress that can developed in the component under the demanded load. A typical safety factor used for a steel shaft in an industrial electric motor design, for example, may be 1.5 or 2 . As Smith (1976) indicated, anticipating the maximum load and applying a fixed SF based upon experience with the materials being considered, generally lead to conservative designs. However, when there is little experience with the materials, such as in the case of introducing new technology, the safety factor may not assure a good design. The same concept applies tothe introduction of new manufacturing methods. New technologies require adequate characterization of the uncertainties in the strength of components and variations in the strength of the materials. A safety factor contains no information about the actual risk or probability of failure. Two components with the same safety factor could have very different reliabilities. As an example, the same steel part could be supplied by two different manufacturers with different heat treatment operations. As equation 4.16 would predict, the manufacturer with stricter process control and therefore less variation in the strength, would produce a more reliable component. Derating in electronic components is equivalent to the safety factor in mechanical design. In this case, a selected component is used below its rated load level by controlling the design of the system, as to effect the loads on the components, or by selecting components with higher than the required rating. Hence, a parameter we use to select components for a design can be derated as follows: $$ P_{\text {Allowable }}=D R F \bullet P_{\text {Rated }} $$ where $P_{\text {Allowable }}$ is a specific component parameter of interest, such as operating voltage, $D R F$ is derating factor and $P_{\text {Rated }}$ is the supplied value of the parameter. Capacitors for example may be derated for applied voltage by a factor of 0.8 for an industrial application or by as much as 0.5 for a spacecraft application. Semiconductors may be constrained to operate at junction temperature of $80^{\circ} \mathrm{C}$ or $100^{\circ} \mathrm{C}$, when they are rated to operate at $125^{\circ} \mathrm{C}$. Derating may reduce the potential for overstress and may also increase life, if the wear out mechanisms of the device are sensitive to the derated parameters. Once again, $D R F$ values are generally selected by experience with components in a specific application. However, as technologies change, rules to select a $D R F$ for a component may no longer be applicable. Derating may be over conservative or may not provide the anticipated increase in design margin even though they will significantly affect the system design. As an example, temperature reduction through active cooling systems to control junction temperature, can impart significant costs. In general, $D R F$ s effectively suffer from the same problems as the safety factor approach to mechanical design. # 4.2.5 Multiple Load Reliability Equations 4.10 and 4.11 were derived for a single load application. In the event we have multiple load applications, we must modify our integral as follows: $$ R=\int_{0}^{\infty} f_{L}(S)\left[\int_{0}^{2} f_{L}(L) d L\right]^{n} d S $$ where $n$ represents the number of loading applications on the component. Equation 4.18 cannot be solved in closed form, but can be integrated using numerical methods, given functions for the available strength $p d f$ and demanded load $p d f$. Lets reconsider our case of a normally distributed demanded load and a normally distributed available strength. We can plot the solution of equation 4.18, as shown in Figure 4.14. Here the probability of failure per load application is plotted against the Safety Margin. Each contour represents a line of constant Loading Roughness. Figure 4. 14 is developed considering that values of $n$ are large. Similar plots can be seen in Carter (1986) and O'Connor (1991). The reliability for $n$ load applications is then: $$ R=\left(1-p_{f}\right)^{n} $$ Equation 4.20 may be used to calculate reliability, given a value, $p_{f}$, extracted from Figure 4.14. Figure 4.14 Safety Margin versus Probability of Failure per Load Application at different values of Loading Roughness. The demanded load and variable strength pdfs were taken as normally distributed # 4.2.6 A Method Design for Intrinsic Reliability Against Overstress If we examine our plot of probability of failure per load application versus the safety margin. We can see that there is a critical value, $S M_{C}$, at the point our loading roughness curve approaches a vertical asymptote. The region to the right of this value, defines the region of intrinsic reliability, where the probability of failure per load application, $p_{f}$, approaches zero. This is summarized in Figure 4.15. We can also see that immediately to the left of $S M_{C}$, that small changes in the Safety Margin result in large changes in the probability of failure, $p_{f}$. This region is not very practical for design purposes. However, if we can determine $S M_{C}$, at a given value of $L R$, we can design a component to be intrinsically reliable for multiple load applications, against overstress failure. Design curves can be generated for various distributions, as shown in Carter (1986) and O'Connor (1991). This concept can be illustrated clearly, using an example.

The data are taken from a large data set of more than 1800 samples. (Fuchs and Stevens 1980) # 5.4 Fatigue Models Fatigue modeling of components is essential to designing reliable components. There are three different approaches to fatigue modeling. These include the S-N Diagram, the MansonCoffin Equation and Linear Elastic Fracture Mechanics. We will review the basic elements of each of these in turn. ### 5.4.1 S-N Diagrams for Materials Let's begin our discussion of fatigue models with the simplest approach. The S-N diagram is easiest to understand and manipulate and is widely used for design purposes. The S-N diagram is created by plotting the log of cycles to failure versus the log of the stress amplitude created by the fluctuating load. Let's initially consider a rotating bending test on small materials characterization samples of low alloy steel with polished surfaces. If we test several conditions recording the cycles to failure, we can construct a plot of mean cycles to failure versus applied stress amplitude. We will observe the characteristics shown in Figure 5.9. Figure 5.9 S-N Curve that would be typical of a low alloy steel. On the S-N diagram, we will define the stress amplitude for $N_{f}$ cycles to failure. We will also adopt $S$ for stress. We then define the fatigue strength, $S_{f}$ as the alternating stress causing failure at $N_{f}$ cycles and $S_{e}$ as the notation for the endurance limit. These are common notations used in design of mechanical components when using the S-N diagram. The S-N curve can be characterized by three distinct regions. From 1 cycle to approximately $10^{3}$ cycles is the region of low cycle fatigue in which the applied stress amplitude results in relatively short life. A break point or change in slope will occur at about $10^{3}$ cycles. From this point, until approximately $10^{6}$ cycles, we have a region of high cycle fatigue in which the applied stress amplitude produces longer, but limited life. Beyond $10^{6}$ cycles, we can see that the applied stress amplitude approaches a constant value and does not limit the life of the material. This point, at which we transition to infinite life, is known as the endurance limit, $S_{e}$. The S-N curve approach to modeling fatigue behavior in design of structural components is usually applied to the high cycle regime. We should also note that not all materials will have an endurance limit. Most non-ferrous materials will not have a distinct endurance limit. However, we can see that it may be desirable to design a steel structural component with infinite life, provided we can tolerate the extra weight and cost and appropriately measure the endurance limit. The straight line behavior from $10^{3}$ to $10^{6}$ cycles on the S-N Diagram is often represented by the following simple power law relationship: $$ S*{f}=C N*{f}^{b} $$ where, C and b are materials properties and $N_{f}$ is the number of cycles to failure. The two constants can be extracted from our S-N Diagram. As we can imagine, the fatigue life at $10^{0}$ cycles will closely correlate to the ultimate strength of the material. In fact, as previously discussed, $\frac{1}{2}$ cycle is a single stress reversal. This is approximately the condition of a tensile test. So, we can expect that the ultimate strength, $\sigma_{u}$, to approximate the fatigue strength at a single stress reversal.The break point at $10^{3}$ cycles is often taken as a fraction of the ultimate strength for estimating the high cycle $\mathrm{S}-\mathrm{N}$ curve for a small rotating bending test specimen. (Plotting techniques for fitting data to a distribution are described in greater detail in Chapter 12.)# 5.4.8 Fatigue Crack Propagation As we have discussed, a fatigue crack will grow in a stable manner until it reaches a critical length. This is stage II fatigue crack growth. Then, the remaining supporting section will fail by fracture. We can estimate this critical crack size, as we have shown in the previous example problem. Let's now turn our attention to estimating the number of cycles a crack will take to grow from crack initiation to fracture over the course of stage II stable crack growth. Under fluctuating loads, we can estimate the stress range which a component will see in service or test. We can expect that the stress intensity factor will have a corresponding range and that equation 5.26 can be modified to reflect this as follows: $$ \Delta K_{I}=a \bullet \Delta \sigma \sqrt{\pi a} $$ where $\Delta \sigma$ is the stress range under fatigue conditions and $\Delta K_{I}$ is the corresponding stress intensity range. A plot of the log of stress intensity range versus the log of the rate of crack growth per cycle, $\frac{d a}{d N}$, will yield a sigmoidal curve similar to the plot in Figure 5.19. The linear region of this curve will fit the power law model known as the Paris Equation (Paris and Erdogan 1963). $$ \frac{d a}{d N}=A\left(\Delta K_{I}\right)^{n} $$ where $A$ and $n$ are constants that are material properties. $n$ is the slope of the linear region of the sigmoidal crack growth curve. Another important feature of the crack growth curve is the limiting or threshold value of the stress intensity range, $\Delta K_{I t h}$. The crack will not propagate at stress intensities below this level. Figure 5.19 Crack growth rate plotted against stress intensity. This type of plot is commonly called da/dN curve.We should recall that fatigue testing used to characterize the stress-life or $S-N$ curve for materials is generally performed using fully reversed loading, where the stress ratio $\mathrm{R}=-1$. However, crack growth experiments are conducted under different conditions. Generally, materials tests are conducted on compact specimens similar to our component in Figure 5.15, under conditions of $R=0$. This is due to the fact that the crack will not propagate under compressive loads. $K_{j}$ has no real physical meaning for $\sigma<0$. We can expect for components, that the $\frac{d a}{d N}$, curve will shift to the left for $R \geq 0$. In order to apply the Paris Equation (equation 5.32), we must integrate to find the value of the number of cycles to failure. We integrate from the initial suspected crack size to the critical crack size: $$ N_{f}=A \int_{a_{i}}^{a_{f}} \frac{d a}{(\Delta K)^{n}} $$

Example 7.1 Lets consider Zn . What is the electrode potential of the half reaction for Zn at $60^{\circ} \mathrm{C}$ in a solution containing 2 g of $\mathrm{Zn}^{+2}$ ions per liter of electrolyte? | The atomic weight of Zn is 65.37 grams per mole. Then $C_{Z n}=(2 \mathrm{~g} / l) /(65.37 \mathrm{~g} / \mathrm{mole})=0.0306 \mathrm{M}$. The temperature is $273+60=333 \mathrm{~K}$. From the Galvanic series we see that $E^{\circ}=-0.76 \mathrm{~V}$. The valence for Zn is 2 . Then from the Nernst equation: $$ E_{Z n}=-0.76+(0.0257 / 2)(333 / 298) \ln (0.0306)=-0.81 \mathrm{~V} $$ Here we see the effect on the half cell reaction of a dilute solution of the corroding ion, relative to the hydrogen electrode, at $60^{\circ} \mathrm{C}$. Let us now recall the concept of free energy. The free energy is a thermodynamic state function. When a chemical corrosion reaction occurs, a state change occurs, and the free energy change is the maximum useful energy resulting from the reaction. The magnitude may be thought of as the driving force of the reaction. If a reaction is spontaneous, the net change in free energy is negative. The relationship between the free energy change and the electrode potential is: $$ \Delta G=n E F $$ $F$ is the Faraday Constant and $F=96,487$ Joules/Volt mol of $\mathrm{e}^{-}$. We can now assess for any condition whether or not a corrosion reaction will take place or not, provided we know the concentration of the species involved in the corrosion process.

Example 7.2 Determine if Zn will corrode in a Hydrochloric Acid solution of $\mathrm{pH}=2$ with a $0.01 \mathrm{M} \mathrm{ZnCl}_{2}$ concentration at room temperature. Assume that the corrosion product is hydrogen gas. The attack of Zn is an HCl solution is show below in Figure 7.2. This may be termed general attack. Lets examine this situation by looking at the half cell reactions and applying the Nernst Equation to calculate the cell potential, $E_{\text {cell }}$. From the Galvanic Series, the anode reaction, expressed as the oxidation of Zn is: $$ \mathrm{Zn} \rightarrow \mathrm{Zn}^{++}+2 \mathrm{e}^{-} $$ The standard half-cell potential for the oxidation of Zn is -0.76 V . Then from the Nernst equation $$ \begin{aligned} & E_{Z n}=E_{Z n}^{\circ}+\frac{0.0257}{n} \ln C \\ & E_{Z n}=-0.76+\frac{0.257}{2} \ln (0.01) \\ & E_{Z n}=-0.82 \mathrm{~V} \end{aligned} $$ The standard half-cell reaction for the oxidation of hydrogen is 0.0 V . This is the reference point for the Galvanic series as we discussed earlier. For a solution, we can recall that the pH $=-\log \left[\mathrm{H}^{+}\right]$, where $\left[\mathrm{H}^{+}\right]$is the hydrogen ion concentration. Then, the Nernst equation for the half cell reaction of hydrogen oxidation is expressed as $E_{H 2}=-0.0592 \mathrm{pH}$. $$ \begin{aligned} & E_{H 2}=-0.0592 p H \\ & E_{H 2}=-0.12 \mathrm{~V} \end{aligned} $$ Recalling that the half cell potentials are both stated as oxidation reactions: $$ E_{\text {Cell }}=E_{\text {Anode }}-E_{\text {Cathode }}=-0.82-(-0.12)=-0.70 \mathrm{~V} $$ Figure 7.2 Corrosion attack of zinc in hydrochloric acid (Hcl). We can now examine the free energy change of the proposed cell: $$ \begin{aligned} & \Delta \mathrm{G}=n E F=2 \mathrm{~mol} \text { elec }(-0.70 \mathrm{~V})(96,487 \mathrm{~J} / \mathrm{Vmol} \text { elec }) \\ & \Delta \mathrm{G}=-135 \mathrm{~kJ} \end{aligned} $$ We can see that the proposed corrosion process will spontaneously take place with a large driving force. One tool we may use to further study the themodymanics of corrosion is the Pourbaix diagram. This type of diagram is a plot of potential versus pH of the electrolyte, usually water, under standard conditions at $25^{\circ} \mathrm{C}$. The Pourbaix diagram will show the relative stability of the metal and its oxides, hydroxides, hydrides or other potential products of the corrosion process. The results of calculating cell potential from the Nernst equation can be examined for electrolytes of different pH . Regions of immunity will be evident, as well as the potential for passivation. Passivation occurs when a thin resistant film forms on the surface of the metal, inhibiting corrosion. In fact, this is a necessary step in imparting corrosion resistance to stainless steel alloys. In this case, passivation is implemented into a surface treatment process.# 7.1.2 Types of Galvanic Cells ## Dissimilar Electrode Cells The wide variety of materials and processes used in systems may lead to the formation of several types of cells in a corrosive environment. One of the most common types of cells is the dissimilar metal or dissimilar electrode cell. Two dissimilar metals in contact will result in corrosion of the anode in the presence of an electrolyte. There are many examples of dissimilar electrode cells in engineering practice. In microelectronic devices, gold wires bonded to aluminum bond pads form a potentially destructive couple. If we examine the Galvanic series, we can see Al and Au are quire far apart and that Al is lower in the series, or anodic. In this case, a small amount of moisture present in a microelectronic package will serve as an electrolyte and can result in severe corrosion of the aluminum bond pad, destroying the circuit. Another example of a dissimilar metal electrode cell can be seen from observing galvanized or zinc coated steel. In this case, the Zn coating over the surface of the steel will be anodic to the Fe based steel. If the coating is damaged, the underlying steel is exposed to potential electrolytes. The Zn surface, however will corrode. As long as there is Zn present the steel is protected.

Example 11.2 A engineer wishes to compare the effects of surface finishing process improvements on fatigue life of a critical automobile components by running fatigue tests. Determine an appropriate experiment layout. Recalling Chapter 5, we can model surface effects on fatigue life according to: $$ S_{a}=K_{a} S_{f}^{\prime}=C k_{a} N_{f}^{b} $$ where $S_{a}$ is the applied alternating stress, $k_{a}$ is the surface factor and $N_{f}$ is the number of cycles to failure. $C$ and $b$ are constants representing material properties. Now, we can simply take the natural log of both sides of the equation 11.23 and we see that: $$ \ln S_{a}=\ln C+\ln k_{a}+b \ln N_{f} $$ In a fatigue experiment we control the load which produces the alternating stress, $S_{a}$, in the component and measure the life, $N_{f}$ Therefore, solving for $\ln N_{f,}$, we see the following: $$ \ln N_{f}=C^{*}-\frac{1}{b} \ln k_{a}-\frac{1}{b} \ln S_{a} $$ This is of the following linear form: $$ y=\beta_{a}+\beta_{1} x_{1}+\beta_{2} x_{2} $$ From equations 11.25 and 11.26 , we see there are two factors of interest $x_{1}$ and $x_{2}$, representing surface finish and load conditions respectively. The number of runs required is $i_{r}=2^{2}=4$ runs required to determine the constants $C^{*}$ and $b$ and the effect of the process improvement. We may not be able to directly control the surface finish factor, $k_{a}$. Rather, we may be primarily interested in comparing two different surface finishing processes. In this case, we may evaluate the effect as a qualitative variable and simply let $x_{1}=+1$ for the improved finishing Process $A$ and $x_{1}=-1$ for the original finishing Process $B$, when performing the regression analysis. $\beta_{1}$ would then represent the effect of process improvement. For load conditions, we substitute the values of alternating stress selected for the tests, with - representing the lowest value and + representing the highest value. $\beta_{2}$ would then represent the effect of load conditions. We can derive the constants for the $S-N$ curve. The experiment would be conducted according to Table 11.5. If we have 6 factors to examine in a fatigue experiment, we will need $i_{r}=2^{6}=64$ experimental runs to perform a full 2 level factorial experiment. On the other hand, we may only be interested in fitting a fatigue model that includes main effects. We can then elect to scale down the experiment by running a fractional factorial. As an example, for an experiment with five factors $(k=5)$, our model will have $m=6$ regression parameters to include the 6 main effects and a regression constant. To fit a simple model with 6 regression parameters, we will need a minimum of 1 degree of freedom to examine error. This will require a minimum of 7 data points to analyze the main effects. We do not need the entire set of 64 runs and all treatments combinations to achieve our objective. In this case, we can reduce the experimental design by constructing a fractional factorial. In doing so, we naturally expect to sacrifice our ability to examine all the interactions, but we will be able to perform a regression analysis to fit the model of interest and include the main effects. As an example, we could construct $\frac{1}{8}$ factorial having $\frac{64}{8}=8$ runs, at treatments with 2 levels for our 5 factors. The experiment would be constructed using the following layout, leaving 2 degrees of freedom: Table 11.6 Design Table for A Fractional Factorial with 5 Factors | Experimental Run | Factor $\boldsymbol{x}_{\mathbf{1}}$ | Factor $\boldsymbol{x}_{\mathbf{2}}$ | Factor $\boldsymbol{x}_{\mathbf{3}}$ | Factor $\boldsymbol{x}_{\mathbf{4}}$ | Factor $\boldsymbol{x}_{\mathbf{5}}$ | | :--------------- | :----------------------------------- | :----------------------------------- | :----------------------------------- | :----------------------------------- | :----------------------------------- | | 1 | + | - | - | + | + | | 2 | + | + | - | - | - | | 3 | + | + | + | - | + | | 4 | - | + | + | + | - | | 5 | + | - | + | + | - | | 6 | - | + | - | + | + | | 7 | - | - | + | - | + | | 8 | - | - | - | - | - | Layouts for fractional factorial experiments may be found in many references. We can easily construct a $\frac{1}{2}$ factorial by the method described by O'Connor (1991). First, we construct the full factorial layout. Then, we construct the full response table with all interactions. Next, we select an interaction that we will eliminate from the design. We can usually eliminate the highest order interaction, as it is unlikely to be significant or have much physical meaning. We eliminate all of the rows of the design in which the selected interaction has a $(-)$ value. We will be left with half of the required runs and treatment combinations. Similarly, we can again reduce the $\frac{1}{2}$ factorial to a $\frac{1}{4}$. Further reductions are possible depending upon the original size of the design table. We need to be fully aware of the fact that we are losing information in the process of creating a fractional design and that we are incurring some risks. If we follow O'Connor's (1991)procedure, we will see that several contrasts in our resulting design will appear identical, after reducing the original design. In this case, we say that the effects associated with the like contrasts in a fractional design are confounded. In other words, we cannot distinguish differences between the confounded effects. If higher order interactions are not significant, then this fact does not matter. We will distinguish the main effects. However, if these higher order effects are significant, we run the risk of the second or third order interaction contributing to the estimated main effect. We may draw an erroneous conclusion. Therefore, we should judiciously select interactions for elimination and carefully assess confounded contrasts based on engineering knowledge of the physical processes involved.

Do apply SEDs to estimate failure mechanism model parameters. Do include discrete and qualitative independent factors in the design. Evans and Kyoung-Taeg Lee In Chapter 10, we examined the basic elements of testing and test design issues. Then, in Chapter 11, we turned our attention to multiple factors, multiple test conditions and test design for model development using designed experiments. We will now address accelerated testing and the statistical analysis of data from accelerated tests. Accelerated testing is the process of applying loads in testing that exceed the loads that are encountered in service. The result is a decreased time to failure of the material, component or system in testing. The benefit is a reduction in the test time, for the evaluations of product life by wear out failure mechanisms. It is unreasonable to expect to test a product in development under expected field loads, since we expect most products to last many years. Yet, we must assure their integrity in a short time, during design phases. In fact, virtually all life tests are conducted under some form of acceleration. As an example, we may elevate the test temperature for a corrosion test leading to rapid deterioration of component test samples. Or, we may elevate both voltage and temperature in testing microcircuits, to evaluate the integrity of the deposited dielectrics used in the circuits. In any event, to understand the relationship of the test to the reliability of a system when it is fielded, we must be able to develop a relationship between test time and field life. To do this effectively, we must understand the impact of the accelerated loading conditions on the failure mechanisms active in the system. In this chapter, we will discuss the development of acceleration factors for tests. In addition, we will discuss the analysis of data from testing and the projection of the data to field conditions. This is an essential and key aspect of effective reliability assessment and becomes necessary to confirm dominant failure mechanisms and to validate models used for design. ### 12.1 Acceleration Factors The effects of acceleration must be examined for each dominant mechanism acting on the components in a system. An acceleration factor for a failure mechanism can be determined from the failure mechanism models we have developed in previous chapters. We can then apply the acceleration factor to data accumulated in test to assess the relationship between the test life and field life. In general, we can say the relationship between test time and field life can be expressed for a given failure mechanism (FM) as: $$ A F*{F M}=\frac{t*{f(\text { field })}}{t\_{f(\text { test })}} $$ In Chapter 11, we broadly categorized our models into three classes. Keeping in mind there are always exceptions, our models may fit into one of following three categories: - Arrhenius Models - Stress Power Law Models - Mixed Models Diffusion driven processes and chemical processes, such as corrosion, will often have an Arrhenius relationship or exhibit a mixed model with mechanical, electrical or chemical stresses acting in concert with temperature to accelerate failure. Power law models, on the other hand, represent fatigue and related processes. In fatigue, increasing the stresses in the component by increasing applied loads, accelerates failure by crack growth. We can determine a relationship between loading conditions through an acceleration transform, developed from failure mechanism models of interest. Let us examine the simple Arrhenius expression. The time to failure for a corrosion process may be expressed as: $$ t*{f}=A^{\*} e^{E*{A} / K T} $$ Recall that $A^{*}$ is a constant, $E_{A}$ is the activation energy, $k$ is Boltzmann's Constant and $T$ is the absolute temperature at which the reaction is occurring. From Chapter 11, we can see that $E_{A}$ is determined by evaluating the time to fail at different temperatures. Now consider that we have determined $E_{A}$ under a series of elevated temperature tests and we wish to project data to field conditions. Applying equation 12.1: $$ \mathrm{AF}=\frac{t*{f \text { field })}}{t*{f(\text { test })}}=\frac{A^{_} e^{E\_{A} / K T(\text { field })}}{A^{_} e^{E\_{A} / K T(\text { test })}} $$ Simplifying: $$ A F=\exp \left[\frac{E_{A}}{K}\left(\frac{1}{T_{\text {field }}}-\frac{1}{T_{\text {test }}}\right)\right] $$ Keep in mind that we have made several assumptions in deriving 12.4. The concentrations of the reacting species have not been considered. We have assumed that they have remained constant between the field conditions and the test conditions. If this assumption is not true, then we must derive a relationship that accounts for concentration differences.

Example 12.1 A heat exchanger was tested under accelerated conditions. The test was conducted at $215^{\circ} \mathrm{C}$, at operating pressures. A leak was detected as a result of pitting after 500 hours of test. The heat exchanger will operate at $125^{\circ} \mathrm{C}$. Assuming the process failure has an activation energy of 1.2 eV , determine the test acceleration factor and estimate the field life from the time of first failure. Applying equation 12.4: $$ \begin{aligned} A F & =\exp \left[\frac{1.2}{86.1 \times 10^{-6}}\left(\frac{1}{398}-\frac{1}{488}\right)\right] \\ & =\exp (6.44) \\ A F & =626 \end{aligned} $$ Then: $$ A F*{F M}=\frac{t*{f(\text { field })}}{t\_{f(\text { test })}} $$ and $$ t\_{f(\text { field })}=626(500)=312,890 \text { hours }=36 \text { years } $$ This is a simple example of an acceleration factor estimate and its application. Loading uncertainties and multiple failure mechanism have not been considered. In general, equation 12.4 would apply to any Arrhenius relationship or mixed model in which the component stresses, other than temperature, remain the same between the field conditions encountered in application and the test conditions. Also, keep in mind that the field loads, in this case temperature, may not be known with precision. In application, as we discussed in Chapter 4, loading conditions are likely to have a lot of associated uncertainty. Let's consider a power law relationship. Recall our simple expression for fatigue life of a material: $$ S*{a}=C N*{f}^{b} $$ where $S_{a}$ is the alternating stress, $N_{f}$ is the cycles to failure and $C$ and $b$ are material properties. Our acceleration factor expression is then: $$ A F=\frac{N*{f(\text { field })}}{N*{f(\text { test })}}=\frac{C^{_} S\_{a(\text { field })}^{1 / b}}{C^{_} S\_{a(\text { test })}^{1 / b}} $$ Simplifying: $$ A F=\left[\frac{S_{a(\text { field })}}{S_{a(\text { test })}}\right]^{\frac{1}{b}} $$ In the case of fatigue, we must know the exponent value $b$, for the material we are considering, to apply an acceleration transform. In comparing low cycle and high cycle fatigue recall that $b($ low cycle $) \neq b($ high cycle $)$. Hence equation 12.7 cannot be applied to transform low cycle fatigue test data to high cycle fatigue component applications. Equation 12.7 is also derived under the assumption that the components or samples used for testing would represent the components used in the field. As discussed in Chapter 5, factors such as manufacturing processes for surface finish and notch designs would contribute substantially to reducing fatigue life. If we consider thermal cycling loads as a source of alternating stresses in the component, then the change in temperature is proportional to the stress amplitude: $$ S\_{a} \propto \Delta T $$ Equation 12.7 then becomes: $$ A F=\left[\frac{\Delta T_{(\text {field })}}{\Delta T_{(\text {test })}}\right]^{\frac{1}{b}} $$ Once again, 12.9 assume that the same fatigue process is active in the field as in the test. We cannot compare low cycle and high cycle fatigue or failure processes in which creep may dominate the deformation. In this case, more complex transforms are necessary.We have shown at this point that we can derive an acceleration transform from a failure mechanism model and we have derived some simple expressions for Arrhenius and Power Law failure mechanism models. These expressions are well known and often broadly applied. However, we must always keep in mind that the test conditions must represent the field conditions to apply an acceleration transform. We are also interested in high levels of reliability, not necessarily in mean life. Figure 12.1 graphically depicts our objectives in interpreting accelerated test data. As Figure 12.1 reflects, we apply an AF assuming that we know the field loading conditions with certainty. While this is true for the test, it is often not the case for a system or product. As an example, consider a washing machine. The weight of the clothing the consumer places in the wash tub will probably vary considerably from consumer to consumer and with each use of the machine. This is explored in greater detail in later sections. # 12.2 Analysis of Data It is essential to determine in the process of analysis which probability distribution that best fits a set of data accumulated from a single test condition. There are two approaches - qualitative and quantitative - that will be presented in this section. In accelerated life testing, the random variable of interest is of course time to failure of the components, sub-systems or systems subjected to the test loads. However, plotting techniques can also be applied to other random variables such as process parameters or strength. In this section, several different types of random variables will be used to demonstrate the analysis techniques and procedures. ### 12.2.1 Probability and Hazard Plotting Although quantitative approaches, including the Chi-squared and Kolmogorov-Smirnov test have been developed, qualitative probability and hazard plotting methods are widely used in practice due to their simplicity. These techniques provide pictorial representations of the data, as well as: - an evaluation of the reasonableness of the assumed probability model - estimates of the percentiles of the distribution or probability of failure at different times - estimates of the distribution parametersPlotting techniques are very simple to use and easy to demonstrate. For a given pdf, the data are plotted on special graph paper designed for that distribution. If the assumed model is correct, the plotted points will tend to fall in a straight line. If the model is inadequate, however, the plot will not be linear and the extent and type of departures can be seen. Once a model appears to fit the data reasonably well, percentiles and parameter values can be estimated from the plot. The procedure and underlying theory of probability plotting are illustrated first. Next, probability plots for normal, lognormal, Weibull and extreme value distributions are considered. Probability plot for singly censored data and hazard plots for multiply censored data are given at the end of the section. # Procedure for Probability Plotting The following steps are involved in preparing a probability plot from a given set of data: - Step 1: Obtain the appropriate probability paper ${ }^{1}$ designed for the distribution under examination. - Step 2: Rank the observations, $x_{(i)}^{\prime} z$, such as times to failure, from smallest to largest in magnitude. Thus, if $x_{1}, x_{2}, \ldots, x_{n}$, are the original unordered observations then the ordered observations, $x_{(1)}, x_{(2)}, \ldots, x_{(n)}$, are such that $x_{(1)} \leq x_{(2)} \leq \ldots \leq x_{(n)}$. - Step 3: Plot the $x_{(i)}^{\prime} z$ on the probability paper versus plotting position, where the plotting position $=(i-0.5) 100 / n$. - Step 4: If a straight line appears to fit the data, draw such a line on the graph 'by eye'. If the selected $p d f$ is correct, the points should cluster around the line, although there will be some deviations. If the plot deviates appreciably from linearity, the chosen pdf does not adequately describe the given data. Systematic departures are indications that the model is inadequate and the another model should be used. The determination of what can and cannot be considered a straight line is a subjective matter, and two people using the same plot may arrive at somewhat different conclusions. But, the larger the sample size, the easier it will be to make the correct decision.
