After each sample, the observations are ordered and relabeled $x_{(i)}, i=1,2, \cdots, n$, where $x_{(i)}$ is the value of the $i^{\text {th }}$ smallest observation. Then, the expected value of $x_{(i)}$ can be shown to be $$ E\left[x_{(i)}\right]=\frac{n!}{(i-1)(\mathrm{n}-i)} \int*{0}^{1} x*{(i)} f\left(x*{(i)}\right) F\left(x*{(i)}\right)^{i-1}\left[1-F\left(x_{(i)}\right)\right]^{n-1} d x\_{(i)} $$ For example, if $x$ is uniformly distributed over the interval $(0,1)$, then equation (12.12) reduces to: $$ E\left[x_{(i)}\right]=\frac{i}{n+1} $$ For distributions for which $E\left[x_{(i)}\right]$ cannot be determined exactly, the following approximation is frequently used: $$ E\left[x_{(i)}\right]=F^{-1}\left\{\frac{i-c}{n-2 c+1}\right\} $$ where $F^{-1}\left\{\frac{i-c}{n-2 c+1}\right\}$ is the value of $x$, such that $\frac{i-c}{n-2 c+1}=\int_{c}^{x} f(u) d u$ and $E\left[x_{(i)}\right]$ is a number which depends on $n$ and $f(x)$. For a sample of size $n$, the first ordered observation $x(1)$ is a one-sample estimate of $E\left[x_{(1)}\right], x_{(2)}$ is a one-sample estimate of $E\left[x_{(2)}\right]$, and so on. Thus the ordered observed values, when plotted against their expected values, would lie on approximately a straight line, and the linearity of the plot of the observations versus their expected values provides an evaluation of the adequacy of a chosen model for the $p d f$ of the data. The construction of specially scaled probability paper has obviated the need for actually calculating expected values for each distribution. This paper is scaled in such a fashion that the ordered observations can be plotted directly against $(i-c) 100 /(n-2 c+1)$, without the need of determining $E\left[x_{(i)}\right]$. In general, the exact value of $c$ depends on $n$ and $f(x)$, but $c=\frac{1}{2}$ has been found to be generally acceptable for a wide variety of distributions and sample sizes. Figure 12.2 Normal probability plot for measured cement container weights.# Normal Probability Plot Normal probability papers are specially designed papers where the plotted points will cluster around a straight line if the data are from the normal distribution. If the plotted points tend to fall in a straight line, we can estimate percentiles $\left(x_{p}\right.$ satisfying $\left.P\left(X \leq x_{p}\right)=p\right.$, given $\left.p\right)$ and percentages failing by the probability plot. To determine percentiles for any random variable we analyze, we enter the plot on the probability scale at the desired percentage and go to the fitted line and then to the corresponding point on the data scale to read the percentile estimate. To determine percentage failing, enter the plot on the data scale at that time. Go to the fitted line, and then go to the corresponding point on the probability scale to read the estimate. In fact, the methods of estimating percentiles and percentages failing are the same for all the probability plots, and thus the estimation of percentiles and percentages is omitted hereafter. The mean and standard deviation are estimated as follows. The mean $\mu$ of a normal distribution equals the median ( $50^{\text {th }}$ percentile), since the distribution is symmetric. To estimate, $\sigma$, the standard distribution, estimate the mean and the $16^{\text {th }}$ percentile. The estimate of $\sigma$ is the difference between the mean and the $16^{\text {th }}$ percentile, since for any normal distribution the standard deviation equals approximately the difference between them.

We can note, from these figures, that: - The variance of the points in the tails (extreme low or high plotted values) will be larger than that of the points at the center of the distribution. Thus, the relative linearity of the plot near the tails of the distribution will often seem poorer than at the center of the distribution even if the correct model has been chosen. - The plotted points are ordered and hence are not independent. Thus the plot may consist of a series of successive points above and below the line, even if the chosen model is correct. - Even though the correct model has been chosen, the plot appears to diverge from linearity due to random variations, especially when the sample size is small. - When there is a systematic departure from a straight line, an examination of a plot can give some information about the shape of a more appropriate model. For example, the plots of Figure 12.3-(c) and (d) show that the values in both tails are too large, and thus the data suggest that a model skewed to the right should be chosen. Figure 12.4 Lognormal Probability Plot of BGA fatigue test data. # Weibull Probability Plotting The importance of the Weibull distribution has been emphasized in Chapter 3. The Weibull distribution may be the most widely used lifetime distribution model. Its popularity maybe due to the flexibility of the distribution to represent many types of failure patterns. That is, the Weibull distribution hazard function is monotone increasing if $\beta>1$, decreasing if $\beta<1$, and constant for $\beta=1$ and for this case, the Weibull distribution reduces to the exponential distribution. In addition, if $\beta=3.5$, the distribution is similar to the normal distribution and it is similar to the lognormal distribution if $2.5<\beta<3.5$. So, in analyzing times to failure from testing or field conditions, the Weibull distribution is an excellent place to start. In Chapter 2, the Weibull cumulative distribution function was defined as $$ F(x)=1-\exp \left[-\left(\frac{x}{\mu}\right)^{\beta}\right], x>0 $$ where $\mu$ and $\beta$ are the scale and shape parameters, respectively. Therefore, we can obtain $$ \frac{1}{1-F(x)}=\exp \left[\left(\frac{x}{\mu}\right)^{\beta}\right] $$ and $$ \ln \ln \left[\frac{1}{1-F(x)}\right]=\beta \ln x-\beta \ln \mu $$ Thus, for any Weibull variate, $\ln \{\ln [1 /\{1-F(x)\}]\}$ will plot as a straight line against the natural logarithms of the observations. To avoid the need for computing $\ln \{\ln [1 /\{1-F(x)\}]\}$ and $\ln x$, the axes of the probability paper are scaled so that ( $\mathrm{i}-0.5) 100 / n$ can be plotted on the ordinate, corresponding to $\ln \{\ln [1 /\{1-F(x)\}]\}$, and the observed values can be plotted on the abscissa, corresponding to $\ln x$.The scale parameter $\mu$ is the $63^{\text {th }}$ percentile, since $F(\mu)=1-e^{-1} \approx 0.63$. In addition, from equation (12.17), the shape parameter $\beta$,is the slope of the fitted line. The slope can be estimated by $$ \hat{\beta}=\frac{W*{2}-W*{1}}{z*{2}-z*{1}} $$ where $W_{2}$ and $W_{1}$ are two values of $\ln \{\ln [1 /\{1-F(x)]]\}$ and where $z_{2}$ and $z_{1}$ are the corresponding values of $\ln x$ on the plotted line. In the commercial Weibull probability paper, $\beta$ can be estimated by using the point labelled 'origin', which will be explained below. In equation (12.18), the hat symbol, ${ }^{\circ}$, denotes the estimator of the parameter of interest, $\beta$.

The step by step procedure of using the hazard paper is as follows: - Obtain the hazard paper designed for the distribution under examination - Order the n data from smallest to largest without regard as to which are censoring or failure times. Label the data with reverse ranks; that is, label the first ordered data with n , the second data with $n-1, \ldots$, and the $n^{\text {th }}$ with 1 . - Calculate a hazard value for each failure time as $100 / k$, where $k$ is its reverse rank. - Calculate the cumulative hazard value for each failure time as the sum of its hazard value and the cumulative hazard value of the preceding failure time. - Plot the cumulative hazard against failure time on the chosen hazard paper. If the plot of failure times is roughly straight, one may conclude that the distribution adequately fits the data. The fitted line in the hazard paper can estimate then, percentiles and distribution parameters. Figure 12.10 Cumulative Weibull hazard plot of failure times for an electrical device.The Weibull hazard function is $$ h(x)=\frac{f(x)}{1-\mathbf{F}(x)}=\frac{\beta}{\mu}\left(\frac{x}{\mu}\right)^{\beta-1} $$ and thus the Weibull cumulative hazard function is $$ H(x)=\int\_{0}^{\infty} \frac{\beta}{\mu}\left(\frac{t}{\mu}\right)^{\beta-1} d t=\left(\frac{x}{\mu}\right)^{\beta} $$ Then, time $x$ as a function of $H$ is $$ \log x=\frac{1}{\beta} \log H+\log \mu $$ This show that $\log x$ is a linear function of $\log H$. Thus, Weibull hazard paper is a log-log graph paper, and the axes of the hazard paper are scaled so that cumulative hazard value (calculated by the above procedure) can be plotted on the ordinate, corresponding to $\log H$, and the failure times can be plotted on the abscissa, corresponding to $\log x$. For $H=100 \%$, the corresponding time $x$ equals $\mu$, which is used to estimate $\mu$ graphically. For example, the estimate of $\mu$ is 120 . The slope of the straight line equals to $1 / \beta$, and thus the shape parameter can be estimated by the formula similar to equation (12.19). When using the commercial Weibull hazard paper, $\beta$ can be estimated by using the dot in the upper left of the paper. That is, if we draw a straight line parallel to the fitted line, so that it passes both through the dot and through the shape parameter scale, the value on the shape parameter is the estimate of $\beta$. In Figure 12.10, the estimate of $\beta$ is about 2. # 12.2.2 Goodness-of-Fit Tests Goodness-of-fit tests are statistical hypothesis tests that are used to assess formally whether the observations are from a particular distribution. Goodness-of-fit tests can be used to test the following null hypothesis: $\mathrm{H}_{0}: X_{i}^{\prime} \mathrm{s}$ are from a particular distribution $\mathrm{F}_{0}(x)$ ## Chi-square Test The most widely used goodness-of-fit test is the chi-square test, which was originally proposed by Karl Pearson (1990). To compute the chi-square test statistic, we must first divide the entire range of the fitted distribution model into adjacent intervals $\left[a_{0}, a_{1}\right),\left[a_{1}, a_{2}\right), \ldots$, $\left[a_{k 1}, a_{k}\right)$, where $a_{0}=0$ and $a_{k}=\infty$. Then we tally $N_{j}:$ number of $X_{i}^{\prime} s$ in the $j^{\text {th }}$ interval $\left(a_{j-1}, a_{j}\right)$ for $j=1,2, \ldots, k$. (Note that $\sum_{i=1}^{k} N_{j}=n$, where n is the sample size). Next, we compute the expected proportion $p_{j}$ of the $X_{i}^{\prime} s$ that would fail in the $j^{\text {th }}$ interval if we were sampling from the fitted distribution. Then $$ p*{j}=\int*{a*{i-1}}^{a*{j}} f(x) d x $$where $\mathrm{f}(x)$ is the probability density function of the fitted distribution. Finally, the test statistic is $$ \chi^{2}=\sum_{j=1}^{k} \frac{\left(N_{j}-n p_{j}\right)^{2}}{n p_{j}} $$ Since $\mathrm{np}_{\mathrm{j}}$ is the expected number of $n X_{j}^{\prime} s$ that would fall in the $\mathrm{j}^{\text {th }}$ interval if $\mathrm{H}_{0}$ was true, we would expect $\chi^{2}$ to be small if the fit is good. Therefore, we reject $\mathrm{H}_{0}$ if $\chi^{2}$ is too large. The precise form of the test depends on whether or not we have estimated any of the parameters of the fitted distribution from the sample. # Parameter Known Case When all parameters of the fitted distribution are known (usually of little practical use in reliability engineering), reject $H_{0}$ if $\chi^{2}>\chi_{k-1,1-\alpha}^{2}$ (Figure 12.11), where $\chi_{k-1,1-\alpha}^{2}$ is the $(1-\alpha)^{\text {th }}$ percentile for a chi-square distribution with $k-1$ degrees of freedom(df). Values for $\chi_{k-1,1-\alpha}^{2}$ can be found in the Appendix. ## Parameter Unknown Case When some or all of the parameters of the fitted distribution are unknown, parameters should be first estimated to calculate $p_{j}$ of equation (12.24). The most popular estimation method is the Maximum Likelihood Estimation (MLE) and the estimation procedures for normal, lognormal and Weibull distributions are summarized in the Appendix. Then, when the number of unknown parameters is $m$, we reject $\mathrm{H}_{0}$ if $\chi^{2}>\chi_{k-m-1,1-\alpha}^{2}$.

engineering is the KolmogonovSmirnov(K-S) test which compares an empirical distribution function with the fitted distribution function. To compute the K-S Statistic, we should first define an empirical distribution. That is, empirical distribution function from $X_{1}, X_{2}, \ldots ., X_{n}$ is $$ F_{n}(x)=\frac{\text { number of } X^{\prime} s \leq x}{n} $$ for all real values $x$. Thus $F_{n}(x)$ is a step function such that $F_{n}\left(x_{(i)}\right)=\frac{i}{n}$ for $=1,2, \ldots, n$. If $F(x)$ is the fitted distribution function, a natural assessment of goodness-of-fit is some kind of measure of the closeness between the functions $F_{n}(x)$ and $F(x)$. The K-S test statistic $\mathrm{D}_{n}$, is simply the largest distance between $F_{n}(x)$ and $F(x)$ for all values of $x$ and is defined by $$ D_{n}=\max _{x}\left|F_{n}(x)-F(x)\right| $$Clearly, a large value of $D_{n}$ indicates a poor fit, so that the form of the test is to reject the null hypothesis $H_{0}$ if $D_{n}$ exceeds some constant $d_{n, 1-\alpha}$, which can be found in the Appendix. Again, the precise form of the test depends on whether or not we have estimated any of the parameters of the fitted distribution from the sample. But, the difference of the critical values between parameter known and unknown cases is usually negligible in this case.

For this reason, acceleration factors are not very predictive. An alternative approach is to apply simulation. The technique outlined in Chapter 3 can be applied to model the test conditions and test failure distribution. We simulate test conditions through applying Monte Carlo simulation. A test simulation includes the primary sources of variability expected in materials properties and manufacturing processes, that affect the component we wish to evaluate. The simulation is exercised on the failure mechanism models, which represent the component. In testing, we will know the test loads with certainty and they can be considered as such in the simulation of the test. We then generate a simulated test distribution and compare it to our actual test data. Next, we assess the validity of our model. With a validated model, we now simulate the field conditions, allowing the loads to become random variables and considering their expected variations. Critical components for this process might be selected from a Failure Modes and Effects Analysis (FMEA) of the system or sub-system under development. Figure 12.13 Process of test simulation and projection of test data to field conditions.# 12.4 Risks in Accelerated Testing In the application of accelerated testing, we must be aware of the inherent risks that may lead to error. When elevated loads are applied to a component or system in testing, we run the risks of over acceleration and failure mechanism shifts. Over acceleration results when the dominant failure mechanism is no longer representative of what is expected in application or under field loading conditions. As an example, we can consider the effects of raising the temperature on diffusion processes. In a polycrystalline metal, grain boundary diffusion dominates at lower temperatures. The primary transport of atoms is along grain boundaries and interfaces. However at higher temperatures, bulk diffusion dominates and the primary path of diffusion is through the crystal lattice. Each of these two processes has different activation energy. Hence, if we measure activation energy for bulk diffusion, when in fact, grain boundary diffusion is the primary mode of transport, we would introduce significant error in projecting test results to lower temperatures. Diffusion in polycrystalline silver for example, shifts from grain boundary to bulk lattice diffusion at about $700^{\circ} \mathrm{C}$ and the activation energy for grain boundary diffusion is about half of the activation energy for bulk diffusion (Reed-Hill 1973). At this temperature, over acceleration is not a concern for product tests, but we need to be aware of the shift, if we are conducting materials tests to measure diffusion kinetics. On the other hand, aluminum shifts at much lower temperatures. In general, we should be concerned about temperature over acceleration for diffusion driven mechanisms in metals, when we exceed test temperatures of $0.5 \mathrm{~T}_{\mathrm{mp}}$ where $\mathrm{T}_{\mathrm{mp}}$ is the melting point (Lall 1998). Another concern is the potential to shift from one dominant failure mechanism to another when test loads are increased above application loading conditions. Let's examine Figure 12.14. This figure shows a plot of mission life versus normalized operating temperature for a Figure 12.14 Plot of operating mission life versus normalized operating temperature for various failure mechanisms occurring in a microelectronic device. (Courtesy of CALCE Center, University of Maryland).microelectronic device. The mean life of the device is plotted for each potential failure mechanism. If we consider a test conducted at condition B, we can see that Time Dependent Dielectric Breakdown (TDDB) of the dielectric will dominate. Now, let's consider operating conditions at a lower temperature. At operating conditions, Point A shows that the dominant mechanism at the operating temperature is Stress Driven Diffusive Voiding (SDDV). This clearly illustrates the risk of mechanism shifting under accelerated loads, when we have competing causes of failure. If we assess life based upon TDDB, as extracted from accelerated tests of the device, we would project a life in excess of $10^{6}$ hours. However under the field conditions, we might expect the device to fail from SDDV at about 20,000 hours. The risk of error increases with increasing complexity of the system or component and with the introduction of new technologies. In addition, our example does not consider uncertainty. A comprehensive process of reliability assessment is needed to avoid error. As we discussed in Chapter 1, we must anticipate causes of failure. Modeling the failure processes then becomes essential, as Figure 12.13 illustrates. Following construction of models, we can appropriately design testing. For our example shown, we might elect to reduce the test temperature or run a series of tests at different temperatures. Following execution of testing, failure analysis must be used to confirm the failure mechanism and validate the modeling process. Comparison to field failure histories and known active mechanisms is also very useful. # 12.3 Do's and Don'ts in Design Do consider the limitations of acceleration factor models in projecting test data. Do recall an acceleration factor applies to a single dominant mechanism. Do model the accelerated test conditions and assess dominant mechanisms in test. Do examine all data to assess field failure modes and mechanisms. Do perform failure analysis of test items. Do plot data at all test conditions and compare the slope of the plots. Do failure analysis of outliers that do not fit models and plots. Do begin analysis with the Weibull distribution and then evaluate other distributions as appropriate. Do segregate failure modes from test data and apply censoring as appropriate. Do consider the impact of sample size on fitting distributions and estimating parameters. Don't perform plotting without a Goodness of Fit test. Don't forget there is a risk of over acceleration when increasing loads, such as temperature and mechanical stress. Don't perform accelerated testing without failure analysis of samples to confirm the failure mechanism. Don't apply acceleration factor models without careful analysis, when there are competing causes of failure. ## References Evans, J.W., Cushing, M.J, Lall,P., Bauernschub, R.,'A Physics of Failure Approach to Addressing Device Reliability in Accelerated Testing', IEEE MCM Conference, Santa Cruz, CA, 1995. Sze, S.M., VLSI Technology, McGraw-Hill, 1988.# 13 Failure Analysis of Assemblies and Devices Michael Pecht and Patrick McCluskey Significant improvements in the reliability of systems can be achieved by retrieving fielded assemblies and examining them to determine the root cause of failures and the extent of degradation which has occurred over time. In addition, it is important to examine root cause of failure as a result of accelerated testing to verify dominant failure mechanisms. Root cause failure analysis employs a number of non-destructive and destructive analytical techniques to identify the locations at which failures occur, characterize the modes in which failures occur, and provide clues as to the fundamental mechanisms by which failures occur. This information highlights the weak links in a system or product. These problems can then be modified, through corrective action to provide increased reliability. Because of the importance of failure analysis and degradation assessments in reliability growth, this chapter will focus primarily on describing the tools and techniques for systematically conducting such a failure analysis for reliability assessment. The identification of the damage mechanisms, which are most likely to cause failure, and the sites at which the damage is the most pronounced in fielded assemblies is also a necessary part of a focused accelerated test program. Accelerated test programs can be used to qualify new assemblies, thereby eliminating those assemblies most likely to fail in the field. In addition, failure analysis becomes an essential part of to determining the expected life of a new assembly, or to determine the remaining life of an assembly, which has been stored or used for an extended period of time. The benefit of the focused accelerated test program is that it allows the proper test loads and stresses to be selected. This benefit is enabled by effective use of failure analysis in a reliability assessment program. In this chapter, we will focus on failure analysis methods and tools. We initially examine an example of the overall process of failure analysis and then identify procedures, theory and information that each failure analysis tool can provide. Many examples in this chapter are specifically related to electronic assemblies and devices. However, the processes and tools are much the same for failure analysis of mechanical assemblies. The reader may wish to refer back to Chapter 9 to further see how these tools are implemented in the analysis of failures. ### 13.1 A Systematic Approach to Root Cause Failure Analysis Root cause failure analysis is only successful if it is approached in a systematic way. The process begins with the most non-destructive techniques and then proceeds to the more destructive techniques, allowing the gathering of unique data from each technique through-out the process. This data, when properly analyzed, leads to the mechanism for the failure. The use of destructive techniques early in the process is discouraged, as it can result in the loss of valuable information that might be required later. We also include a section on reliability modeling, where we draw attention to some important factors to be considered in the modeling process. Two real life examples are presented: a reliability study of a system in a power plant and an availability analysis of a gas compression system. ### 1.1 Lifetime Models In reliability we are mainly concerned with devices or systems that fail at an unforeseen or unpredictable (this term is defined precisely later) random age of $T>0$. This random variable is assumed to have a distribution $F, F(t)=$ $P(T \leq t), t \in \mathbb{R}$, with a density $f$. The hazard or failure rate $\lambda$ is defined on the support of the distribution by $$ \lambda(t)=\frac{f(t)}{\bar{F}(t)} $$ with the survival function $\bar{F}(t)=1-F(t)$. The failure rate $\lambda(t)$ measures the proneness to failure at time $t$ in that $\lambda(t) \triangle t \approx P(T \leq t+\triangle t \mid T>t)$ for small $\triangle t$. The (cumulative) hazard function is denoted by $\Lambda$, $$ \Lambda(t)=\int_{0}^{t} \lambda(s) d s=-\ln \{\bar{F}(t)\} $$ The well-known relation $$ \bar{F}(t)=P(T>t)=\exp \{-\Lambda(t)\} $$ establishes the link between the cumulative hazard and the survival function. Modeling in reliability theory is mainly concerned with additional informationabout the state of a system, which is gathered during the operating time of the system. This additional information leads to updated predictions about proneness to system failure. There are many ways to introduce such additional information into the model. In the following sections some examples of how to introduce additional information and how to model the lifetime $T$ are given. # 1.1.1 Complex Systems As will be introduced in detail in Chap. 2, a complex system comprises $n$ components with positive random lifetimes $T_{i}, i=1,2, \ldots, n, n \in \mathbb{N}$. Let $\Phi:\{0,1\}^{n} \rightarrow\{0,1\}$ be the structure function of the system, which is assumed to be monotone. The possible states of the components and of the system, "intact" and "failed," are indicated by " 1 " and " 0 ," respectively. Then $\Phi_{t}=\Phi\left(\mathbf{X}_{t}\right)$ describes the state of the system at time $t$, where $\mathbf{X}_{t}=\left(X_{t}(1), \ldots, X_{t}(n)\right)$ and $X_{t}(i)$ denotes the indicator function $$ X_{t}(i)=I\left(T_{i}>t\right)= \begin{cases}1 & \text { if } \quad T_{i}>t \\ 0 & \text { if } \quad T_{i} \leq t\end{cases} $$ which is 1 , if component $i$ is intact at time $t$, and 0 otherwise. The lifetime $T$ of the system is then given by $T=\inf \left\{t \in \mathbb{R}_{+}: \Phi_{t}=0\right\}$.

Example 1.1. As a simple example the following system with three components is considered, which is intact if component 1 and at least one of the components 2 or 3 are intact: In this example $\Phi_{t}=X_{t}(1)\left\{1-\left(1-X_{t}(2)\right)\left(1-X_{t}(3)\right)\right\}$ is easily obtained with $T=\inf \left\{t \in \mathbb{R}_{+}: \Phi_{t}=0\right\}=T_{1} \wedge\left(T_{2} \vee T_{3}\right)$, where as usual $a \wedge b$ and $a \vee b$ denote $\min \{a, b\}$ and $\max \{a, b\}$, respectively. The additional information about the lifetime $T$ is given by the observation of the state of the single components. As long as all components are intact, only a failure of component 1 leads to system failure. If one of the components 2 or 3 fails first, then the next component failure is a system failure. Under the classical assumption that all components work independently, i.e., the random variables $T_{i}, i=1, \ldots, n$, are independent, certain characteristics of the system lifetime are of interest: - Determining the system lifetime distribution from the known component lifetime distributions or at least finding bounds for this distribution (see Sects. 2.1 and 2.2).- Are certain properties of the component lifetime distributions like increasing failure rate (IFR) or increasing failure rate average (IFRA) preserved by forming monotone systems? One of these closure theorems states, for example, that the distribution of the system lifetime is IFRA if all component lifetimes have IFRA distributions (see Sect.2.2). - In what way does a certain component contribute to the functioning of the whole system? The answer to this question leads to the definition of several importance measures (see Sect. 2.1). # 1.1.2 Damage Models Additional information about the lifetime $T$ can also be introduced into the model in a quite different way. If the state or damage of the system at time $t \in \mathbb{R}_{+}$can be observed and this damage is described by a random variable $X_{t}$, then the lifetime of the system may be defined as $$ T=\inf \left\{t \in \mathbb{R}_{+}: X_{t} \geq S\right\} $$ i.e., as the first time the damage hits a given level $S$. Here $S$ can be a constant or, more general, a random variable independent of the damage process. Some examples of damage processes $X=\left(X_{t}\right)$ of this kind are described in the following subsections. ## Wiener Process The damage process is a Wiener process with positive drift starting at 0 and the failure threshold $S$ is a positive constant. The lifetime of the system is then known to have an inverse Gaussian distribution. Models of this kind are especially of interest if one considers different environmental conditions under which the system is working, as, for example, in so-called burn-in models. An accelerated aging caused by additional stress or different environmental conditions can be described by a change of time. Let $\tau: \mathbb{R}_{+} \rightarrow \mathbb{R}_{+}$be an increasing function. Then $Z_{t}=X_{\tau(t)}$ denotes the actual observed damage. The time transformation $\tau$ drives the speed of the deterioration. One possible way to express different stress levels in time intervals $\left[t_{i}, t_{i+1}\right), 0=t_{0}<t_{1}<$ $\ldots<t_{k}, i=0,1, \ldots, k-1, k \in \mathbb{N}$, is the choice $$ \tau(t)=\sum_{j=0}^{i-1} \beta_{j}\left(t_{j+1}-t_{j}\right)+\beta_{i}\left(t-t_{i}\right), t \in\left[t_{i}, t_{i+1}\right), \beta_{v}>0 $$ In this case it is seen that if $F_{0}$ is the inverse Gaussian distribution function of $T=\inf \left\{t \in \mathbb{R}_{+}: X_{t} \geq S\right\}$, and $F$ is the distribution function of the lifetime $T_{a}=\inf \left\{t \in \mathbb{R}_{+}: Z_{t} \geq S\right\}$ under accelerated aging, then $F(t)=$ $F_{0}(\tau(t))$. A generalization in another direction is to consider a random time change, which means that $\tau$ is a stochastic process. By this, randomly varying environmental conditions can be modeled.# Compound Point Processes Processes of this kind describe so-called shock processes where the system is subject to shocks that occur from time to time and add a random amount to the damage. The successive times of occurrence of shocks, $T_{n}$, are given by an increasing sequence $0<T_{1} \leq T_{2} \leq \ldots$ of random variables, where the inequality is strict unless $T_{n}=\infty$. Each time point $T_{n}$ is associated with a real-valued random mark $V_{n}$, which describes the additional damage caused by the $n$th shock. The marked point process is denoted $(T, V)=\left(T_{n}, V_{n}\right), n \in \mathbb{N}$. From this marked point process the corresponding compound point process $X$ with $$ X_{t}=\sum_{n=1}^{\infty} I\left(T_{n} \leq t\right) V_{n} $$ is derived, which describes the accumulated damage up to time $t$. The simplest example is a compound Poisson process in which the shock arrival process is Poisson and the shock amounts $\left(V_{n}\right)$ are i.i.d. random variables. As before, the lifetime $T$ is the first time the damage process $\left(X_{t}\right)$ hits the level $S$. If we go one step further and assume that $S$ is not deterministic and fixed, but a random failure level, then we can describe a situation in which the observed damage process does not carry complete information about the (failure) state of the system; the failure can occur at different damage levels $S$. Another way to describe the failure mechanism is the following. Let the accumulated damage up to time $t$ be given by the shock process $X_{t}$ as in (1.2). If the system is up at $t-$ just before $t$, the accumulated damage equals $X_{t-}=x$ and a shock of magnitude $y$ occurs at $t$, then the probability of failure at $t$ is $p(x+y)$, where $p(x)$ is a given $[0,1]$-valued function. In this model failures can only occur at shock times and the accumulated damage determines the failure probability. ### 1.1.3 Different Information Levels It was pointed out above in what way additional information can lead to a reliability model. But it is also important to note that in one and the same model different observation levels are possible, i.e., the amount of actual available information about the state of a system may vary. The following examples will show the effect of different degrees of information. ### 1.1.4 Simpson's Paradox This paradox says that if one compares the death rates in two countries, say A and B , then it is possible that the crude overall death rate in country A is higher than in B although all age-specific death rates in B are higher than in A . This can be transferred to reliability in the following way. Considering a twocomponent parallel system, the failure rate of the system lifetime may increasealthough the component lifetimes have decreasing failure rates. The following proposition, which can be proved by some elementary calculations, yields an example of this. Proposition 1.2. Let $T=T_{1} \vee T_{2}$ with i.i.d. random variables $T_{i}, i=1,2$, following the common distribution $F$, $$ F(t)=1-e^{-u(t)}, t \geq 0, u(t)=\gamma t+\alpha\left(1-e^{-\beta t}\right), \alpha, \beta, \gamma>0 $$ If $2 \alpha e^{\alpha}<\left(\frac{\gamma}{\beta}\right)^{2}<1$, then the failure rate $\lambda$ of the lifetime $T$ increases, whereas the component lifetimes $T_{i}$ have decreasing failure rates. This example shows that it makes a great difference whether only the system lifetime can be observed (aging property: IFR) or additional information about the component lifetimes is available (aging property: DFR). The aging property of the system lifetime of a complex system does not only depend on the joint distribution of the component lifetimes but also, of course, on the structure function. Instead of a two-component parallel system, consider a series system where the component lifetimes have the same distributions as in Proposition 1.2. Then the failure rate of $T_{\text {ser }}=T_{1} \wedge T_{2}$ decreases, whereas $T_{\text {par }}=T_{1} \vee T_{2}$ has an IFR. # 1.1.5 Predictable Lifetime The Wiener process $X=\left(X_{t}\right), t \in \mathbb{R}_{+}$, with positive drift $\mu$ and variance scaling parameter $\sigma$, is a popular damage threshold model. The process $X$ can be represented as $X_{t}=\sigma B_{t}+\mu t$, where $B$ is standard Brownian motion. If one assumes that the failure level $S$ is a fixed known constant, then the lifetime $T=\inf \left\{t \in \mathbb{R}_{+}: X_{t} \geq S\right\}$ follows an inverse Gaussian distribution with a finite mean $E T=S / \mu$. One criticism of this model is that the paths of $X$ are not monotone. As a partial answer, one can respond that maintenance actions also lead to improvements and thus $X$ could be decreasing at some time points. A more severe criticism from the point of view of the available information is the following. It is often assumed that in this model the paths of the damage process can be observed continuously. But this would make the lifetime $T$ a predictable random time (a precise definition follows in Chap. 3), i.e., there is an increasing sequence $\tau_{n}, n \in \mathbb{N}$, of random time points that announces the failure. In this model one could choose $\tau_{n}=\inf \left\{t \in \mathbb{R}_{+}: X_{t} \geq S-1 / n\right\}$, and take $n$ large enough and stop operating the system at $\tau_{n}$ "just" before failure, to carry out some preventive maintenance, cf. Fig. 1.1. This does not usually apply in practical situations. This example shows that one has to distinguish carefully between the different information levels for the model formulation (complete information) and for the actual observation (partial information).
