In practical applications, it is often preferable to compute $1-\mathrm{PA}_{S 0}(t)$ instead of $\mathrm{PA}_{S 0}(t)$. # 2.3.5 Parallel Models with Const. Failure Rates \& Load Sharing In the redundancy structures investigated in the previous sections, all elements were operating under the same conditions. For this type of redundancy, called active (parallel) redundancy, the assumed statistical independence of the elements implies, in particular, that there is no load sharing. This assumption does not arise in many practical applications, for example, at component level or in the presence of power elements. The investigation of the reliability function in the case of load sharing or of other kinds of dependency involves the use of stochastic processes. The situation is simple if one can assume that the failure rate of each element can change only when a failure occurs (e.g. because of load sharing). In this case, for a nonrepairable item (system) the general model for a $k$-out-of-n redundancy is a death process as given in Fig. 2.12 (birth and death as in Fig. 6.13 on p. 215 for the repairable case with constant failure \& repair rates). $Z_{0}, \ldots, Z_{n-k+1}$ are the states of the process. In state $Z_{i}, i$ elements are down. At state $Z_{n-k+1}$ the system is down. Figure 2.12 Diagram of the transition probabilities in $(t, t+\delta t]$ for a $k$-out-of-n redundancy, nonrepairable, constant failure rates during the sojourn time in each state (not necessarily at a state change), ideal failure detection \& switch ( $t$ arbitrary, $\delta t \rightarrow 0$, Markov process, $Z_{n-k+1}$ down state)Assuming $\lambda=$ failure rate of an element in the operating state and $\lambda_{r}=$ failure rate of an element in the reserve state $\left(\lambda_{r} \leq \lambda\right)$, the model of Fig. 2.12 considers in particular the following cases: 1. Active redundancy without load sharing (independent elements) $$ v_{i}=(n-i) \lambda, \quad i=0, \ldots, n-k $$ $\lambda$ is the same for all states. 2. Active redundancy with load sharing $(\lambda=\lambda(i))$ $$ v_{i}=(n-i) \lambda(i), \quad i=0, \ldots, n-k $$ $\lambda(i)$ increases (in general) at each state change. 3. Warm (lightly loaded) redundancy $\left(\lambda_{r}<\lambda\right)$ $$ v_{i}=k \lambda+(n-k-i) \lambda_{r}, \quad i=0, \ldots, n-k $$ $\lambda$ and $\lambda_{r}$ are the same for all states ( $\lambda(i)$ and/or $\lambda_{r}(i)$ for load sharing). 4. Standby (cold) redundancy $\left(\lambda_{r} \equiv 0\right)$ $$ v_{i}=k \lambda, \quad i=0, \ldots, n-k $$ $\lambda$ is the same for all states ( $\lambda(i)$ possible for operating elements). For a standby redundancy, it is assumed that the failure rate in the reserve state is $\equiv 0$ (the reserve elements are switched on when needed). Warm redundancy is somewhere between active and standby ( $0<\lambda_{r}<\lambda$ ). However, it should be noted that the $k$-out-of-n active, warm, or standby redundancy is only the simplest representatives of the general concept of redundancy; series-parallel structures, voting techniques, bridges, and more complex structures are frequently used (see Sections 2.2.6, 2.3.1-2.3.4, and 6.6-6.8 with repair rate $\mu=0$, for some examples); moreover, redundancy can also appear in other forms, e.g. at software level, and the benefit of redundancy can be limited by the involved failure modes as well as by control and switching elements (see Section 6.8 for some examples). According to Appendix A7.5.3.1 (p. 509) and considering Fig. 2.12, let $$ \mathrm{P}_{i}^{\prime}(t)=\operatorname{Pr}\left\{\text { the process is in state } Z_{i} \text { at time } t\right\} $$ be the state probabilities $(i=0, \ldots, n-k+1) . \quad \mathrm{P}_{i}^{\prime}(t)$ is obtained by considering the process at two adjacent time points $t \& t+\delta t$, making use of the memoryless property given by the constant failure rate assumed between consecutive state changes (Eq. (A6.29)). The function $\mathrm{P}_{i}^{\prime}(t)$ satisfies thus the following difference equation $$ \mathrm{P}_{i}^{\prime}(t+\delta t)=\mathrm{P}_{i}^{\prime}(t)\left(1-v_{i} \delta t\right)+\mathrm{P}_{i-1}^{\prime}(t) v_{i-1} \delta t+\mathrm{o} \delta t, \quad i=0, \ldots, n-k+1, v_{-1}=v_{n-k+1}=0 $$where $\mathrm{o}(\delta t)$ denotes a quantity having an order higher than that of $\delta t$ (Eq.(A7.89)). For $\delta t \rightarrow 0$, there follows a system of differential equations describing a death process $$ \begin{aligned} & \dot{\mathrm{P}}_{0}^{\prime}(t)=-\mathrm{v}_{0} \mathrm{P}_{0}^{\prime}(t) \\ & \dot{\mathrm{P}}_{i}^{\prime}(t)=-\mathrm{v}_{i} \mathrm{P}_{i}^{\prime}(t)+\mathrm{v}_{i-1} \mathrm{P}_{i-1}^{\prime}(t), \quad i=1, \ldots, n-k \\ & \dot{\mathrm{P}}_{n-k+1}^{\prime}(t)=\mathrm{v}_{n-k} \mathrm{P}_{n-k}^{\prime}(t) \end{aligned} $$ Assuming the initial conditions $\mathrm{P}_{i}^{\prime}(0)=1$ and $\mathrm{P}_{j}^{\prime}(0)=0$ for $j \neq i$ at $t=0$, the solution (generally obtained using Laplace transform) leads to $\mathrm{P}_{j}^{\prime}(t), j=0, \ldots, n-k+1$. From which, using $\mathrm{P}_{i j}^{\prime}(t) \equiv \mathrm{P}_{j}^{\prime}(t)$ to better emphasize the dependence to the initial condition at $t=0$ (Eq. A7.116)), the reliability function $\mathrm{R}_{S i}(t)$ follows as $$ \mathrm{R}_{S i}(t)=\sum_{j=0}^{n-k} \mathrm{P}_{i j}^{\prime}(t)=1-\mathrm{P}_{i(n-k+1)}^{\prime}(t), \quad i=0, \ldots, n-k $$ and the mean time to failure from Eq. (2.9). Assuming, for instance, $\mathrm{P}_{0}(0)=1$ as initial condition, the Laplace transform of $\mathrm{R}_{S 0}(t)$, $$ \tilde{\mathrm{R}}_{S 0}(s)=\int_{0}^{\infty} \mathrm{R}_{S 0}(t) e^{-s t} d t $$ is given by (with $\tilde{\mathrm{P}}_{n-k+1}^{\prime}(s)$ obtained recursively from Eq. (2.57)) $$ \tilde{\mathrm{R}}_{S 0}(s)=\frac{\left(s+\mathrm{v}_{0}\right) \ldots\left(s+\mathrm{v}_{n-k}\right)-\mathrm{v}_{0} \ldots \mathrm{v}_{n-k}}{s\left(s+\mathrm{v}_{0}\right) \ldots\left(s+\mathrm{v}_{n-k}\right)} $$ The mean time to failure follows then from (Eq. (2.59) with $s=0$ ) $$ M T T F_{S 0}=\tilde{\mathrm{R}}_{S 0}(0) $$ yielding (using $d y / d s=y \cdot d(\ln y) / d s$ with $\mathrm{y}=\left(s+\mathrm{v}_{0}\right) \cdots\left(s+\mathrm{v}_{n-k}\right)$ in the numerator) $$ M T T F_{S 0}=\sum_{i=0}^{n-k} \frac{1}{\mathrm{v}_{i}} $$ Thereby, $S$ stands for system and 0 specify the initial condition $\mathrm{P}_{0}^{\prime}(0)=1$. A $k$-out-of- $n$ standby redundancy (Eq.(2.54)) leads to (Tab. A9.7b,Eq.(A6.102)) $$ \mathrm{R}_{S 0}(t)=\sum_{i=0}^{n-k} \frac{(k \lambda t)^{i}}{i!} e^{-k \lambda t} $$ and (Eqs. $(2.54) \&(2.62))$ $$ M T T F_{S 0}=\frac{n-k+1}{k \lambda} $$ Equation (2.63) gives the probability for up to $n-k$ failures (i.e. $0,1, \ldots, n-k$ ) in $(0, t]$ by constant failure rate $k \lambda$, and shows the relation existing between the Poisson distribution and the occurrence of exponentially distributed events (Appendix A7.2.5).A $k$-out-of- $n$ active redundancy without load sharing yields (Eqs. Failure modes analysis is essential where redundancy appears, among other to identify parts which are in series to the ideal redundancy (in the reliability block diagram), to discover interactions between elements or modules, and to find appropriate measures to avoid failure propagation (secondary failures). Protection against secondary failures can be realized at component level with decoupling elements such as diodes (

Example 2.3 on p. 32), resistors, capacitors. Other possibilities are the introduction of standby elements which are activated at failure of working elements, the use of different technologies for redundant elements, etc. As a general rule, all parts which are essential for basic functions (e. g. interfaces \& monitoring circuitries) have to be designed with care; adherence to appropriate design guidelines is important (Chapter 5), and detection \& localization of hidden failures (faults) as well as avoidance of false alarms is mandatory. The above considerations applies, in particular, for equipment \& systems with high reliability or safety requirements, as used in aerospace, automotive \& nuclear fields. In digital systems, fault tolerance can often be obtained using error correcting codes (e. g. [4.22]). For software, $N$-version and $N$ self configuring programming, realized by different independent designers, is often used for a majority redundancy.# 2.4 Reliability Allocation and Optimization With complex equipment and systems, it is important to allocate reliability goals at subsystem and assembly levels early in the design phase. Such an allocation motivates the design engineer to consider reliability aspects at all system levels. Allocation is simple if the item (system) has no redundancy and its components have constant failure rates. Considering that the system's failure rate $\lambda_{S 0}$ is constant and equal to the sum of the failure rates of its elements (Eq. (2.19)), the allocation of $\lambda_{S 0}$ can be done as follows: 1. Break down the system into elements $E_{1}, \ldots, E_{n}$. 2. Define a complexity factor $k_{i}$ for each element $\left(0 \leq k_{i} \leq 1, k_{1}+\ldots+k_{n}=1\right)$. 3. Determine the duty cycle $d_{i}$ for each element ( $d_{i}=$ operating time of element $E_{i} /$ operating time of the system). 4. Allocate the system's failure rate $\lambda_{S 0}$ among elements $E_{1}, \ldots, E_{n}$ according to $$ \lambda_{i}=\lambda_{S 0} k_{i} / d_{i}, \quad \lambda_{S 0}=\sum_{i=1}^{n} \lambda_{i} d_{i} $$ $k_{1}=\ldots=k_{n}=1 / n$ and $d_{1}=\ldots=d_{n}=1$ yields $\lambda_{i}=\lambda_{S 0} / n$. Often it is necessary to consider cost aspects. Assuming that for element $E_{i}$ the cost relation to the failure rate is of the form $c_{i}=\mathrm{f}_{i}\left(\lambda_{i}\right)$, e. g. $c_{i}=b_{i} / \lambda_{i}$, cost optimization ask for the minimization of $C=\sum_{i} c_{i}=\sum_{i} \mathrm{f}_{i}\left(\lambda_{i}\right)$. For the case of a series system with elements $E_{1}$ and $E_{2}$, this leads to take $\lambda_{1}$ as solution of $$ d\left(\mathrm{f}_{1}\left(\lambda_{1}\right)+\mathrm{f}_{2}\left(\lambda_{S 0}-\lambda_{1}\right)\right) / d \lambda_{1}=0 $$ and $\lambda_{2}=\lambda_{S 0}-\lambda_{1}$. For a series system with elements $E_{1}, \ldots, E_{n}$, the method of the Lagrange multiplier, with $\phi\left(\lambda_{1}, \ldots, \lambda_{n}, \alpha\right)=\mathrm{f}_{1}\left(\lambda_{1}\right)+\ldots+\mathrm{f}_{n}\left(\lambda_{n}\right)+\alpha \cdot\left(\lambda_{S 0}-\lambda_{1}-\ldots-\lambda_{n}\right)$, yields $\lambda_{1}, \ldots, \lambda_{n}$ as solution of following system of $n+1$ algebraic equations $$ \left\{\begin{array}{l} \lambda_{S 0}-\lambda_{1}-\ldots-\lambda_{n}=0 \\ \frac{\partial \phi}{\partial \lambda_{i}}=0, \quad i=1, \ldots, n \end{array}\right. $$ For instance, $c_{i}=\mathrm{f}_{i}\left(\lambda_{i}\right)=b_{i} / \lambda_{i}$ yields $\lambda_{i}=\lambda_{S 0} /\left(1+\sum_{j \neq i} \sqrt{b_{j} / b_{i}}\right), i, j=1, \ldots, n$. Other methods, e. g. based on linear or nonlinear programming can be used. Complexity and duty cycle can be integrated in $c_{i}=\mathrm{f}_{i}\left(\lambda_{i}\right)$, considering also empirical data as well as aspects of technological risk and failure effect (consequence). Should individual element failure rates not be constant and / or the system contain redundancy, allocation reliability goals is more laborious, see e. g. [2.34(1965)]. In the case of repairable series - parallel structures, one can often assume that the failure rate at equipment and systems level is basically fixed by the series elements (Sections 6.6 - 6.7, in particular Eqs. (6.93) \& (6.88),

More complicated is the situation when the reliability function $\mathrm{R}(t)$ is required. For electronic components it is possible to operate with the failure rate, since models and data are often available. This is seldom the case for mechanical parts, although failure rate models for some parts and units (bearings, springs, couplings, etc.) have been developed, see e. g. [2.26, 2.27]. If no information about failure rates is available, a general approach based on the stress-strength method, often supported by finite element analysis, can be used. Let $\xi_{L}(t)$ be the stress (load) and $\xi_{S}(t)$ the strength, a failure occurs at the time $t$ for which $\left|\xi_{L}(t)\right|>\left|\xi_{S}(t)\right|$ holds for the first time. ${ }^{*}$ Often, $\xi_{L}(t)$ and $\xi_{S}(t)$ can be considered as deterministic values and the ratio $\xi_{S}(t) / \xi_{L}(t)$ is the safety factor. In many practical applications, $\xi_{L}(t)$ and $\xi_{S}(t)$ are random variables, often stochastic processes. A practical oriented procedure for the reliability analysis of mechanical systems in these cases is: ${ }^{*}$ 1. Definition of the system and of its associated mission profile. 2. Formulation of failure hypotheses (buckling, bending, etc.) and validation of them using an FMEA/FMECA (Section 2.6); failure hypotheses are often correlated, and this dependence must be identified and considered. 3. Evaluation of the stresses applied with respect to the critical failure hypotheses. 4. Evaluation of the strength limits by considering also dynamic stresses, notches, surface condition, etc. 5. Calculation of the system reliability (Eqs. (2.74) - (2.80)). 6. Elimination of reliability weaknesses and return to step 1 or 2, as necessary. More than one $(n>1)$ failure hypothesis that can be correlated, stresses and strength $>0$; the reliability function is given by $$ \begin{aligned} & \mathrm{R}_{S 0}(t)=\operatorname{Pr}\left\{\left(\xi_{S_{1}}(x)>\xi_{L_{1}}(x)\right) \cap\left(\xi_{S_{2}}(x)>\xi_{L_{2}}(x)\right) \cap \ldots\right. \\ & \cap\left(\xi_{S_{n}}(x)>\xi_{L_{n}}(x)\right), \quad 0<x \leq t\}, \quad \mathrm{R}_{S 0}(0)=1 . \end{aligned} $$ Equation (2.75) can take a complicated form, according to the degree of dependence. However, the method based on the failure rate, introduced in Section 2.2, is easier to be used and works reasonably well in many practical applications dealing with electronic and electromechanical equipment and systems.# 2.6 Failure Modes Analyses Failure rate analyses (Sections 2.1-2.5) basically do not account for the effect (consequence) of a failure. To understand the mechanism of system failures and in order to identify potential weaknesses of a fail-safe concept or a fail-safe procedure, it is necessary to perform a failure modes and effects analysis, at least where redundancy appears and for critical parts of the item considered. Such an analysis is termed FMEA (Failure Modes and Effects Analysis) or FMECA (Failure Modes, Effects, and Criticality Analysis) if also the failure severity is of interest. If failures and defects have to be considered, fault modes should be used, allowing errors/ flaws as possible causes as well. An FMEA/FMECA consists of the systematic analysis of failure (fault) modes, their causes, effects (consequences), and criticality [2.80, 2.81, 2.83, 2.84, 2.86-2.93, 2.96-2.99], including common mode \& common cause as well. For critical applications (e.g. safety related), all parts of the item considered (one after the other) are investigated, in one run or in several steps (design FMEA/FMECA, process FMEA/ FMECA); see e.g. Tables 3.4 \& A10.1 and Section 3.3 for some considerations on failure modes of electronic components. Possibilities to avoid failures (faults) or to minimize (mitigate) their consequence must be analyzed and corresponding corrective (or preventive) actions have to be realized. The criticality describes the severity of the consequence of a failure (fault) and is designated by categories or levels which are function of the risk for damage or performance loss (Fig. 2.13). The FMEA/FMECA is a bottom-up (inductive) procedure, performed as a teamwork with designer \& reliability engineers. The procedure is established in international standards [2.89]. It is easy to understand but can become time-consuming for complex equipment and systems. For this reason it is recommended to concentrate efforts to critical parts, in particular where redundancy appears. Table 2.5 shows a procedure for an FMEA/FMECA. Basic are steps 3 to 8 . Case 2 applies when preventive maintenance can be performed without interruption of the operation or, approximately, during periodic non operating times. ### 4.5 Basic Models for Spare Parts Provisioning Spare parts provisioning is important for systems with long useful life or when short repair times and / or independence from the manufacturer is required (spare part is used here e. g. for line replaceable unit (LRU), see p.116). Basically, a distinction is made between centralized and decentralized logistic support. Also important is to take into account whether spare parts are repairable or not. This section presents the basic models for the provision of nonrepairable and of repairable spare parts. For nonrepairable spare parts, the cases of centralized and decentralized logistic support are considered in order to quantify the advantage of a centralized logistic support with respect to a decentralized one. More general maintenance strategies are discussed in Section 4.6, and cost specific aspects in Sections 4.5-4.7. ### 4.5.1 Centralized Logistic Support, Nonrepairable Spare Parts In centralized logistic support, spare parts are stocked at one place. The basic problem can be formulated as follows,at time $t=0$, the first part is put into operation, it fails at time $t=\tau_{1}$ and is replaced (in a negligible time) by a second part which fails at time $t=\tau_{1}+\tau_{2}$ and so forth; asked is the number $n$ of parts which must be stocked in order that the requirement for parts during the cumulative operating time $T$ is met with a given (fixed) probability $\gamma$. To answer this question, the smallest integer $n$ must be found for which $$ \operatorname{Pr}\left\{\tau_{1}+\ldots+\tau_{n}>T\right\} \geq \gamma $$ holds. In general, $\tau_{1}, \ldots, \tau_{n}$ are assumed to be independent positive random variables with the same distribution function $\mathrm{F}(x)(\mathrm{F}(0)=0$, density $\mathrm{f}(x)) \&$ finite mean $\mathrm{E}\left[\tau_{i}\right]=\mathrm{E}[\tau]=$ MTTF $\& \operatorname{Var}\left[\tau_{i}\right]=\operatorname{Var}[\tau]$. If the number of parts is calculated from $$ n=T / M T T F $$ the requirement can only be covered (for $T$ large) with a probability of 0.5 . Thus, more than $T / M T T F$ parts are necessary to meet the requirement with $\gamma>0.5$. According to Eq. (A7.12), valid for renewal processes, the probability as per Eq. (4.9) can be expressed by the $(n-1)$ th convolution of the distribution function $\mathrm{F}(t)$ with itself, i. e. $$ \begin{aligned} & \operatorname{Pr}\left\{\tau_{1}+\ldots+\tau_{n}>T\right\}=1-\mathrm{F}_{n}(T) \\ & \text { with } \quad \mathrm{F}_{1}(T)=\mathrm{F}(T) \quad \text { and } \quad \mathrm{F}_{n}(T)=\int_{0}^{T} \mathrm{~F}_{n-1}(T-x) \mathrm{f}(x) d x, \quad n>1 \end{aligned} $$ Of the distribution functions $\mathrm{F}(x)$ used in reliability theory, a closed, simple form for the function $\mathrm{F}_{n}(x)$ exists only for the exponential, gamma, and normal distribution functions, yielding a Poisson, gamma, and normal distribution, respectively. Results of Sections 4.5.1-4.5.3, in particular those on decentralized logistic support, can be extended to cover the case of systems with different spare parts.# 4.6 Maintenance Strategies Maintenance strategies can be very different according to the objective to be reached (type of maintenance policies, minimization of system down time or spare parts, availability maximization by given cost and / or logistic support, etc.). Among possible maintenance strategies [2.34, 4.0, 4.1, 4.2, 4.6, 4.8, 4.14, 4.18, 4.30, 6.3, A7.4(1962)], this section unifies and extends basic repair/replacement policies. Preliminary investigations on a new, approach for mission oriented high safety systems (Active System Control ASC, superimposing a periodic check to preventive maintenance) are introduced in [4.26], with practical realizations in [4.4], see also [5.77]. Cost aspects related to maintenance strategies and to spare parts provisioning are considered in this section and in Section 4.7. For undetected fault times one can refer to Eqs. (A6.30) and (6.223) for a practical application. In the following it is assumed that the item considered is new at $t=0$, its failurefree time $\tau>0$ has distribution function $\mathrm{F}(x)$, density $\mathrm{f}(x)$, and finite mean $\mathrm{E}[\tau] \&$ variance $\operatorname{Var}[\tau]$. Furthermore, in Sections 4.6.1 \& 4.6.2, repairs/replacements are performed in a negligible time. Section 4.6.1 considers the case in which the item is as-good-as-new after each maintenance action, planned (preventive maintenance) or at failure (repair). In section 4.6.2, the item is as-good-as-new only after planned maintenance actions, but as-bad-as-old after repairs (minimal repair at failure). Considerations with finite repair/replacement times are in Sections 4.6.3 \& 6.8.2. ${ }^{+)}$ ### 4.6.1 Complete renewal at each maintenance action This section assumes that each maintenance action, planned or at failure, is of negligible length and brings the item considered to as-good-as-new, as a whole, yielding a renewal point for the underlying point process. ${ }^{*+1}$ Among possible strategies to avoid wear-out failures or effects of sudden failures, replacements can be performed, basically, ${ }^{*++1}$ (a) at a given (fixed) operating time $T_{P M}$ or at failure if the operating time is shorter than $T_{P M}$ (age replacement, Fig. 4.5a), (b) at given (fixed) time points $T_{P M}, 2 T_{P M}, \ldots$ or at failure (block replacement, Fig. 4.5b), (fix) only at given time points $T_{P M}, 2 T_{P M}, \ldots$ (fix replacement, Fig. 4.5c), (of) only at failure (ordinary renewal process without truncation). Example 6.3 Show that for a repairable one-item structure in continuous operation (Assumption (6.1)), the limit $$ \lim _{t \rightarrow \infty} \mathrm{PA}_{S}(t)=P A_{S}=\frac{M T T F}{M T T F+M T T R} $$ is valid for any distribution function $\mathrm{F}(x), \mathrm{F}_{A}(x), \mathrm{G}(x), \mathrm{G}_{A}(x)$ satisfying conditions (6.8) (6.12), and for which $\mathrm{f}(x), \mathrm{f}_{A}(x), \mathrm{g}(x), \mathrm{g}_{A}(x)$ go to 0 as $x \rightarrow \infty$. ## Solution Using the renewal density theorem Eq. (A7.31), by considering Fig. A7.3 (p. 491), it follows that $$ \lim _{t \rightarrow \infty} \mathrm{~h}_{\text {duu }}(t)=\lim _{t \rightarrow \infty} \mathrm{~h}_{\text {dud }}(t)=\frac{1}{M T T F+M T T R} $$ Furthermore, applying the key renewal theorem Eq.(A7.29) to $\mathrm{PA}_{S}(t)$ given by Eq.(6.42) yields $$ \begin{aligned} \lim _{t \rightarrow \infty} \mathrm{PA}_{S}(t) & =p\left(1-1+\frac{\int_{0}^{\infty}(1-\mathrm{F}(x)) d x}{M T T F+M T T R}\right)+(1-p) \frac{\int_{0}^{\infty}(1-\mathrm{F}(x)) d x}{M T T F+M T T R} \\ & =p \frac{M T T F}{M T T F+M T T R}+(1-p) \frac{M T T F}{M T T F+M T T R}=\frac{M T T F}{M T T F+M T T R} \end{aligned} $$ The limits $1 /(M T T F+M T T R)$ and $M T T F /(M T T F+M T T R)$ can also be obtained from the final value theorem of the Laplace transform (Table A9.7a), considering for $s \rightarrow 0$ $$ \begin{array}{ll} \hat{\mathrm{f}}(s)=1-s M T T F+\mathrm{o}(s), & \hat{\mathrm{f}}_{A}(s)=1-s \mathrm{E}\left[\tau_{0}\right]+\mathrm{o}(s) \\ \hat{\mathrm{g}}(s)=1-s M T T R+\mathrm{o}(s), & \hat{\mathrm{g}}_{A}(s)=1-s \mathrm{E}\left[\tau_{0}^{\prime}\right]+\mathrm{o}(s) \end{array} $$ with $\mathrm{o}(s)$ as per Eq. (A7.89) and using Eq. (A7.50). When considering $\hat{\mathrm{g}}(\lambda)$ for availability calculations, the approximation given by Eq. (6.54) often leads to $P A_{S}=1$, already by simple redundancy structures. In these cases, Eq. (6.113) has to be used. Supplementary results: For $t \rightarrow \infty, 1 /(M T T F+M T T R)$ holds also for $h_{\text {udu }}(t), h_{\text {udd }}(t), h_{\text {ud }}(t)$ $=p h_{\text {udu }}(t)+(1-p) h_{\text {udd }}(t) \& h_{d u}(t)=p h_{\text {duu }}(t)+(1-p) h_{\text {dud }}(t)$ (see also Eqs. (A7.60) \& (A7.177)). In the case of constant failure \& repair rates $\left(\lambda(x)=\lambda \equiv \lambda_{S 0} \& \mu(x)=\mu \equiv \mu_{S}\right)$ Eq. (6.42) yields (Eq. (A7.50), Table A9.7b) $$ \mathrm{PA}_{S}(t)=\frac{\mu}{\lambda+\mu}+\left(p-\frac{\mu}{\lambda+\mu}\right) e^{-(\lambda+\mu) t}=P A_{S}+\left(p-P A_{S}\right) e^{-(\lambda+\mu) t} $$ Thus, for this important case, the convergence of $\mathrm{PA}_{S}(t)$ toward $P A_{S}=\mu /(\lambda+\mu)$is exponential with a time constant $1 /(\lambda+\mu)<1 / \mu=M T T R$. In particular, for $p=1$, i. e. for $\mathrm{PA}_{S}(0)=1$ and $\mathrm{PA}_{S}(t) \equiv \mathrm{PA}_{S 0}(t)$, it follows that $$ \mathrm{PA}_{S 0}(t)-P A_{S}=\frac{\lambda}{\lambda+\mu} e^{-(\lambda+\mu) t} \leq \frac{\lambda}{\mu} e^{-\mu t}=\lambda M T T R e^{-t / M T T R} $$ Generalizing the distribution function $\mathrm{G}(x)$ of the repair time and/or $\mathrm{F}(x)$ of the failure-free time, $\mathrm{PA}_{S 0}(t)$ can oscillate damped (as in general for the renewal density $\mathrm{h}(t)$ given by Eq. (A7.18)). However, for constant failure rate $\lambda$ and providing $\lambda M T T R$ sufficiently small and some rather weak conditions on the density $\mathrm{g}(x)$, lower and upper bounds on $\mathrm{PA}_{S 0}(t)$ can be found [6.25] $$ \mathrm{PA}_{S 0}(t) \geq \frac{1}{1+\lambda M T T R}-c_{l} \frac{\lambda M T T R}{1+\lambda M T T R} e^{-(\lambda+1 / M T T R) t}, \quad t \geq 0 $$ and $$ \mathrm{PA}_{S 0}(t) \leq \frac{1}{1+\lambda M T T R}+c_{u} \frac{\lambda M T T R}{1+\lambda M T T R} e^{-(\lambda+1 / M T T R) t}, \quad t \geq 0 $$ $c_{l}=1$ holds for many practical applications ( $\lambda M T T R \ll 0.1$ ). Sufficient conditions for $c_{u}=1$ are given in [6.25]. However, conditions on $c_{u}$ are less important as on $c_{l}$, since $\mathrm{PA}_{S 0}(t) \leq 1$ is always true. The case of a gamma distribution with density $\mathrm{g}(x)=\alpha^{\beta} x^{\beta-1} e^{-\alpha x} / \Gamma(\beta)$, mean $\beta / \alpha$, and shape parameter $\beta \geq 3$, leads, for instance, to $\left|\mathrm{PA}_{S 0}(t)-P A_{S}\right| \leq \lambda M T T R e^{-t / M T T R}$ at least for $t \geq 3 M T T R=3 \beta / \alpha\right.$. # 6.2.5 Steady-State Behavior For $$ p=\frac{M T T F}{M T T F+M T T R}, \quad \mathrm{~F}_{A}(x)=\frac{1}{M T T F} \int_{0}^{x}(1-\mathrm{F}(y)) d y, \quad \mathrm{G}_{A}(x)=\frac{1}{M T T R} \int_{0}^{x}(1-\mathrm{G}(y)) d y $$ as initial conditions / distribution at $t=0$, the alternating renewal process describing the time behavior of a one-item repairable structure is stationary (in steadystate), see Appendix A7.3. Example 6.4 Show that for a repairable one-item structure in steady-state, i.e. with $p, \mathrm{~F}_{A}(x)$, and $\mathrm{G}_{A}(x)$ as per Eq. (A7.50) and (6.57) yields $$ \begin{aligned} & \tilde{\mathrm{PA}}_{S}(s)=\frac{M T T F}{M T T F+M T T R}\left(\frac{1}{s}-\frac{1-\tilde{\mathrm{f}}(s)}{s^{2} M T T F}+\frac{\frac{1-\tilde{\mathrm{f}}(s)}{s M T T F} \cdot \tilde{\mathrm{~g}}(s)}{1-\tilde{\mathrm{f}}(s) \cdot \tilde{\mathrm{g}}(s)} \cdot \frac{1-\tilde{\mathrm{f}}(s)}{s}\right) \\ & +\frac{M T T R}{M T T F+M T T R} \cdot \frac{\frac{1-\tilde{\mathrm{g}}(s)}{s M T T R}}{1-\tilde{\mathrm{f}}(s) \cdot \tilde{\mathrm{g}}(s)} \cdot \frac{1-\tilde{\mathrm{f}}(s)}{s}, \end{aligned} $$ and finally $$ \tilde{\mathrm{PA}}_{S}(s)=\frac{M T T F}{M T T F+M T T R}\left(\frac{1}{s}-\frac{1-\tilde{\mathrm{f}}(s)}{s^{2} M T T F}\right)+\frac{[1-\tilde{\mathrm{f}}(s)][\tilde{\mathrm{g}}(s)-\tilde{\mathrm{f}}(s) \cdot \tilde{\mathrm{g}}(s)+1-\tilde{\mathrm{g}}(s)]}{s^{2}(M T T F+M T T R)[1-\tilde{\mathrm{f}}(s) \cdot \tilde{\mathrm{g}}(s)]} ; $$ from which $$ \tilde{\mathrm{PA}}_{S}(s)=\frac{M T T F}{M T T F+M T T R} \cdot \frac{1}{s}=\frac{P A_{S}}{s} $$ and thus $\mathrm{PA}_{S}(t)=P A_{S}$ for all $t \geq 0$. ### 6.3 Systems without Redundancy The reliability block diagram of a system without redundancy (series structure/ system/model) consists of the series connection of all its elements $E_{1}, \ldots, E_{n}$, see Fig. 6.4. Each element $E_{i}$ in Fig. 6.4 is characterized by the distribution functions $\mathrm{F}_{i}(x)$ for the failure-free time and $\mathrm{G}_{i}(x)$ for the repair time. ${ }^{*}$ ### 6.3.1 Series Structure with Constant Failure and Repair Rates In this section, constant failure and repair rates are assumed, i. e. $$ \mathrm{F}_{i}(x)=1-e^{-\lambda_{i} x}, \quad x>0, \mathrm{~F}_{i}(x)=0 \text { for } x \leq 0 $$ and $$ \mathrm{G}_{i}(x)=1-e^{-\mu_{i} x}, \quad x>0, \mathrm{G}_{i}(x)=0 \text { for } x \leq 0 $$ [^0] [^0]: *) It can be noted that for a series structure, assumption (6.2) of no further failures at system down implies also assumption (6.3) of only one repair crew. Figure 6.4 Reliability block diagram for a series structure (system without redundancy) holds for $i=1, \ldots, n$. Because of Eqs. (6.58) and (6.59), the stochastic behavior of the system is described by a time-homogeneous Markov process (Appendix A7.5). Let $Z_{0}$ be the system up state and $Z_{i}$ the state in which element $E_{i}$ is down. Taking assumption (6.2) into account, i. e. of no further failures at system down, the corresponding diagram of transition probabilities in $(t, t+\delta t]$ (p.503) is given by Fig. 6.5 (see also footnote on p. 189). Equations of Table 6.2 can be used to obtain the expressions for the reliability function, point availability and interval reliability. With $U=\left\{Z_{0}\right\}, \widetilde{U}=\left\{Z_{1}, \ldots, Z_{n}\right\}$ and the transition rates according to Fig. 6.5, the reliability function (see Table 6.2 on p. 173 for notation) follows from $$ \mathrm{R}_{S 0}(t)=e^{-\lambda_{S 0} t}, \quad \text { with } \quad \lambda_{S 0}=\sum_{i=1}^{n} \lambda_{i} $$ Figure 6.5 Diagram of the transition probabilities in $(t, t+\delta t]$ for a repairable series structure with elements $E_{1}, \ldots, E_{n}$, constant failure \& repair rates $\lambda_{i} \& \mu_{i}$, ideal failure detection and switch, no further failures at system down (and thus also only one repair crew; $Z_{1}, \ldots, Z_{n}$ down states (absorbing for reliability calculation), arbitrary $t, \delta t \downarrow 0$, Markov process)and thus, for the mean time to failure, $$ M T T F_{S 0}=1 / \lambda_{S 0} $$ The point availability is given by $$ \mathrm{PA}_{S 0}(t)=\mathrm{P}_{00}(t) $$ with $\mathrm{P}_{00}(t)$ from (Table 6.2) $$ \begin{aligned} & \mathrm{P}_{00}(t)=e^{-\lambda_{S 0} t}+\sum_{i=1}^{n} \int_{0}^{t} \lambda_{i} e^{-\lambda_{S 0} x} \mathrm{P}_{i 0}(t-x) d x \\ & \mathrm{P}_{i 0}(t)=\int_{0}^{t} \mu_{i} e^{-\mu_{i} x} \mathrm{P}_{00}(t-x) d x, \quad i=1, \ldots, n \end{aligned} $$ yielding for the Laplace transform (Table A9.7) of $\mathrm{PA}_{S 0}(t)$ $$ \tilde{\mathrm{PA}}_{S 0}(s)=\tilde{\mathrm{P}}_{00}(s)=\frac{1}{s\left(1+\sum_{i=1}^{n} \frac{\lambda_{i}}{s+\mu_{i}}\right)} $$ From Eq. (6.64) there follows the asymptotic \& steady-state value of the point and average availability $P A_{S}=A A_{S}=\lim _{s \rightarrow 0} s \tilde{\mathrm{PA}}_{S 0}(s)$ $$ P A_{S}=A A_{S}=\frac{1}{1+\sum_{i=1}^{n} \frac{\lambda_{i}}{\mu_{i}}} \approx 1-\sum_{i=1}^{n} \frac{\lambda_{i}}{\mu_{i}} $$ Because of the constant failure rate of all elements, the interval reliability can be directly obtained from Eq. (6.27) by $$ \operatorname{IR}_{S 0}(t, t+\theta)=\mathrm{PA}_{S 0}(t) e^{-\lambda_{S 0} \theta} $$ with the asymptotic \& steady-state value $$ \operatorname{IR}_{S}(\theta)=P A_{S} e^{-\lambda_{S 0} \theta} $$ where (Eq. Example 6.5 A system consists of elements $E_{1}$ to $E_{4}$ which are necessary for the fulfillment of the required function (series structure). Assume constant failure rates $\lambda_{1}=10^{-3} \mathrm{~h}^{-1}, \lambda_{2}=0.5 \cdot 10^{-3} \mathrm{~h}^{-1}, \lambda_{3}=$ $10^{-4} \mathrm{~h}^{-1} \& \lambda_{4}=2 \cdot 10^{-3} \mathrm{~h}^{-1}$, and that for all elements the repair time is lognormally distributed with parameters $\lambda=0.5 \mathrm{~h}^{-1}$ and $\sigma=0.6$. Considering that no further failures can occur at system down (the system is disconnected), give the reliability function for a mission of duration $t=168 \mathrm{~h}$, the mean time to failure, the asymptotic \& steady-state values of the point and average availability, and the asymptotic \& steady-state values of the interval reliability for $\theta=12 \mathrm{~h}$. ## Solution The system failure rate is $\lambda_{S 0}=\lambda_{1}+\lambda_{2}+\lambda_{3}+\lambda_{4}=36 \cdot 10^{-4} \mathrm{~h}^{-1}$, according to Eq. (6.60). The reliability function follows as $\mathrm{R}_{S 0}(t)=e^{-0.0036 t}$, from which $R_{S 0}(168 \mathrm{~h}) \approx 0.55$. The mean time to failure is $M T T F_{S 0}=1 / \lambda_{S 0} \approx 278 \mathrm{~h}$. The mean time to repair is obtained from Table A6.1 as $\mathrm{E}\left[\tau^{\prime}\right]=\left(e^{\sigma^{2} / 2}\right) / \lambda=M T T R \approx 2.4 \mathrm{~h}$. For the asymptotic \& steady-state values of the point and average availability as well as for the interval reliability for $\theta=12 \mathrm{~h}$ it follows from Eqs. (6.71) and (6.67) that $P A_{S}=A A_{S}=1 /\left(1+36 \cdot 10^{-4} \cdot 2.4\right) \approx 0.991$ and $\operatorname{IR}_{S}(12) \approx 0.991 \cdot e^{-0.0036 \cdot 12} \approx 0.95$ ### 6.3.3 Series Structure with Arbitrary Failure \& Repair Rates Generalization of repair and failure-free time distribution functions leads to a nonregenerative stochastic process. This model can be investigated using supplementary variables, or by approximating the distribution functions of the failure-free time in such a way that the involved stochastic process can be reduced to a regenerative process. Using for the approximation an Erlang distribution function (Eq. (A6.102)) leads to a semi-Markov process (Appendix A7.6). As an example, let's consider the case of a two-element series structure ( $E_{1}, E_{2}$ ) and assume that the repair times are arbitrary, with densities $\mathrm{g}_{1}(x)$ and $\mathrm{g}_{2}(x)$, and the failure-free times have densities $$ \mathrm{f}_{1}(x)=\lambda_{1}^{2} x e^{-\lambda_{1} x}, \quad x>0, \mathrm{f}_{1}(x)=0 \text { for } x \leq 0 $$ and $$ \mathrm{f}_{2}(x)=\lambda_{2} e^{-\lambda_{2} x}, \quad x>0, \mathrm{f}_{2}(x)=0 \text { for } x \leq 0 $$ Equation (6.73) is the density of the sum of two exponentially distributed random time intervals with density $\lambda_{1} e^{-\lambda_{1} x}$ (see Eq. (A6.102)). Under these assumptions, the two-element series structure corresponds to a 1-out-of-2 standby redundancy $E_{1^{\prime}} \& E_{1^{\prime \prime}}$ with constant failure rate $\lambda_{1}$ and repair only at the failure of both elements $E_{1^{\prime}} \& E_{1^{\prime \prime}}\left(\mathrm{g}_{1}(x)\right.$ is the density of the repair function for $E_{1^{\prime}} \& E_{1^{\prime \prime}}$ ), in series with an element $\left(E_{2}\right)$ with constant failure rate $\lambda_{2}$. It consists of two elements $E_{1}$ and $E_{2}$, one of which is in the operating state and the other in reserve, when not under repair or waiting for repair. When a failure occurs, one element is repaired while the other continues operation. The system is down when an element fails when the other is being repaired or waiting for repair. Assuming ideal failure detection \& switching, the reliability block diagram is a parallel connection of elements $E_{1} \& E_{2}$ (Fig. 6.7). Investigations in this section are based on assumptions (6.1)-(6.7). This implies that the system has only one repair crew, repair of a redundant element is performed on-line \& begins at failure occurrence, and repaired elements are as-good-as-new. Distribution functions of repair and failure-free times are generalized step by step, beginning with exponential, up to the case in which the process involved has only one regeneration state. Preventive maintenance, switching, incomplete coverage \& common cause failures are considered in Section 6.8, travel time on pp. 204 \& 528. ### 6.4.1 1-out-of-2 Redundancy with Const. Failure \& Repair Rates Because of the constant failure and repair rates, the time behavior of the 1-out-of-2 redundancy can be described by a time-homogeneous Markov process. Example 6.8 Let the density $\mathrm{g}(x)$ of the repair time $\tau^{\prime}$ of a system with constant failure rate $\lambda>0$ be continuous and assume furthermore that $\lambda \mathrm{E}\left[\tau^{\prime}\right]=\lambda M T T R \ll 1$ and $\lambda \operatorname{Var}\left[\tau^{\prime}\right]<M T T R$. Investigate the quantity $\tilde{\mathrm{g}}(\lambda)$ for $\lambda \rightarrow 0$. ## Solution For $\lambda \rightarrow 0, \lambda M T T R<<1 \& \lambda \operatorname{Var}\left[\tau^{\prime}\right]<M T T R$, the 3 first terms of the series expansion of $e^{-\lambda t}$ lead to $$ \tilde{\mathrm{g}}(\lambda)=\int_{0}^{\infty} \mathrm{g}(t) e^{-\lambda t} d t=\int_{0}^{\infty} \mathrm{g}(t)\left(1-\lambda t+\frac{(\lambda t)^{2}}{2}\right) d t=1-\lambda \mathrm{E}\left[\tau^{\prime}\right]+\mathrm{E}\left[\tau^{\prime 2}\right] \lambda^{2} / 2 $$ From this, follows the approximate expression (Eq. (A6.45)) $$ \tilde{\mathrm{g}}(\lambda)=1-\lambda M T T R+\lambda^{2}\left(M T T R^{2}+\operatorname{Var}\left[\tau^{\prime}\right]\right) / 2 $$ In many practical applications, $$ \tilde{\mathrm{g}}(\lambda)=1-\lambda M T T R $$ is a sufficiently good approximation, however not in calculating steady-state availability (Eq. (6.114) would give for Eq. (6.110) $P A_{S}=1$, thus Eq. (6.113) has to be used). Example 6.9 In a 1-out-of-2 warm redundancy with $E_{1}=E_{2}=E$ let the failure rates in the operating and reserve state be constant ( $\lambda$ and $\lambda_{r}$ ). For the repair time let us assume that it is distributed according to $\mathrm{G}(x)=1-e^{-\mu^{\prime}(x-\psi)}$ for $x>\psi$ and $\mathrm{G}(x)=0$ for $x \leq \psi$, with $M T T R \equiv 1 / \mu>\psi$. Assuming $\lambda \psi \ll 1$, investigate the influence of $\psi$ on the mean time to failure $M T T R_{S 0}$ and on the asymptotic \& steady-state value of the point availability $P A_{S}$. ## Solution With $$ \tilde{\mathrm{g}}(\lambda)=\int_{\psi}^{\infty} \mu^{\prime} e^{-\mu^{\prime}(t-\psi)-\lambda t} d t=\frac{\mu^{\prime}}{\lambda+\mu^{\prime}} e^{-\lambda \psi}=\frac{\mu^{\prime}}{\lambda+\mu^{\prime}}(1-\lambda \psi) $$ and considering $M T T R=\int_{0}^{\infty} x \mathrm{~g}(x) d x=\int_{\psi}^{\infty} x \mu^{\prime} e^{-\mu^{\prime}(x-\psi)} d x=\psi+\frac{1}{\mu^{\prime}}=\frac{1}{\mu}$; i. e. $\mu^{\prime}=\mu /(1-\mu \psi)$ and thus $\tilde{\mathrm{g}}(\lambda)=\mu(1-\lambda \psi)^{\prime} /(\lambda+\mu(1-\lambda \psi))$, Eq. (6.108) and Eq. (6.110) lead to the approximate expressions $$ M T T F_{S 0, \psi>0}=\frac{2 \lambda+\lambda_{r}+\mu(1-\lambda \psi)}{\lambda\left(\lambda+\lambda_{r}\right)} $$ and $$ P A_{S, \psi>0}=\frac{\mu\left(\lambda+\lambda_{r}+\mu(1-\lambda \psi)\right)}{\left(\lambda+\lambda_{r}\right)\left(\lambda+\mu(1-\lambda \psi)\right)+\mu^{2}(1-\lambda \psi)}=1-\frac{\lambda\left(\lambda+\lambda_{r}\right)(1-\mu \psi))}{\mu\left(\lambda+\lambda_{r}+\mu(1-\lambda \psi)\right)} $$ On the other hand, $\psi=0$ leads to $1-\tilde{\mathrm{g}}(\lambda)=\lambda /(\lambda+\mu)$ and thus (Eqs. (6.92) and (6.87)) $$ M T T F_{S 0, \psi=0}=\frac{2 \lambda+\lambda_{r}+\mu}{\lambda\left(\lambda+\lambda_{r}\right)} \quad \text { and } \quad P A_{S, \psi=0}=\frac{\mu\left(\lambda+\lambda_{r}+\mu\right)}{(\lambda+\mu)\left(\lambda+\lambda_{r}\right)+\mu^{2}} $$ Assuming $\mu \gg \lambda, \lambda_{r}$, yields (considering $\lambda \psi<\lambda / \mu<<1$ ) $$ \frac{M T T F_{S 0, \psi>0}}{M T T F_{S 0, \psi=0}}=1-\lambda \psi \quad \text { and } \quad \frac{P A_{S, \psi>0}}{P A_{S, \psi=0}}=1+\lambda \psi \frac{\lambda+\lambda_{r}}{\mu}=1 $$Equation (6.115) allows the conclusion to be made that, for $\lambda$ MTTR $<<1$, the shape of the distribution function of the repair time has (for unchanged MTTR) a small influence on results at system level, in particular on the mean time to failure $M T T F_{S 0}$ and on the asymptotic \& steady-state point and average availability $P A_{S}=A A_{S}$ of a 1-out-of-2 redundancy. Above conclusion can often be extended to more complex structures.

Fault coverage is defined as the proportion of faults that can be detected and localized under given conditions. ${ }^{+)}$ It applies in particular to redundant structures. A fault coverage greater as 0.95 is often required for complex equipment. Lacks in the detection and/or localization lead to hidden faults, often not covered by automatic or semi-automatic diagnosis, and thus localizable only at a repair or preventive maintenance. Hidden faults can cause a serious reduction of the advantage given by a redundancy, see e.g. Eqs. (6.220) \& (6.222) or (6.228) \& (6.229)). As a general rule, fault coverage has to be investigated on a case-by-case basis, considering the aspects of false detection and /or localization (or alternatively false alarm), and no detection and/or localization possible (or alternatively no alarm emitted). Following an illustrative example, this section discusses some basic models for incomplete coverage. ${ }^{*+}$ A way to compensate incomplete coverage is given at the end of the 3 th footnote on this page and illustrated with 2 new models $\mathbf{c} \& \mathbf{d}$ of Table 6.12 (p. 256), implying the realization of an operation monitoring as per Table 4.1 with suitable BIT/BITE (see remarks on pp. $250 \& 255$ ). However, for critical applications, majority redundancy remains the best way to compensate incomplete coverage (in a 2-out-of-3 redundancy, the first failure is captured on line and no switch is necessary, see pp. 49, 31, 222-25). Consider first the case of a 1-out-of-2 active redundancy with two different elements $E_{1} \& E_{2}$, and assume that failures of $E_{1}$ can be localized and repaired only at a repair of $E_{2}$ or at a preventive maintenance (PM). (6.209); $\lambda_{0}=\lambda_{\sigma}=0$ yields results as for an ideal switch.# 6.8.6 Fault Tolerant Reconfigurable Systems Fault tolerant (resilient) structures are able to detect and localize faults (failures \& defects) and reconfigure themselves to continue operation with minimum loss of performance and / or safety (graceful degradation); see e. g. [2.36, 4.4, 4.26, 5.77]. Such a characteristic must be built in during design \& development. Typical examples of fault tolerant systems are safety circuits and power \& telecommunication networks. Following a short discussion on ideal reconfiguration, this section deals with reconfiguration occurring at given fixed times (phased-mission systems) or at failure by considering also imperfect switching in Section 6.8.6.3. Investigation is based on tools introduced in Appendix A7, summarized in Table 6.2; constant failure and repair rates are assumed, yielding to Markov processes. Procedures are illustrated on a case-by-case basis using diagrams of transition rates. ### 6.8.6.1 Ideal Case Each redundant structure belongs to a fault tolerant reconfigurable structure and must be validated for this purpose during design \& development, for instance with an FMEA (Section 2.6). For the redundant structures investigated in Sections 2.2, 2.3.1-2.3.5, 6.4-6.7 and Appendix A7, independent elements (p.52), ideal fault coverage, ideal switching, and no reduction of system performance at failure of a redundant element was assumed. Because of these assumptions, investigations often lead to series - parallel structures (Sections $6.6 \& 6.7$ ). Imperfect switching, incomplete coverage, and items (systems) with more than two states or failure modes are considered in Sections 2.3.6, 6.8.3-6.8.5, 6.8.6.3. Sections 6.8.6.2 and 6.8.6.3 investigate time and failure censored reconfiguration, and Section 6.8.6.4 considers reward \& frequency/duration aspects. In addition, Sections 6.8.7-6.8.9 deal with common cause failures, basic considerations on reliability networks, and a general procedure for complex repairable systems. Alternative investigation methods for complex systems and aspects of human reliability \& risk management are introduced in Sections $6.9,6.10$ and 6.11 , respectively. ### 6.8.6.2 Time Censored Reconfiguration (Phased-Mission Systems) In some practical applications, systems are used for different required functions. If each required function can be considered separately from one another, investigation is performed by considering a reliability block diagram (if it exist) for each required function (p. 29). Otherwise, if mission phases follow each other, investigation must consider the system reconfiguration at the end of each phase and one define this as a phased-mission system. Investigation of phased-mission systems can be more time-consuming as stated e. g. in [2.7,2.18,6.24,6.33,6.41], dealing with binary state assignment (basically limited to totally independent elements (p. 52)),considering time dependent failure or repair rates (breaking the Markov property), using semi-Markov processes (of limited validity), or missing Assumption 4 below (important when transferring state probabilities at the end of phase $k$ to initial probabilities for phase $k+1$ ). A lower bound $R_{S 0_{I}}$ on the reliability $R_{S 0}$ for the whole mission is obtained by connecting the reliability block diagrams for each phase in series for the whole mission duration. An upper bound on $R_{S 0}$ is given by the smaller of the reliability for each phase, taken separately, by assuming that all elements involved are as-good-as-new at begin of the phase considered; thus, $$ R_{S 0_{I}} \leq R_{S 0} \leq R_{S 0_{u}}=\min \left(R_{S 0, k}\right)^{*)} \quad k=1, \ldots, n \text { (for } n \text { phases) } $$ Examples 6.23-6.25 illustrate basic aspects. For the availability, Eq.(6.246) applies. Following some general assumptions in Point (i), a practice oriented procedure for reliability and availability analysis of repairable phased-mission systems, which considers standby redundancy and arbitrary repair strategy, is given in Point (ii). (i) General assumptions: 1. Failure \& repair rates $\left(\lambda_{i} \& \mu_{i}\right)$ of all elements are constant during the sojourn time in any state within each phase, but can change (stepwise) at a state (or phase) change because of change in configuration, component use, stress, repair strategy or other; for all elements it holds that $\lambda_{i} \ll \mu_{i}$. 2. At the beginning of the phased-mission all elements are as-good-as-new. 3. Phase duration $T_{1}, \ldots, T_{n}$ are given (fixed) values, each of them so large that asymptotic \& steady-state values for availability can be assumed for each phase $\left(T_{1}, \ldots, T_{n} \gg \max \left(10 / \mu_{i}\right)\right.$ for all elements (Section 6.2.5 \& Eq. (6.88)). 4. For availability investigation, not used elements in a phase are either as-good-as-new and put in standby (failure rate $\lambda \equiv 0$ ) at begin of the phase, or repaired (Assumption 3) and then put in standby (repair priority on elements used); for reliability investigation, down states at system level are absorbing states and the above rule holds for elements which have not caused system down. 5. The system has only one repair crew and no further failures can occur at system down; system down is an absorbing state for reliability; for availability, the system is restored to an operating state according to a given repair strategy. 6. Fault coverage, switch \& logistic support are ideal, no preventive maintenance. 7. For each phase, a reliability block diagram exists. Reduction of above assumptions is possible, for instance, on the basis of the models discussed in Sections 6.8.2-6.8.5. Thus, $$ \mathrm{R}_{S 0}\left(T_{1}\right)=\mathrm{P}_{1,0}^{-}\left(T_{1}\right)=e^{-\lambda_{1} T_{1}} \quad \text { and } \quad \mathrm{P}_{1,1}^{-}\left(T_{1}\right)=1-e^{-\lambda_{1} T_{1}} $$ $\mathrm{P}_{1,1}^{-}(t)$ follows from $\mathrm{P}_{1,0}^{-}(t)+\mathrm{P}_{1,1}^{-}(t)=1$. Similarly, for phase 2 with $t$ starting at $t=T_{1}$, $$ \stackrel{\circ}{\mathrm{P}}_{2,0}^{-}\left(t-T_{1}\right)=-\lambda_{2} \mathrm{P}_{2,0}^{-}\left(t-T_{1}\right), \quad \text { with } \quad \mathrm{P}_{2,0}^{-}(0)=\mathrm{P}_{1,0}^{-}\left(T_{1}\right)=e^{-\lambda_{1} T_{1}} $$ yielding $\mathrm{P}_{2,0}^{-}\left(t-T_{1}\right)=e^{-\lambda_{1} T_{1}} e^{-\lambda_{2}\left(t-T_{1}\right)}, \quad T_{1}<t \leq T_{1}+T_{2}$, and thus $$ \mathrm{R}_{S 0}\left(T_{1}+\mathrm{T}_{2}\right)=\mathrm{P}_{2,0}^{-}\left(T_{1}+T_{2}\right)=e^{-\lambda_{1} T_{1}} e^{-\lambda_{2} T_{2}}=e^{-\left(\lambda_{1} T_{1}+\lambda_{2} T_{2}\right)}=R_{S 0} $$ ##

For reliability investigation, calculate the reliability function $\mathrm{R}_{1,0}\left(T_{1}\right)$ at the end of phase 1 starting in state $Z_{1,0}$ at $t=0$ in the same way as for a one mission system (Table 6.2), as well as states probabilities $\mathrm{P}_{1, j}^{\prime}\left(T_{1}\right)$ for all up states $Z_{1, j}$; if $Z_{1, j}$ (possibly with further as-good-as-new elements used inphase 2) is an up state in phase $2, \mathrm{P}_{1, j}^{\prime}\left(T_{1}\right)$ becomes the probability $\mathrm{P}_{2, j}^{\prime}(0)$ to start phase 2 in $Z_{2, j}$; if $Z_{1, j}$ is a (system) down state in phase $2, \mathrm{P}_{1, j}^{\prime}\left(T_{1}\right)$ adds to the initial probability of starting phase 2 in the (system) down state; if $Z_{1, j}$ does not appear in phase $2, \mathrm{P}_{1, j}^{\prime}\left(T_{1}\right)$ adds to the initial probability in state $Z_{2,0}$ to give $\mathrm{P}_{2,0}^{\prime}(0)$ (from rule 2 above and verifying that for each phase the sum of all states probabilities is 1 ); reliability calculation must take care of elements which are not used in the phase considered and can act as standby redundancy $(\lambda \equiv 0)$ for working elements; continuing in this way, the reliability $R_{S 0}$ for the whole mission starting phase 1 in $Z_{1,0}$, follows as $$ R_{S 0}=\sum_{Z_{j} \in U_{n}} \mathrm{P}_{n, j}^{\prime}\left(T_{n}\right), \quad U_{n}=\text { set of up states in phase } n $$ 5. If a state $Z_{k, i}$ does not appear in the phase $k+1$, the general rule 4 applies. 6. To avoid ambiguities, $x$ starting by $x=0$ at the begin of each phase has to be used. Besides cases with ideal fault coverage, ideal switching, and no system performance reduction at failure (Sections 2.2, 2.3, and 6.4-6.7), more complex structures often arise in practical applications (see Sections 6.8.3-6.8.5 for some examples). Such structures must be investigated on a case-by-case basis, and an FMEA/FMECA (Section 2.6) is mandatory to validate investigations. Often it is necessary to consider that after a reconfiguration, the system performance is reduced, i. e. reward and frequency/duration aspects have to be involved in the analysis. They have the advantage of great flexibility (type of redundancy and repair strategy, incomplete coverage or switch, common cause failures, etc.). Further tools are known to model repairable systems, e. g. based on dynamic fault trees or Petri nets. For very large or complex systems, a numerical solution or Monte Carlo simulation can become necessary. Many of these tools are similar in performance and versatility (Petri nets are equivalent to Markov models), other have limitations (fault trees apply basically to totally independent elements, and Monte Carlo simulations delivers only numerical solutions), so that choice of the tool is related to the personal experience of the analyst (see e. g. [A2.6 (61165, 60300-3-1), 6.103 (31010), 6.39 (2005)] for comparisons). However, modeling large complex systems requires a close cooperation between project and reliability engineers. After a review of totally independent elements, Sections 6.9.2-6.9.5 discuss dynamic fault trees, BDD, event trees \& Petri nets. Sections 6.9.6-6.9.7 consider then numerical solutions \& approximate expressions for large systems. Tools and models for human reliability \& risk management are introduced in Sections 6.10 \& 6.11. ### 6.9.1 Systems with Totally Independent Elements Totally independent elements (totally IE) assumes that there is only active redundancy and each element operates, and if repairable is repaired to as-good-as-new, independently from each other. Elements are boxes in the reliability block diagram and total independence implies that each element has its own repair crew and continues operation during repair of failed elements. This does not exclude that the (physically) same element can appear more times in a reliability block diagram (Examples $2.2 \& 2.3$ ). The reliability function $\mathrm{R}_{\mathrm{S} 0}(t)$ of nonrepairable (up to system failure) systems with totally independent elements has been investigated in Section 2.3.4. As stated with Eq. (2.48), equations for $\mathrm{R}_{\mathrm{S} 0}(t)$ are also valid for the point availability $\mathrm{PA}_{\mathrm{S} 0}(t)$ of repairable systems, substituting $\mathrm{PA}_{i}(t)$ to $\mathrm{R}_{i}(t)$. This rule gives an upper bound on $\mathrm{PA}_{\mathrm{S} 0}(t)$ if each element does not have its own repair crew. Except for series structures, $\mathrm{R}_{\mathrm{S} 0}(t)$ for repairable systems cannot be obtained using Boolean methods, see pp. 293-94 for a possible approximation. ### 6.9.2 Static and Dynamic Fault Trees A fault tree (FT) is a graphical representation of the conditions or other factors causing or contributing to the occurrence of a defined undesirable event, referred astop event. In its original form, as introduced in Section 2.6 (p. 76), a fault tree contains only static gates (essentially AND \& OR for coherent systems) and is termed static fault tree. Such a fault tree can handle combinatorial events, qualitatively (similar as for an FMEA, Section 2.6) or quantitatively (with Boolean functions, Section 2.3.4). As in the current literature [2.85, 6.38, A2.6(IEC61025)], " 0 " will be used also here for operating and " 1 " for failure (this in contrast to the notation used in Sections $2.2 \& 2.3$ for reliability investigations based on the reliability block diagram with 1 for up and 0 for down). With this notation, AND gates represent in fault trees a parallel structure with active redundancy and OR gates a series structure (Figs. 2.14, 6.40-6.42). In setting up a fault tree, a reliability block diagram can be useful. However, fault trees can also consider external events. Figure 6.40 gives two examples with corresponding static fault trees (see Table 2.1 and

Example 6.30 for calculations based on the reliability block diagram, Section 6.9.3 for calculations based on binary decision diagrams). Static fault trees can be used to calculate reliability and point availability for the case of totally independent elements (see discussion on p. 280). For instance, reliability calculation leads to (nonrepairable up to system failure) $$ 1-\mathrm{R}_{S 0}(t)=1-\prod_{i=1}^{n} \mathrm{R}_{i}(t) \quad \text { or } \quad \overline{\mathrm{R}}_{S 0}(t)=1-\prod_{i=1}^{n}\left(1-\overline{\mathrm{R}}_{i}(t)\right), \quad \mathrm{R}_{i}(0)=1 $$ for the series structure with independent elements $E_{1}, \ldots, E_{n}$, and to $$ 1-\mathrm{R}_{S 0}(t)=1-\sum_{i=k}^{n}\binom{n}{i} \mathrm{R}^{i}(t)(1-\mathrm{R}(t))^{n-i} \quad \text { or } \quad \overline{\mathrm{R}}_{S 0}(t)=1-\sum_{i=k}^{n}\binom{n}{i}(1-\overline{\mathrm{R}}(t))^{i} \overline{\mathrm{R}}(t)^{n-i} $$ for the $k$-out-of-n active redundancy with identical and independent elements $E_{1}=$ $\ldots=E_{n}=E$ (Eqs. (2.17) \& (2.23), $\overline{\mathrm{R}}_{i}(t)=1-\mathrm{R}_{i}(t)=$ failure probability). For complex structures, calculation uses binary decision diagrams (based on the Shannon decomposition of the fault tree structure function, see Section 6.9.3) or minimal path or cut sets (Eqs. (2.42), (2.44)), often supported by computer programs. However, because of their basic structure, static fault trees cannot handle states or time dependencies, in particular standby redundancy \& repair strategy. For these cases, it is necessary to extend static fault trees, adding so called dynamic gates to obtain dynamic fault trees. Important dynamic gates are [2.85, 6.38, A2.6 (IEC 61025)]: - Priority AND gate (PAND), the output event (failure) occurs only if all input events occur and in sequence from left to right. - Sequence enforcing gate (SEQ), the output event occurs only if input events occur in sequence from left to right and there are more than two input events. - Spare gate (SPARE), the output event occurs if the number of spares is less than required. Further gates (choice gate, redundancy gate, warm spare gate) have been suggested, Figure 6.40 a) Reliability block diagram and static fault tree for a 2-out-of-3 active redundancy with switch element; b) Functional block diagram \& static fault tree for a redund. computer system [6.30]; Notes: " 0 " holds for operating (up), " 1 " for failure (down) e.g. in [6.38]. All above dynamic gates requires a Markov analysis, i. e. states probabilities must be calculated by a Markov approach (constant failures \& repair rates), yielding results used as occurrence probability for the basic event replacing the corresponding dynamic gate. Use of dynamic gates in dynamic fault tree analysis, with corresponding computer programs, has been carefully investigated, e. g. in $[2.85,6.36,6.38]$. Fault tree analysis (FTA) is an established methodology for reliability and availability calculation emerging in the 1960's with investigations on nuclear power plants. However, it is basically limited to totally independent elements (active redundancy, nonrepairable up to system failure for reliability, repairable with a repair crew for each element for availability), and the necessity to use Markov approaches to solve dynamic gates can further reduce its utility in practical applications. Quite generally, FTA has the same limitations as those of methods based on binary considerations (fault trees, reliability block diagrams, binary decision diagrams, etc.). However, all these tools are sufficient for some applications, and can give a valid support in generating transition rates diagrams for Markov analysis. So once more, combination of investigation tools is often a good way to solve difficult problems.# 6.9.3 Binary Decision Diagrams A binary decision diagram (BDD) is a directed acyclic graph obtained by successive Shannon decomposition (Eq. (2.38)) of a Boolean function. It applies in particular to the structure functions developed in Section 2.3.4 for coherent systems, using minimal path or cut sets. This allows for easy calculation of the reliability function $\mathrm{R}_{S 0}(t)$ for the nonrepairable case (Eqs. (2.45), (2.47)) or point availability $\mathrm{PA}_{S 0}(t)$ for repairable totally independent elements (Eqs. (2.45), (2.48)). Frequently, BDDs are used to calculate $\mathrm{R}_{S 0}(t)$ or $\mathrm{PA}_{S 0}(t)$ for systems completely described by a fault tree with corresponding fault tree structure function $\phi_{F T}\left(\zeta_{1}, \ldots, \zeta_{n}\right) . \quad \phi_{F T}\left(\zeta_{1}, \ldots, \zeta_{n}\right)$ follows from a fault tree, see e.g. Figs. $6.41 \& 6.42$, or from the corresponding reliability block diagram, considering " 0 " for operating (up) and " 1 " for failure (down). In relation to fault trees, a BDD is created starting from the top event, i. e. from $\phi_{F T}\left(\zeta_{1}, \ldots, \zeta_{n}\right)$, down to the sink boxes using the Shannon decomposition (Eq. (2.38)) of the fault tree structure function at the node considered. Each node refers to a variable of $\phi_{F T}\left(\zeta_{1}, \ldots, \zeta_{n}\right)$ and has 2 outgoing edges, 0 -edge for operating and 1-edge for failure. Input to a node can be one or more outgoing edges from other nodes. The BDD terminates in 2 sink boxes labeled 0 for operating (up), 1 for failure (down). Indication 0 or 1 and an arrow help to identify the outgoing edge. Figure 6.41 gives two basic reliability block diagrams with corresponding fault trees, $\phi_{F T}$, and BDDs; to obtain $\mathrm{R}_{S 0}(t)$, one moves from the top of the BDD following all possible paths down to the sink box " 0 ", taking in a multiplicative way $\mathrm{R}_{i}(t)$ or $\widetilde{\mathrm{R}}_{i}(t)=1-\mathrm{R}_{i}(t)$ according to the value 0 or 1 assumed by the variable $\zeta_{i}$ involved (similar is for $\widetilde{\mathrm{R}}_{S 0}(t)$; for $\mathrm{PA}_{S 0}(t)$ consider Eq. (2.48)). However, considering the uncertainties involved in the risk assessmentprocess, and that risk acceptance has often an important subjective component, planing, realizing \& checking/monitoring barriers that avoid or at least mitigate risk causes or effects/consequences, during the life cycle of a system, is the most effective way to improve protection against harm. Ideally, the system should be conceived to have a fail-safe behavior (pp. 66, 72, 158) with respect to system intrinsic critical failures and hazards triggered by system's personnel (operation, maintenance, support) or external events (attacks, natural catastrophes). For this purpose, besides appropriate control \& fail-safe procedures, barriers (hardware and/or software) are introduced to avoid or at least mitigate risk causes or effects. Barriers can be active or passive, and are realized for instance by - observing design rules (Chapter 5), in particular to avoid failure propagation, - realizing redundancy with different elements, to avoid common cause failures, and by performing a careful investigation of all possible failure modes (as a general rule, redundant elements of fault tolerant equipment and systems must be designed and realized independently from each other, in critical cases with different technologies, tools and personnel, for hardware and software), - introducing majority redundancies (also for actuators), - introducing efficient alarm and fail-safe procedures (e. g. shut-off circuitries), - supporting/bypassing humans by critical decisions, at least with two-step actions, - improving technical controls through preventive maintenance, - improving administrative controls, - improving risk awareness and communication (through motivation \& training), - restricting access to sensitive parts, and/or reinforcing guarding. Identification, realization, evaluation, and monitoring of barriers must be performed during all life cycle phases, using tools for failures (fault) modes \& effects/ consequences analysis (Sections 2.6 \& 6.10), in particular FMEA / FMECA (pp. 72 - 75), FTA (pp. 76, 280-82), BDD (pp.283-85) \& ETA (p.286), and experience shows that combination of investigation tools is often necessary to improve solutions. However, $100 \%$ risk mitigation (i. e. risk avoidance) is generally not possible ${ }^{*}$, and a compromise between conflicting needs must be found to fix the acceptable risk (or safety) level for a given system. As often used for MTTR estimation or demonstration (p. 409), efficacy of barriers should be checked by introducing selected critical failures or external hazards; tests which can deliver important results useful to support modeling efforts. [^0] [^0]: *) For instance, assuming failure as cause and fire as consequence, neither a redundancy as barrier for cause nor a firewall or sprinkler as barrier for consequence can reach a $100 \%$ risk mitigation.# 7 Statistical Quality Control \& Reliability Tests Statistical quality control \& reliability (RAMS) tests are performed to estimate or demonstrate quality and reliability characteristics on the basis of data collected from sampling tests. Estimation leads to point or interval estimate, marked with ${ }^{\wedge}$ in this book; demonstration is a test of a given hypothesis on an unknown characteristic. Estimation \& demonstration of an unknown probability is given in Section 7.1 for a defective probability $p$ and in Section 7.2.1 for some reliability figures. Procedures for steady-state availability estimation \& demonstration are in Section 7.2.2. Estimation \& demonstration of a constant failure rate $\lambda$ (or $M T B F$ for $M T B F \equiv 1 / \lambda$ ) are discussed in depth in Sections 7.2.3. The case of an MTTR is considered in Section 7.3. Basic models for accelerated tests are introduced in Section 7.4, with regard also to multiple failure mechanisms. Goodness-of-fit tests based on graphical \& analytical procedures are summarized in Section 7.5. General reliability data analysis, including test on nonhomogeneous Poisson processes and trend tests, are discussed in Section 7.6; models for reliability growth in Section 7.7. A careful introduction to the mathematical foundations for this chapter is in Appendix A8. Selected examples illustrate the practical aspects, and to simplify the notation, sample is used for random sample (taken from a very large, homogeneous lot), mean for expected value \& independent for mutually, statistically, stochastically independent; furthermore, indices $S_{i}$ (p.3) are omitted in this chapter ( $S_{0}$ is assumed for $R, R(t), P A, \lambda, M T B F$ ), and estimated (or empirical) values are marked with ^. ### 7.1 Statistical Quality Control One of the main purposes of statistical quality control is to use sampling tests to estimate or demonstrate the defective probability $p$ of a given item, to a required accuracy and often on the basis of tests by attributes (i. e. tests of type good/bad). However, considering $p$ as an unknown probability, a broader field of applications can be covered by the same methods. Other topics, such as tests by variables and statistical processes control [7.1-7.5], are not considered in this book. In this section, $p$ is considered as a defective probability (see footnote on p. 1). It will be assumed that all elements of the sample are independent and have the same defective probability (i. e. the lot is homogeneous and much larger than the sample), allowing the use of the binomial distribution (Appendix A6.10.7, pp. 465-67).# 7.1.1 Estimation of a Defective Probability $p$ Let $n$ be the size of a (random) sample from a large homogeneous lot. If $k$ defective items have been observed within the sample of size $n$, then (Eq. (A8.29)) $$ \hat{p}=k / n, \quad k=0,1,2, \ldots, n $$ is the maximum likelihood point estimate of the defective probability $p$ for an item in the lot under consideration. $\hat{p}=k / n$ is unbiased ( $\mathrm{E}[\hat{p}]=\mathrm{E}[k] / n=p$, Eq. (A6.122)) and $k$ is a sufficient statistic (delivers the complete information about $p$, Appendix A8.2.1). Furthermore, $\operatorname{Var}[\hat{p}]=\operatorname{Var}[k] / n^{2}=p(1-p) / n$ (Eq. (A6.123)). For a given confidence level $\gamma=1-\beta_{1}-\beta_{2}\left(0<\beta_{1}<1-\beta_{2}<1\right)$, the lower $\hat{p}_{l}$ and upper $\hat{p}_{u}$ limit of the confidence interval for $p$ can be obtained from $$ \sum_{i=k}^{n}\binom{n}{i} \hat{p}_{l}^{i}\left(1-\hat{p}_{l}\right)^{n-i}=\beta_{2} \quad \text { and } \quad \sum_{i=0}^{k}\binom{n}{i} \hat{p}_{u}^{i}\left(1-\hat{p}_{u}\right)^{n-i}=\beta_{1} $$ for $0<k<n$, and from $$ \hat{p}_{l}=0 \quad \text { and } \quad \hat{p}_{u}=1-\sqrt[n]{\beta_{1}} \quad \text { for } \quad k=0 \quad\left(\gamma=1-\beta_{1}\right) $$ or from $$ \hat{p}_{l}=\sqrt[n]{\beta_{2}} \quad \text { and } \quad \hat{p}_{u}=1 \quad \text { for } \quad k=n \quad\left(\gamma=1-\beta_{2}\right) $$ see Eqs. (A8.37) to (A8.40) and the remarks given there. $\beta_{1}$ is the risk that the true value of $p$ is larger than $\hat{p}_{u}$ and $\beta_{2}$ the risk that the value of $p$ is smaller than $\hat{p}_{l}$, see

Example 7.1 for an application. The confidence level is nearly equal to (but not less than) $\gamma=1-\beta_{1}-\beta_{2}$. It can be considered as the relative frequency of cases in which the interval $\left[\hat{p}_{l}, \hat{p}_{u}\right]$ overlaps (covers) the true value of $p$, in an increasing series of repetitions of the experiment of taking a random sample of size $n$ from the same homogeneous lot (p. 554). The main concern of this test is to check a zero hypothesis $H_{0}: p<p_{0}$ against an alternative hypothesis $H_{1}: p>p_{1}$ on the basis of the following agreement between producer and consumer, the lot should be accepted with a probability nearly equal to (but not less than) $1-\alpha$ if the true (unknown) defective probability $p$ is lower than $p_{0}$, but rejected with a probability nearly equal to (but not less than) $1-\beta$ if $p$ is greater than $p_{1}\left(p_{0}, p_{1}>p_{0}\right.$, and $0<\alpha<1-\beta<1$ are given (fixed) values).$p_{0}$ is the specified defective probability and $p_{1}$ is the maximum acceptable defective probability. $\alpha$ is the allowed producer's risk (type I error), i. e. the probability of rejecting a true hypothesis $H_{0}: p<p_{0} . \beta$ is the allowed consumer's risk (type II error), i. e. the probability of accepting the hypothesis $H_{0}: p<p_{0}$ when the alternative hypothesis $H_{1}: p>p_{1}$ is true. Verification of the agreement stated above is a problem of statistical hypothesis testing (Appendix A8.3) and can be performed, for instance, with a simple two-sided sampling plan or a sequential test. In both cases, the basic model is the sequence of Bernoulli trials, as introduced in Appendix A6.10.7 (pp. 465-66). # 7.1.2.1 Simple Two-sided Sampling Plan The procedure (test plan) for the simple two-sided sampling plan is as follows (Appendix A8.3.1.1): 1. From $p_{0}, p_{1}, \alpha \& \beta$, determine the smallest integer $c$ and the value $n$ satisfying $$ \sum_{i=0}^{c}\binom{n}{i} p_{0}^{i}\left(1-p_{0}\right)^{n-i} \geq 1-\alpha $$ and $$ \sum_{i=0}^{c}\binom{n}{i} p_{1}^{i}\left(1-p_{1}\right)^{n-i} \leq \beta $$ 2. Take a sample of size $n$, determine the number $k$ of defective items in the sample, and - reject $H_{0}: p<p_{0}, \quad$ if $k>c$ - accept $H_{0}: p<p_{0}, \quad$ if $k \leq c$. The graph of Fig. 7.2 visualizes the validity of the above rule (see Appendix A8.3.1.1 for a proof). It satisfies inequalities (7.8) \& (7.9), and is known as operating characteristic curve (or acceptance probability curve). For each value of $p$, it gives the probability of having no more than c defective items in a sample of size $n$. Since the operating characteristic curve decreases monotonically in $p$, the risk for a false decision decreases for $p<p_{0}$ and $p>p_{1}$, respectively. It can be shown that the quantities $c$ and $n p_{0}$ depend only on $\alpha, \beta$, and the ratio $p_{1} / p_{0}$ (discrimination ratio). Table 7.3 (p. 335) gives $c$ and $n p_{0}$ for some important values of $\alpha, \beta$ and $p_{1} / p_{0}$ for the case where the Poisson approximation (Eq. (A6.129)) holds, see

Example 7.2 for an application. Using the operating characteristic curve, the Average Outgoing Quality (AOQ) can be calculated. $A O Q$ represents the mean percentage of defective items that reach the customer, assuming that all rejected samples have been $100 \%$ inspected \& the defective items have been replaced by good ones, and is given by Figure 7.2 Operating characteristic curve (acceptance probability curve) as a function of the defective probability $p$ for $p_{0}=2 \%, p_{1}=4 \%, \alpha=\beta \leqq 0.1, n=510, c=14$ as per Table 7.3 (see also Fig. 7.3) $$ A O Q=\operatorname{Pr}\{p \cap \text { acceptance }\}=p \operatorname{Pr}\{\text { acceptance }|p\}=p \sum_{i=0}^{c}\binom{n}{i} p^{i}(1-p)^{n-i} $$ The maximum value of $A O Q$ is the Average Outgoing Quality Limit [7.4, 7.5]. Obtaining the solution of inequalities (7.8) and (7.9) is time-consuming. For small values of $p_{0} \& p_{1}$ (up to a few \%), the Poisson approximation (Eq. (A6.129)) $$ \binom{n}{i} p^{i}(1-p)^{n-i} \approx \frac{(n p)^{i}}{i!} e^{-n p} $$ can be used. Introducing the Poisson approximation in Eqs. (7.8) and (7.9) leads to a Poisson distribution with parameters $m_{1}=n p_{1}$ and $m_{0}=n p_{0}$, which can be solved using a table of the $\chi^{2}$-distribution (Table A9.2). Alternatively, the curves of Fig. 7.3 provide graphical solutions, sufficiently good for practical applications. Exact solutions are in Table 7.3 (p.335). #

The graph of Fig. 7.3 yields the same result: $c=14$, $m_{0} \approx 10.2$ and $m_{1} \approx 20.4$ for $\alpha \approx \beta \leq 0.1$. Results using Table A9.2 lead to $v=30$ $\left(t_{v, q_{2}} / t_{v, q_{1}}=2, q_{1}=\alpha \leq 0.1, q_{2}=1-\beta \geq 0.9\right), \mathrm{F}(20.34)=0.093 \leq \alpha . \mathrm{F}(40.68) \approx 0.906 \geq 1-\beta$ (linear interpolation); thus, $c=\mathrm{v} / 2-1=14$ and $n=20.34 /(2 \cdot 0.01)=1017$. Graphical and analytical methods require a solution by successive approximation: choice of $c$, starting at $c=0$, and check of conditions for $\alpha$ and $\beta$ by considering the ratio $p_{1} / p_{0}$.# 7.1.2.2 Sequential Test The procedure for a sequential test is as follows (Appendix A8.3.1.2): 1. In a Cartesian coordinate system draw the acceptance line $y_{1}(n)=a n-b_{1}$ and the rejection line $y_{2}(n)=a n+b_{2}$, with $$ a=\frac{\ln \frac{1-p_{0}}{1-p_{1}}}{\ln \frac{p_{1}}{p_{0}}+\ln \frac{1-p_{0}}{1-p_{1}}}, \quad b_{1}=\frac{\ln \frac{1-\alpha}{\beta}}{\ln \frac{p_{1}}{p_{0}}+\ln \frac{1-p_{0}}{1-p_{1}}}, \quad b_{2}=\frac{\ln \frac{1-\beta}{\alpha}}{\ln \frac{p_{1}}{p_{0}}+\ln \frac{1-p_{0}}{1-p_{1}}} $$ 2. Select one item after another from the lot, test the item, enter the test result in the diagram drawn in step 1 , and stop the test as soon as either the rejection or the acceptance line is crossed. The advantage of the sequential test is that on average it requires a smaller sample size than the corresponding simple two-sided sampling plan (

Example 7.10 or Fig. 7.8). A disadvantage is that the sample size (test duration) is random. # 7.1.3 One-sided Sampling Plans for the Demonstration of a Defective Probability $p$ The two-sided sampling plans of Section 7.1.2 are fair in the sense that for $\alpha=\beta$, both producer and consumer run the same risk of making a false decision. In practical applications however, one-sided sampling plans are often used, i. e. only $p_{0}$ and $\alpha$ or $p_{1}$ and $\beta$ are specified. In these cases, the operating characteristic curve (acceptance probability curve) is not completely defined. For each value of $c$ $(c=0,1, \ldots)$ a largest $n(n=1,2, \ldots)$ exists which satisfies inequality (7.8) for given $p_{0}$ and $\alpha$, or a smallest $n$ exists which satisfies inequality (7.9) for given $p_{1}$ and $\beta$ (Fig.7.3). One recognizes that the operating characteristic curves become steeper as the value of $c$ increases (Figs. 7.4 or A8.9). Hence, for small values of $c$, the producer (if $p_{0}$ and $\alpha$ are given) or the consumer (if $p_{1}$ and $\beta$ are given) can realize an advantage. Figure 7.4 (obtained from Fig. 7.3, $m=n p$ ) visualizes the reduction of the consumer risk (from $\beta \approx 0.88$ for $c=0$ or $\approx 0.98$ for $c=7$ ) by increasing values of the defective probability $p$ or values of $c$, see Fig 7.9 for a counterpart. When only $p_{0}$ and $\alpha$ or $p_{1}$ and $\beta$ are given, it is usual to set in these cases $$ p_{0}=A Q L \quad \text { and } \quad p_{1}=L T P D $$ respectively, where $A Q L$ is the Acceptable Quality Level and LTPD is the Lot Tolerance Percent Defective (Eqs. (A8.79) to (A8.82)). A large number of one-sided sampling plans for the demonstration of $A Q L$ values are given in national and international standards (IEC 60410, ISO 2859, MIL-STD-105, DIN 40080 [7.3]). Many of these plans have been established empirically. Following remarks can be useful when evaluating such plans: 1. $A Q L$ values are given in $\%$. 2. The values for $n$ and $c$ are in general obtained using the Poisson approximation. 3. Not all values of $c$ are listed, the value of $\alpha$ often decreases with increasing $c$. 4. Sample size is related to lot size, and this relationship is empirical. 5. A distinction is made between reduced tests (level I), normal tests (level II) and tightened tests (level III); level II is normally used; transition from one level to another is often given empirically (e. g. transition from level II to level III is necessary if 2 out of 5 successive independent lots have been rejected and a return to level II follows if 5 successive independent lots are passed). 6. The value of $\alpha$ is not given explicitly (for $c=0$, for example, $\alpha$ is approximately 0.05 for level I, 0.1 for level II, and 0.2 for level III). Figure 7.4 Operating characteristic curves (acceptance probability curves) as a function of the defective probability $p$ for $p_{0}=A Q L=0.65 \%$ with sample sizes $n=20,80,500$ as per Table 7.1 $(\alpha=0.12$ for $c=0, \approx 0.09$ for $c=1, \approx 0.02$ for $c=7$ per Fig. 7.3, Table A9.2 or [A9.1 - A9.6]) Table 7.1 presents some test procedures for $A Q L$ values from IEC 60410 [7.3] and Fig. 7.4 shows the corresponding operating characteristic curves for $A Q L=0.65 \%$ and sample size $n=20,80$, and 500 . Test procedures for demonstration of $L T P D$ values with given (fixed) customer risk $\beta$ are for example in [3.12 (S-19500)]. They are often based on the Poisson approximation (Eq. (A6.129)) and can be easily established using a $\chi^{2}$ - table (Appendix A9.2) or Fig. 7.3. For given $\beta$ and $L T P D$, the values of $n$ and $c$ can be obtained taking in Fig. 7.3 $$ \sum_{i=0}^{c} \frac{(m)^{i}}{i!} e^{-m}=\beta $$ and reading $m=n p=n L T P D$ for $c=0,1,2, \ldots$ (Example: $\beta=0.1 \& L T P D=2 \%$ yields $m \approx 3.9$ for $c=1$, and from this $n \approx 3.9 / 0.02=195$; the procedure is thus: test 195 items and reject $L T P D=2 \%$ if more than 1 defect occur). In addition to the simple one-sided sampling plans described above, multiple one-sided sampling plans are often used to demonstrate $A Q L$ values. In a double one-sided sampling plan, the following procedure is used: 1. Take a first sample of size $n_{1}$ and accept definitely if no more than $c_{1}$ defects occur, but reject definitely if exactly or more than $d_{1}$ defects have occurred. 2. If after the first sample the number of defects is greater than $c_{1}$ but less than $d_{1}$, take a second sample of size $n_{2}$ and accept if there are totally (in the first and second sample) no more than $c_{2}$ defects; elsewhere reject. The operating characteristic curve (acceptance probability curve) for a double onesided sampling plan can be calculated as$$ \begin{aligned} \operatorname{Pr}\{\text { acceptance } \mid p\}= & \sum_{i=0}^{c_{1}}\binom{n_{\mathrm{i}}}{i} p^{i}(1-p)^{n_{1}-i} \\ & +\sum_{i=c_{1}+1}^{d_{1}-1}\left[\binom{n_{\mathrm{i}}}{i} p^{i}(1-p)^{n_{1}-i} \sum_{j=0}^{c_{2}-i}\binom{n_{2}}{j} p^{j}(1-p)^{n_{2}-j}\right] \end{aligned} $$ Multiple one-sided sampling plans are also given in national and international standards, see for example IEC 60410 [7.3] for the following double one-sided sampling plan to demonstrate $A Q L=1 \%$ | Lot size | $n_{1}$ | $n_{2}$ | $c_{1}$ | $d_{1}$ | $c_{2}$ | | --: | :--: | :--: | :--: | :--: | :--: | | $281-500$ | 32 | 32 | 0 | 2 | 1 | | $501-1,200$ | 50 | 50 | 0 | 3 | 3 | | $1,201-3,200$ | 80 | 80 | 1 | 4 | 4 | | $3,201-10,000$ | 125 | 125 | 2 | 5 | 6 | The advantage of multiple one-sided sampling plans is that on average they require smaller sample sizes than would be necessary for simple one-sided sampling plans.
