use the first sampling plan above for $\uparrow$ or below for $\downarrow, c=$ number of allowed defects# 7.2 Statistical Reliability (RAMS) Tests Statistical reliability (RAMS) tests are useful to evaluate the reliability, availability, maintainability, and safety achieved in a given item (system). Early initiation of these tests allows quick identification and cost-effective correction of weaknesses not discovered by reliability (RAMS) analyses. This supports a learning process, often related to a reliability growth program (Section 7.7). However, since reliability (RAMS) tests are generally time-consuming and expensive, they should be coordinated with other tests and performed with test conditions as close as possible to those experienced in the field. As for quality control, a distinction is made between estimation and demonstration of a specific reliability (RAMS) figure. Section 7.2.1 uses results of Section 7.1 for reliability and availability testing for the case of a given (fixed) mission; this applies also to maintainability and safety considered as a probability. In section 7.2.2 a unified method for availability estimation and demonstration for the case of continuous operation is introduced. Section 7.2.3 deals then carefully with estimation and demonstration of a constant failure rate $\lambda$ (or $M T B F$ for the case $M T B F \equiv 1 / \lambda$ ); these results can be used for the safety function given by Eq. (6.330). Estimation and demonstration of an MTTR is discussed in Section 7.3. Accelerated tests (also for multiple failure mechanisms), goodness-of-fit tests, general reliability data analysis \& trend tests, and reliability growth are introduced in Sections 7.4-7.7, respectively. To simplify the notation, indices $S_{i}$ are omitted $\left(R, P A, \lambda, M T B F\right.$ are used for $R_{S 0}, P A_{S}, \lambda_{S 0}, M T B F_{S 0}$ ). ### 7.2.1 Reliability \& Availability Estimation and Demonstration for the Case of a given (fixed) Mission Reliability $(R)$ and availability (asymptotic \& steady-state point and average availability $P A=A A$ ) are often defined as success probability for a given (fixed) mission. Their estimation and demonstration can thus be performed as for an unknown probability $p$ (Section 7.1) by setting, for convenience, $$ p=1-R \quad \text { or } \quad p=1-P A=1-A A $$ For a demonstration, the null hypothesis $H_{0}: pR_{0}$ or $H_{0}: A A>A A_{0}$, which adheres better to the concept of reliability or availability. The same holds for other reliability figure expressed as an unknown probability $p$. Above considerations hold for given (fixed) mission, repeated $n$ times. However, for the case of continuous operation, estimation and demonstration of $\mathrm{R}(t)$ or $\mathrm{PA}(t)$ can leads to a difficulty in defining time points $t_{1}, t_{2}, \ldots, t_{n}$ at which the $n$ observations have to be performed. Sections $7.2 .2 \& 7.2 .3$ deal with continuous operation. Examples 7.3 - 7.6 illustrate some cases of reliability tests for given (fixed) mission.#

(7.9) or Fig. 7.3 with $c=7, n=100$, $p_{1}=0.1$ or $n p_{1}=10$ ). (A two-sided plan with $\alpha \approx \beta \approx 0.15, n=100, c=7$, $p_{0}=0.05$ would ask for $p_{1} \approx 0.11$, Fig.7.3.) ##

Example 7.7), for constant failure rate $\lambda(x)=\lambda$, the (fixed) cumulative operating time $T$ can be partitioned in an arbitrary way from failure-free times of statistically identical and independent items (see note to Table 7.3 on p. 335 for a rule). Following situations can occur in practical applications: 1. Operation of a single item immediately renewed at failure, here $T=t$. 2. Operation of $n$ identical items, each of them being immediately renewed at failure, here $T=n t(n=1,2, \ldots)$. As stated above, for constant failure rate $\lambda(x)=\lambda$ and immediate renewal, the failure process is a homogeneous Poisson process with intensity $\lambda$ for $n=1$, or $n \lambda$ for $n>1$, over the (fixed) time interval $(0, T]$ for $n=1$, or $(0, T / n]$ for $n>1$. Hence, the probability for $k$ failures within the cumulative operating time $T$ is (Eq. (A7.41))$$ \operatorname{Pr}\{k \text { failures within } T \mid \lambda\}=\operatorname{Pr}\{k \text { failures within } T / n \mid n \lambda\}=\frac{(\lambda T)^{k}}{k!} e^{-\lambda T}, \quad \begin{aligned} & k=0,1, \ldots \\ & n=1,2, \ldots \end{aligned} $$ Statistical procedures for the estimation and demonstration of a failure rate $\lambda$ (or for $M T B F$ for the case $M T B F \equiv 1 / \lambda$ ) can thus be based on the evaluation of the parameter $(m=\lambda T)$ of a Poisson distribution. In addition to the case of a given (fixed) cumulative operating time $T$, with immediate renewal, discussed above and investigated in Sections 7.2.3.1-7.2.3.3, for which the number $k$ of failures in $T$ is a sufficient statistic and $\hat{\lambda}=k / T$ is an unbiased estimate for $\lambda$, further possibilities are known. Assuming $n$ identical items new at $t=0$ and labeling the individual failure times as $t_{1}<t_{2}<\ldots$, measured from $t=0$, also following censoring cases can occur in practical applications $(k>1)$ : 1. Fixed number $k$ of failures, the test is stopped at the $k$ th failure and failed items are not renewed; an unbiased point estimate of the failure rate $\lambda$ is (Eq (A8.35)) $$ \begin{aligned} & \hat{\lambda}=(k-1) /\left[n t_{1}+(n-1)\left(t_{2}-t_{1}\right)+\ldots+(n-k+1)\left(t_{k}-t_{k-1}\right)\right] \\ & =(k-1) /\left[t_{1}+\ldots+t_{k}+(n-k) t_{k}\right] . \end{aligned} $$ 2. Fixed number $k$ of failures, the test is stopped at the $k$ th failure and failed items are instantaneously renewed; an unbiased point estimate for $\lambda$ is $$ \hat{\lambda}=(k-1) /\left(n t_{1}+n\left(t_{2}-t_{1}\right)+\ldots+n\left(t_{k}-t_{k-1}\right)=(k-1) / n t_{k}\right. $$ 3. Fixed test time $T_{\text {test }}$, failed items are not renewed; a biased point estimate of the failure rate $\lambda$ (given $k$ items have failed in $\left.\left(0, T_{\text {test }}\right]\right)$ is $$ \hat{\lambda}=k /\left[n t_{1}+(n-1)\left(t_{2}-t_{1}\right)+\ldots+(n-k)\left(T_{\text {test }}-t_{k}\right)\right]=k /\left[t_{1}+\ldots+t_{k}+(n-k) T_{\text {test }}\right] $$ #

Example 7.7 An item with constant failure rate $\lambda$ operates first for a fixed time $T_{1}$ and then for a fixed time $T_{2}$. Repair times are neglected. Give the probability that $k$ failures will occur in $T=T_{1}+T_{2}$. ## Solution The item's behavior within each of the time periods $T_{1}$ and $T_{2}$ can be described by a homogeneous Poisson process with intensity $\lambda$. From Eq. (A7.39) it follows that $$ \operatorname{Pr}\left\{i \text { failures in the time period } T_{i} \mid \lambda\right\}=\frac{\left(\lambda T_{i}\right)^{i}}{i!} e^{-\lambda T_{1}} $$ and, because of the memoryless property of the homogeneous Poisson process $$ \begin{aligned} \operatorname{Pr}\left\{k \text { failures in } T=T_{1}+T_{2} \mid \lambda\right\} & =\sum_{i=0}^{k} \frac{\left(\lambda T_{i}\right)^{i}}{i!} e^{-\lambda T_{1}} \cdot \frac{\left(\lambda T_{2}\right)^{k-i}}{(k-i)!} e^{-\lambda T_{2}} \\ & =e^{-\lambda T} \lambda^{k} \sum_{i=0}^{k} \frac{T_{i}^{i}}{i!} \cdot \frac{T_{2}^{k-i}}{(k-i)!}=\frac{(\lambda T)^{k}}{k!} e^{-\lambda T} \end{aligned} $$ The last part of Eq. (7.26) follows from the binomial expansion of $\left(T_{1}+T_{2}\right)^{k}$. Eq. (7.26) shows that for $\lambda$ constant, the cumulative operating time $T$ can be partitioned in an arbitrary way from failure-free times of statistically identical and independent items (see note to Table 7.3 for a rule).Supplementary result: The same procedure can be used to prove that the sum of two independent homogeneous Poisson processes with intensities $\lambda_{1}$ and $\lambda_{2}$ is a homogeneous Poisson process with intensity $\lambda_{1}+\lambda_{2}$; in fact, $$ \begin{aligned} & \operatorname{Pr}\left\{k \text { failures in }(0, T] \mid \lambda_{1}, \lambda_{2}\right\} \\ & =\sum_{i=0}^{k} \frac{\left(\lambda_{1} T\right)^{i}}{i!} e^{-\lambda_{1} T} \frac{\left(\lambda_{2} T\right)^{k-i}}{(k-i)!} e^{-\lambda_{2} T}=\frac{\left(\left(\lambda_{1}+\lambda_{2}\right) T\right)^{k}}{k!} e^{-\left(\lambda_{1}+\lambda_{2}\right) T} \end{aligned} $$ This result can be extended to nonhomogeneous Poisson processes. # 7.2.3.1 Estimation of a Constant Failure Rate $\lambda$ (or of $M T B F$ for $M T B F \equiv 1 / \lambda)^{*}$ Let's consider an item with a constant failure rate $\lambda(x)=\lambda$. If during the given (fixed) cumulative operating time $T^{* \prime}$ exactly $k$ failures have occurred, the maximum likelihood point estimate for the unknown parameter $\lambda$ follows as (Eq. (A8.46)) $$ \hat{\lambda}=k / T, \quad k=0,1,2, \ldots $$ $\hat{\lambda}=k / T$ is unbiased, i. e. $\mathrm{E}[\hat{\lambda}]=\lambda, k$ is a sufficient statistic $\& \operatorname{Var}[\hat{\lambda}]=\operatorname{Var}[k] / T^{2}=\lambda / T$ (Example A6.21, Eqs. (A6.40), (A6.46), Appendix A8.2.1). For a given confidence level (p.554) $\gamma=1-\beta_{1}-\beta_{2}\left(0<\beta_{1}<1-\beta_{2}<1\right)$ and $k>0$, lower $\hat{\lambda}_{l}$ and upper $\hat{\lambda}_{u}$ limits of the confidence interval for $\lambda$ can be obtained from (Eqs. (A8.47)-(A8.51)) $$ \sum_{i=k}^{\infty} \frac{\left(\hat{\lambda}_{l} T\right)^{i}}{i!} e^{-\hat{\lambda}_{l} T}=\beta_{2} \quad \text { and } \quad \sum_{i=0}^{k} \frac{\left(\hat{\lambda}_{u} T\right)^{i}}{i!} e^{-\hat{\lambda}_{u} T}=\beta_{1} $$ or from $$ \hat{\lambda}_{l}=\frac{\chi_{2 k, \beta_{2}}^{2}}{2 T} \quad \text { and } \quad \hat{\lambda}_{u}=\frac{\chi_{2(k+1), 1-\beta_{1}}^{2}}{2 T} $$ using the quantile of the $\chi^{2}$-distribution (Table A9.2). For $k=0$, Eq. (A8.49) yields $$ \hat{\lambda}_{l}=0 \quad \text { and } \quad \hat{\lambda}_{u}=\frac{\ln \left(1 / \beta_{1}\right)}{T} . \quad \text { with } \gamma=1-\beta_{1} $$ Figure 7.6 gives confidence limits $\hat{\lambda}_{l} / \hat{\lambda} \& \hat{\lambda}_{u} / \hat{\lambda}$ for $\beta_{1}=\beta_{2}=(1-\gamma) / 2$, with $\hat{\lambda}=k / T$, useful for practical applications; see

Example 7.8 for an application. For the case $M T B F \equiv 1 / \lambda, M T \bar{B} F=T / k, k \geq 1$, is biased; unbiased is, for $\lambda T \gg 1$, $M T \bar{B} F=T /(k+1) \quad(\mathrm{E}[T /(k+1)]=\left(1-e^{-\lambda T}\right) / \lambda$, Eqs. (A6.40), (A6.39), (A7.41)). For practical applications, $M T \bar{B} F_{l} \approx 1 / \hat{\lambda}_{u}$ and $M T \bar{B} F_{u} \approx 1 / \hat{\lambda}_{l}$ can often be used. Example 7.8 In testing a subassembly with constant failure rate $\lambda, 4$ failures occur during $T=10^{4}$ cumulative operating hours (footnote on p. 330). Find the confidence interval for $\lambda$ for a confidence level $\gamma=0.8\left(\beta_{1}=\beta_{2}=0.1\right)$. ## Solution From Fig. 7.6 it follows that for $k=4$ and $\gamma=0.8, \hat{\lambda}_{l} / \hat{\lambda} \approx 0.44$ and $\hat{\lambda}_{u} / \hat{\lambda} \approx 2$. With $T=10^{4} \mathrm{~h}$, $k=4$, and $\hat{\lambda}=4 \cdot 10^{-4} \mathrm{~h}^{-1}$, the confidence limits are $\hat{\lambda}_{l} \approx 1.7 \cdot 10^{-4} \mathrm{~h}^{-1}$ and $\hat{\lambda}_{u} \approx 8 \cdot 10^{-4} \mathrm{~h}^{-1}$. Supplementary result: Corresponding one-sided conf. interval is $\lambda \leq 8 \cdot 10^{-4} \mathrm{~h}^{-1}$ with $\gamma=0.9$.In the above considerations (Eqs. (7.28) - (7.32)), the cumulative operating time $T$ was given (fixed), independent of the individual failure-free times and the number $n$ of items involved (Type I (time) censoring, see also footnote on p. 330). The situation is different when the number of failures $k$ is given (fixed), i. e. when the test is stopped at the occurrence of the $k$ th failure (Type II (failure) censoring). Here, the cumulative operating time is a random variable (term $(k-1) / \lambda$ of Eqs. (7.23) \& (7.24)). Using the memoryless property of homogeneous Poisson processes, it can be shown that the quantities $\left(t_{i}-t_{i-1}\right), i=1,2, \ldots, k, t_{0}=0$, are independent observations of exponentially distributed random variables with parameters $n \lambda$ for Eq.(7.24) and $(n-i+1) \lambda$ for Eq.(7.23), respectively. This is necessary and sufficient to prove that the $\hat{\lambda}$ given by Eqs. (7.23) and (7.24) are maximum likelihood estimates for $\lambda$. For confidence intervals, results of Appendix A8.2.2.3 can be used (directly for the case of Eq. (7.24)). In some practical applications, system's failure rate confidence limits as a function of component's failure rate confidence limits is asked. Monte Carlo simulation can help. However, for a series system with $n$ elements, constant failure rates $\lambda_{1}, \ldots, \lambda_{n}$, time censoring, and same observation time $T$, Eqs. (2.19), (7.28) \& (7.27) yield $\hat{\lambda}_{S 0}=\hat{\lambda}_{1}+\ldots+\hat{\lambda}_{n}$. Furthermore, for given (fixed) $T, 2 T \lambda_{i}\left(\lambda_{i}\right.$ considered here as random variable, Appendix A8.2.2.2) has a $\chi^{2}$-distribution with $2\left(k_{i}+1\right)$ degrees of freedom (Eqs. (A8.48) \& (A8.51), Table A9.2); thus, $2 T \lambda_{S 0}$ has a $\chi^{2}$-distribution with $\Sigma 2\left(k_{i}+1\right)$ degrees of freedom (Appendix A9.2, Example A6.15). From this, and considering the shape of the $\chi^{2}$-distribution (Tab. A9.2, [A9.2, A9.3]), it holds, empirically, that $\operatorname{Pr}\left\{\lambda_{S 0} \leq \hat{\lambda}_{1_{u}}+\ldots+\hat{\lambda}_{n_{u}}\right\} \geq \gamma$, with $\hat{\lambda}_{i_{u}}$ obtained from $\operatorname{Pr}\left\{\lambda_{i} \leq \hat{\lambda}_{i_{u}}\right\}=\gamma$ for $\gamma \approx 0.7, i=1, \ldots, n(\gamma \approx 0.78$ in [7.17]). Extensions to different observation times $T_{i}$, series-parallel structures, Erlangian distributed failure-free times are investigated in [7.17]. Estimation of $\lambda / \mu$ as approximation for unavailability is given in Section 7.2.2.1. # 7.2.3.2 Simple Two-sided Test for the Demonstration of a Constant Failure Rate $\lambda$ (or of $M T B F$ for the case $M T B F \equiv 1 / \lambda)^{*}$ In the context of an acceptance test, demonstration of a constant failure rate $\lambda$ (or of $M T B F$ for the case $M T B F \equiv 1 / \lambda$ ) is often required, not merely its estimation as in Section 7.2.3.1. The main concern of this test is to check a zero hypothesis $H_{0}: \lambda<\lambda_{0}$ against an alternative hypothesis $H_{1}: \lambda>\lambda_{1}$ on the basis of the following agreement between producer and consumer, items should be accepted with a probability nearly equal to (but not less than) $1-\alpha$ if the true (unknown) failure rate $\lambda$ is less than $\lambda_{0}$, but rejected with a probability nearly equal to (but not less than) $1-\beta$ if $\lambda$ is greater than $\lambda_{1}$ $\left(\lambda_{0}, \lambda_{1}>\lambda_{0}\right.$, and $0<\alpha<1-\beta<1$ are given (fixed) values). However, estimation and demonstration of specific parameters, for instance MTTR (mean time to repair, used for mean time to restoration in this book, see p. 113) is important for practical applications. From Eqs. (A8.6) and (A8.10), the empirical mean and variance of $\tau^{\prime}$ are given by $$ \hat{\mathrm{E}}\left[\tau^{\prime}\right]=\frac{1}{n} \sum_{i=1}^{n} t_{i}^{\prime} $$ and $$ \operatorname{Vár}\left[\tau^{\prime}\right]=\frac{1}{n-1} \sum_{i=1}^{n}\left(t_{i}^{\prime}-\hat{\mathrm{E}}\left[\tau^{\prime}\right]\right)^{2}=\frac{1}{n-1}\left[\sum_{i=1}^{n} t_{i}^{\prime 2}-\frac{1}{n}\left(\sum_{i=1}^{n} t_{i}^{\prime}\right)^{2}\right] $$Both estimates are unbiased, i. e. $\mathrm{E}\left[\hat{\mathrm{E}}\left[\tau^{\prime}\right]\right]=\mathrm{E}\left[\tau^{\prime}\right]=M T T R \& \mathrm{E}\left[\operatorname{Var}\left[\tau^{\prime}\right]\right]=\operatorname{Var}\left[\tau^{\prime}\right]$; furthermore, $\operatorname{Var}\left[\hat{\mathrm{E}}\left[\tau^{\prime}\right]\right]=\operatorname{Var}\left[\tau^{\prime}\right] / n$ (Appendix A8.1.2). As stated above, the repair time $\tau$ ' can often be assumed lognormally distributed with distribution function $$ \mathrm{F}(t)=\operatorname{Pr}\left\{\tau^{\prime} \leq t\right\}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2 \pi}} \int_{-\infty}^{\frac{\ln (\lambda t)}{\sigma}} e^{-x^{2} / 2} d x $$ (Eq. (A6.110)), and mean \& variance given by (Eqs. (A6.112) \& (A6.113)) $$ \mathrm{E}\left[\tau^{\prime}\right]=M T T R=\frac{e^{\sigma^{2} / 2}}{\lambda}, \quad \operatorname{Var}\left[\tau^{\prime}\right]=\frac{e^{2 \sigma^{2}}-e^{\sigma^{2}}}{\lambda^{2}}=M T T R^{2}\left(e^{\sigma^{2}}-1\right) $$ Form Example A6.18 (p. 464) one recognizes that $\ln \tau^{\prime}$ is normally distributed with mean $\ln (1 / \lambda)$ and Variance $\sigma^{2}$. Using Eqs. (A8.24) and (A8.27), the maximum likelihood estimations of $\lambda$ and $\sigma^{2}$ follow as $$ \hat{\lambda}=\left[\prod_{i=1}^{n} \frac{1}{t_{i}^{\prime}}\right]^{1 / n} \quad \text { and } \quad \hat{\sigma}^{2}=\frac{1}{n} \sum_{i=1}^{n}\left[\ln \left(\hat{\lambda} t_{i}^{\prime}\right)\right]^{2} $$ A point estimate for $\lambda$ and $\sigma$ can also be obtained by the method of quantiles. The idea is to substitute some particular quantiles with the corresponding empirical quantiles to obtain estimates for $\lambda$ or $\sigma$. For $t=1 / \lambda, \ln (\lambda t)=0$ and $\mathrm{F}(1 / \lambda)=0.5$, therefore, $1 / \lambda$ is the 0.5 quantile (median) $t_{0.5}$ of the distribution function $\mathrm{F}(t)$ given by Eq. (7.41). From the empirical 0.5 quantile $\hat{t}_{0.5}^{\prime}=\inf \left(t^{\prime}: \hat{\mathrm{F}}_{n}\left(t^{\prime}\right) \geq 0.5\right)$ an estimate for $\lambda$ follows as $$ \hat{\lambda} \approx 1 / \hat{t}_{0.5}^{\prime} $$ Moreover, $t=e^{\sigma} / \lambda$ yields $\mathrm{F}\left(e^{\sigma} / \lambda\right) \approx 0.841(\ln (\lambda t) / \sigma=1$, Table A9.1); thus $e^{\sigma} / \lambda \approx t_{0.841}$ is the 0.841 quantile of $\mathrm{F}(t)$ given by Eq. (7.41). With such figures, cost and scheduling considerations demand the use of accelerated testing for $\lambda$ estimation and demonstration, in particular if reliable field data are not available. An accelerated test is a test in which the applied stress is chosen to exceed that encountered in field operation, but still below the technological limits; this in order to shorten the time to failure of the item considered by avoiding an alteration of the involved failure mechanism (genuine acceleration). In accelerated tests, failure mechanisms are assumed to be activated selectively by increased stress. The quantitative relationship between degree of activation and extent of stress, the acceleration factor $A$, is determined via specific tests. Generally, it is assumed that the stress will not change the type of the failure-free time distribution function of the item under test, but only modify parameters; in the following, this hypothesis is assumed to be valid; however, its verification is mandatory before a statistical evaluation of data (see also p.102). Many electronic component failure mechanisms are activated through a temperature increase. Calculating the acceleration factor $A$, the Arrhenius model can often be used over a reasonably large temperature range (about $0-150^{\circ} \mathrm{C}$ for ICs ). The Arrhenius model is based on the Arrhenius law [7.10,3.43], which states that the rate $v$ of a simple (first-order) chemical reaction depends on temperature $T$ as $$ v=v_{0} e^{-E_{a} / k T} $$ $E_{a}$ and $v_{0}$ are parameters, $k$ is the Boltzmann constant ( $k=8.6 \cdot 10^{-5} \mathrm{eV} / \mathrm{K}$ ), and $T$ the absolute temperature in Kelvin degrees. $E_{a}$ is the activation energy and is expressed in eV . Assuming that the event considered (for example the diffusion between two liquids) occurs when the chemical reaction has reached a given threshold, and the reaction time dependence is given by a function $\mathrm{r}(t)$, the relationship between the times $t_{1}$ and $t_{2}$ necessary to reach at two temperatures $T_{1}$ and $T_{2}>T_{1}$ a given level of the chemical reaction considered can be expressed as $$ v_{1} \mathrm{r}\left(t_{1}\right)=v_{2} \mathrm{r}\left(t_{2}\right) $$ Furthermore, assuming $\mathrm{r}(t) \sim t$, i. e. a linear time dependence, it follows that $$ v_{1} t_{1}=v_{2} t_{2} $$ Substituting in Eq. (7.54) and rearranging, yields $$ \frac{t_{1}}{t_{2}}=\frac{v_{2}}{v_{1}}=e^{\frac{E_{a}}{k}\left(\frac{1}{T_{1}}-\frac{1}{T_{2}}\right)} $$By transferring this deterministic model to the mean times to failure $M T T F_{1}$ and $M T T F_{2}$ or to the constant failure rates $\lambda_{2}$ and $\lambda_{1}$ (using $M T T F=1 / \lambda$ ) of a given item at temperatures $T_{1}$ and $T_{2}$, it is possible to define an acceleration factor $A$ $$ A=M T T F_{1} / M T T F_{2}, \text { or, for time independent failure rate, } A=\lambda_{2} / \lambda_{1} $$ expressed by $$ A=e^{\frac{E_{a}}{k}\left(\frac{1}{T_{1}}-\frac{1}{T_{2}}\right)+)} $$ The right hand sides of Eq. (7.55) applies to the case of a constant (time independent but stress dependent) failure rate $\lambda(t)=\lambda$, for which $\mathrm{E}[\tau]=\sqrt{\operatorname{Var}[\tau]}=1 / \lambda$ holds with $\tau$ as time to failure (p. 457). Assuming that for time dependent failure rates, the left hand sides of Eq. (7.55) applies to mean time to failure $(E[\tau]=M T T F)$ and standard deviation ( $\sqrt{\operatorname{Var}[\tau]}$ ) as well, and that the type of the distribution function is the same at temperatures $T_{1}$ and $T_{2}$ (as stated on p.341), it can be shown that for the distribution functions frequently used in reliability engineering (Table A6.1) the following holds for the parameters: $\lambda_{2}=A \lambda_{1}$ for exponential, Gamma, Weibull, and lognormal; $\beta_{2}=\beta_{1}$ for Gamma and Weibull; $\sigma_{2}=\sigma_{1}$ for lognormal; $m_{2}=m_{1} / A$ $\& \sigma_{2}=\sigma_{1} / A$ for normal distribution (

(7.59a)), corrosion (Peck), and voltage stress (Kemeny) [3.34, 3.56, 3.67] $$ A=\left(\frac{j_{2}}{j_{1}}\right)^{n} e^{\frac{E_{a}}{k}\left(\frac{1}{T_{1}}-\frac{1}{T_{2}}\right)}, \quad A=\left(\frac{R H_{2}}{R H_{1}}\right)^{n} e^{\frac{E_{a}}{k}\left(\frac{1}{T_{1}}-\frac{1}{T_{2}}\right)}, \quad A=e^{\left(C_{0}+\frac{E_{a}}{k T}+C_{1} V / V_{\max }\right)} $$ where $j=$ current density, $R H=$ relative humidity, and $V=$ voltage, respectively (see also Eqs. (3.2) - (3.6) and Table 3.5). Refined models are e. g. in [3.67 \& 2.22]. For cracks propagation, Paris Law [2.77, 2.79] applies in many situations. For damage accumulation, Miner's hypothesis of independent damage increments [3.52] can be used in some applications. Known for conductivefilament formation is the Rudra's model[3.62]. Models for solder joints are discussed e. g. in [3.79(2011), 3.90], see Section 3.4 (p.109) for some considerations. Refinement of the above models is in progress in the context of physics of failures (PoF) [2.15, 3.49, 3.66, 3.67], in particular for ULSI ICs and considering stress dependent parameters and time dependent failure rates, with emphasis on: 1. New oxide \& package related, or externally induced failure mechanisms. 2. Identification and analysis of causes for early failures or premature wear-out. 3. Development of physical models for failure mechanisms and of simplified models for reliability predictions in practical applications. Such efforts will increase physical understanding on components failure rates.In addition to the accelerated tests discussed above, a rough estimate of component life time can often be obtained through short-term tests under extreme stresses (HALT, HAST, etc.). Examples are humidity testing of plastic-packaged ICs at high pressure and nearly $100 \% \mathrm{RH}$, or tests of ceramic-packaged ICs at up to $350^{\circ} \mathrm{C}$. Experience shows that under high stress, life time is often lognormally distributed, thus with strong time dependence of the failure rate (Table A6.1 on p. 447). Highly accelerated stress tests (HAST) and highly accelerated life tests (HALT) can activate failure mechanisms which would not occur during normal operation, so care is necessary in extrapolating results to situations exhibiting lower stresses. Often, the purpose of such tests is to force (not only to activate) failures. They belong thus to the class of semi-destructive or destructive tests, often used at the qualification of prototype to investigate possible failure modes, mechanisms, and/or technological limits. The same holds for step-stress accelerated tests (often used as life tests or in screening procedures), for which, damage accumulation can be more complex as given e. g. by the Miner's hypothesis or in [7.20, 7.28]; a case-by-case investigation is mandatory for all this kind of tests (see also remarks on pp. 102, 341, 342, 406). # 7.5 Goodness-of-fit Tests Let $t_{1}, \ldots, t_{n}$ be $n$ independent observations of a random variable $\tau$ distributed according to $\mathrm{F}(t)$, a rule is asked to test the null hypothesis $H_{0}: \mathrm{F}(t)=\mathrm{F}_{0}(t)$, for a given type I error $\alpha$ (probability of rejecting a true hypothesis $H_{0}$ ), against a general alternative hypothesis $H_{1}: \mathrm{F}(t) \neq \mathrm{F}_{0}(t)$. Goodness-of-fit tests deal with such testing of hypothesis and are often based on the empirical distribution function (EDF), see Appendices A8.3 for an introduction. This section shows the use of Kolmogorov-Smirnov and chi-square tests. Cramér -von Mises tests are summarized on pp. 572 - 73. Trend tests are discussed in Section 7.6. ### 7.5.1 Kolmogorov-Smirnov Test The Kolmogorov-Smirnov test (pp. 545-46, 572) is based on the convergence for $n \rightarrow \infty$ of the empirical distribution function (Eq. (A8.1)) $$ \hat{\mathrm{F}}_{n}(t)= \begin{cases}0 & \text { for } t<t_{(1)} \\ i / n & \text { for } t_{(i)} \leq t<t_{(i+1)}, \\ 1 & \text { for } t \geq t_{(n)}\end{cases} \quad i=1,2, \ldots, n-1 $$ to the true distribution function, and compares the experimentally obtained $\hat{\mathrm{F}}_{n}(t)$ with the given (postulated) $\mathrm{F}_{0}(t) . \quad \mathrm{F}_{0}(t)$ is assumed here to be known and continuous, $t_{(1)}<\ldots<t_{(n)}$ are the ordered observations. The procedure is as follows: Figure 7.11 Largest deviation $y_{1-\alpha}$ between a postulated distribution function $\mathrm{F}_{0}(t)$ and the corresponding empirical distribution function $\hat{\mathrm{F}}_{n}(t)$ at the level $1-\alpha\left(\operatorname{Pr}\left\{D_{n} \leq y_{1-\alpha} \mid \mathrm{F}_{0}(t)\right.\right.$ true $\left.]=1-\alpha\right)$ 1. Determine the largest deviation $D_{n}$ between $\hat{\mathrm{F}}_{n}(t)$ and $\mathrm{F}_{0}(t)$ $$ D_{n}=\sup _{-\infty<t<\infty}\left|\hat{\mathrm{F}}_{n}(t)-\mathrm{F}_{0}(t)\right| $$ 2. From the given type 1 error $\alpha$ and the sample size $n$, use Table A9.5 or Fig. 7.11 to determine the critical value $y_{1-\alpha}$. 3. Reject $H_{0}: \mathrm{F}(t)=\mathrm{F}_{0}(t)$ if $D_{n}>y_{1-\alpha} ;$ otherwise accept $H_{0}$. This procedure can be easily combined with a graphical evaluation of data. For this purpose, $\hat{\mathrm{F}}_{n}(t)$ and the band $\mathrm{F}_{0}(t) \pm y_{1-\alpha}$ are drawn using a probability chart on which $\mathrm{F}_{0}(t)$ can be represented by a straight line. If $\hat{\mathrm{F}}_{n}(t)$ leaves the band $\mathrm{F}_{0}(t) \pm y_{1-\alpha}$, the hypothesis $H_{0}: \mathrm{F}(t)=\mathrm{F}_{0}(t)$ is to be rejected (note that the band width is not constant when using a probability chart). Probability charts are discussed in Appendix A.8.1.3, examples are in Appendix A9.8 and Figs. 7.12 - 7.14.

Life times $t_{1}, \ldots, t_{n}$ of $n$ statistically identical and independent items, all starting at $t=0$ when plotted on the time axis (Figs. 1.1, 7.12, 7.14, A8.1). 2. Failure-free times separating consecutive failure occurrences of a repairable item (system) with negligible repair times, repaired (restored) as a whole to as-good-as-new at each repair; i. e. statistically identical, independent interarrival times with common distribution function $\mathrm{F}(x)$, yielding a renewal process. This situation often occurs in reliability tests; for instance, when only the failed part in a system is repaired to as-good-as-new (p.138-39), and at least one element in the system has a time dependent failure rate; in this case, failure-free times (interarrival times, by negligible repair times) are neither independent nor equally distributed. Except for very large systems, for which the flow of failures can converge to a homogeneous Poisson process (p. 537), the only situation which leads to independent and equally distributed interarrival times is that of case 2 above, which requires constant failure rate for all elements to avoid restoration at each repair of all not failed elements with time dependent failure rate. ##

If a trend in consecutive interarrival times is recognized, but the underlying point process cannot be approximated by a renewal process (including the homogeneous Poisson process (HPP)) or an NHPP, a further possibility is to consider the observed failure time points $t_{1}^{*}<t_{2}^{*}<\ldots$ directly. As shown in Appendix A7.8.5, a mean value function $\mathrm{Z}(t)=\mathrm{E}[\mathrm{v}(t)]$ can be associated to each point process, where $v(t)$ is the count function giving the number of events (failures) occurred in $(0, t]$ $\left(Z_{S}(t)\right.$ and $v_{S}(t)$ for considerations at system level). From the observed failure time points (observed occurrence times) $t_{1}^{*}<t_{2}^{*}<\ldots$, the empirical mean value function $\hat{\mathrm{Z}}(t)=\hat{\mathrm{E}}[\mathrm{v}(t)]$ follows as $$ \hat{\mathrm{Z}}(t)=\hat{\mathrm{E}}[\mathrm{v}(t)]= \begin{cases}0 & \text { for } t<t_{1}^{*} \\ i & \text { for } t_{i}^{*} \leq t<t_{i+1}^{*}, \quad i=1,2, \ldots\end{cases} $$ In a renewal process, the mean value function $\mathrm{Z}(t)$ corresponds to the renewal function $\mathrm{H}(t)$ (Eq. (A7.15)), and the failure intensity $\mathrm{z}(t)=d \mathrm{Z}(t) / d t$ correspond to the renewal density $\mathrm{h}(t)$ (Eqs. (A7.18) \& A7.24)). For a homogeneous Poisson process (HPP), $\mathrm{Z}(t)$ takes the form (Eq. (A7.42)) $$ \mathrm{Z}(t)=\mathrm{E}[\mathrm{v}(t)]=\lambda t $$ Each deviation from a straight line $\mathrm{Z}(t)=a \cdot t$ is thus an indication for a possible trend (except for statistical deviations). As shown in Fig. A7.2 on p. 484 for a renewal process, early failures or wear-out gives a basically different shape of the underlying renewal function, a convex shape for the case of early failures and a concave shape for the case of wear-out. This property can be used to recognize the presence of trends in a point process, by considering the shape of the associated empirical mean value function $\hat{\mathrm{Z}}(t)$ given by Eq. (7.97), see e. g. [7.24] for an application. However, such a procedure remains a very rough evaluation (see e.g. Fig. A7.2); care is thus necessary when extrapolating results, for instance, about a percentage of early failures or the failure rate after an early failure period.# 7.7 Reliability Growth At the prototype qualification tests, the reliability of complex equipment \& systems can be less than expected. Disregarding any imprecision of data or model used in calculating the predicted reliability (Chapter 2), such a discrepancy is often the consequence of weaknesses (errors, flaws, mistakes) during design or manufacturing. For instance, use of components or materials at their technological limits or with internal weaknesses, cooling, interface or EMC problems, transient phenomena, interference between hardware and software, assembling or soldering problems, damage during handling, transportation or testing, etc. Errors and flaws cause defects and systematic failures. Superimposed to these are early failures and failures with constant failure rate (wear-out should not be present at this stage). However, a distinction between deterministic faults (defect \& systematic failures) and random faults (early failures \& failures with constant failure rate) is only possible with a cause analysis; such an analysis is necessary to identify and eliminate causes of observed faults (redesign for defects and systematic failures, screening for early failures, and repair for failures with constant failure rate), and initiates a learning process improving the reliability of the equipment or system considered. Of course, defects and systematic failures can also be randomly distributed on the time axis, e. g. caused by a mission dependent time-limited overload, by software defects, or simply because of the system complexity. However, they still differ from failures, as they are basically independent of operating time (disregarding systematic failures which can appear only after a certain operating time, e. g. as for some cooling or software problems). The aim of a reliability growth program is the cost-effective improvement of the item's reliability through successful correction/elimination of the causes of design or production weaknesses. Early failures should be precipitated with an appropriate screening (environmental stress screening (ESS)), see Section 8.2 for electronic components and Section 8.3 for electronic assemblies, as well as Section 8.4 for cost aspects. Considering that flaws found during reliability growth are in general deterministic (defects and systematic failures), reliability growth is performed during prototype qualification tests and pilot production, seldom for series-produced items (Fig. 7.16). Stresses during reliability growth are often higher than those expected in the field (as for ESS). Furthermore, the statistical methods used to investigate reliability growth are in general basically different from those given in Section 7.2.3 for standard reliability tests to estimate or demonstrate a constant failure rate $\lambda$. This is because during the reliability growth program, design and / or production changes or modifications are introduced in the item(s) considered and statistical evaluation is not restarted after a change or modification. Figure 7.16 Qualitative visualization of a possible reliability growth A large number of models have been proposed to describe reliability growth for hardware and software, see e. g. [5.68, 5.71, 7.31-7.49, A2.6 (61014 \& 61164)], some of which on the basis of theoretical considerations. A practice oriented model, proposed by J.T. Duane [7.36], refined in [7.35 (1975)], and carefully investigated in [A8.1], known also as the AMSAA model, assumes that the flow of events (system failures) constitutes a nonhomogeneous Poisson process (NHPP) with intensity $$ \mathrm{m}(t)=\frac{d \mathrm{M}(t)}{d t}=\alpha \beta t^{\beta-1}, \quad \alpha>0,0<\beta<1, t>0, \mathrm{~m}(t)=0 \text { for } t \leq 0 $$ and mean value function $$ \mathrm{M}(t)=\alpha t^{\beta}, \quad \alpha>0,0<\beta<1, t>0, \mathrm{M}(t)=0 \text { for } t \leq 0 $$ $\mathrm{M}(t)$ gives the expected number of failures in $(0, t] . \mathrm{m}(t) \delta t$ is the probability for one failure (any one) in $(t, t+\delta t]$ (Eq. (7.74)). It can be shown that for an NHPP, $\mathrm{m}(t)$ is equal to the failure rate $\lambda(t)$ of the first occurrence time (Eq. (A7.209)). Thus, comparing Eqs. (7.99) \& (A6.91) one recognizes that for the NHPP described by Eq. (7.99), the first occurrence time has a Weibull distribution; however, $\mathrm{m}(t)$ and $\lambda(t)$ are fundamentally different (see remarks on pp. 7, 356, 390 $-91,441-42,482,540$ ), and all others interarrival times do not follow a Weibull distribution and are neither independent nor identically distributed. Because of the distribution of the first occurrence time, the NHPP process described by Eq. (7.99) is often (improperly) called Weibull process, causing great confusion. Also used is the term power law process. Nonhomogeneous Poisson processes are investigated in Appendix A7.8.2.In the following, an NHPP will be assumed as underlying model; i.e., considering remarks on pp. 535 (point 2) and 138, it is assumed that at each failure the item (system) is repaired in a negligible time to as-bad-as-old (verification of this assumption is mandatory, based also on physical considerations on the nature /causes of failures involved). If the underlying process is an NHPP, estimation of the model parameters ( $\alpha$ and $\beta$ in the case of Eq. (7.99)) can easily be performed using observed data. Let's consider first the time censored case, and assume that up to the given (fixed) time $T, n$ events have occurred at times $0<t_{1}^{*}<t_{2}^{*}<\ldots<t_{n}^{*}<T . \quad t_{1}^{*}, t_{2}^{*}, \ldots$ are the realizations (observations) of the arrival times $\tau_{1}^{*}, \tau_{2}^{*}, \ldots$ and * indicates that $t_{1}^{*}, t_{2}^{*}, \ldots$ are points on the time axis and not independent realizations of a random variable $\tau$ with a given (fixed) distribution function. Considering the main property of an NHPP, i. e. that the number of events in nonoverlapping intervals are independent and distributed according to (Eq. (A7.195), see also the footnote on p. 481) $$ \operatorname{Pr}\{k \text { events in }(a, b]\}=\frac{(\mathrm{M}(b)-\mathrm{M}(a))^{k}}{k!} e^{-(\mathrm{M}(b)-\mathrm{M}(a))}, \quad \begin{aligned} & k=0,1,2 \\ & 0 \leq a<b, \mathrm{M}(0)=0 \end{aligned} $$ and the interpretation of the intensity $\mathrm{m}(t)$ given by Eq. (7.74) or Eq. (A7.194), the following likelihood function (Eq. (A8.24)) can be found for the parameter estimation of the intensity $\mathrm{m}(t)$ $$ \begin{aligned} \mathrm{L} & =\mathrm{m}\left(t_{1}^{*}\right) e^{-\mathrm{M}\left(t_{1}^{*}\right)} \mathrm{m}\left(t_{2}^{*}\right) e^{-\left(\mathrm{M}\left(t_{2}^{*}\right)-\mathrm{M}\left(t_{1}^{*}\right)\right)} \ldots \mathrm{m}\left(t_{n}^{*}\right) e^{-\left(\mathrm{M}\left(t_{n}^{*}\right)-\mathrm{M}\left(t_{n-1}^{*}\right)\right)} e^{-\left(\mathrm{M}(T)-\mathrm{M}\left(t_{n}^{*}\right)\right)} \\ & =e^{-\mathrm{M}(T)} \prod_{i=1}^{n} \mathrm{~m}\left(t_{i}^{*}\right) \end{aligned} $$ Equation (7.102) considers no event ( $k=0$ in Eq. (7.101)) in each of the nonoverlapping intervals $\left(0, t_{1}^{*}\right),\left(t_{1}^{*}, t_{2}^{*}\right), \ldots,\left(t_{n}^{*}, T\right)$ and applies to an arbitrary NHPP. For the Duane model it follows that $$ \mathrm{L}=e^{-\mathrm{M}(T)} \prod_{i=1}^{n} \mathrm{~m}\left(t_{i}^{*}\right)=\alpha^{n} \beta^{n} e^{-\alpha T^{\beta}} \prod_{i=1}^{n} t_{i}^{* \beta-1} $$ or $$ \ln \mathrm{L}=n \ln (\alpha \beta)-\alpha T^{\beta}+(\beta-1) \sum_{i=1}^{n} \ln \left(t_{i}^{*}\right) $$ The maximum likelihood estimates for the parameters $\alpha \& \beta$ are then obtained from $$ \left.\frac{\partial \ln L}{\partial \alpha}\right|_{\alpha=\hat{\alpha}}=0 \quad \&\left.\quad \frac{\partial \ln L}{\partial \beta}\right|_{\beta=\hat{\beta}}=0 $$ yielding $$ \hat{\alpha}=\frac{n}{T^{\beta}} \quad \& \quad \hat{\beta}=\frac{n}{\sum_{i=1}^{n} \ln \left(T / t_{i}^{*}\right)}, \quad \text { (time censoring) } $$An estimate for the intensity of the underlying nonhomogeneous Poisson process is given by $$ \hat{\mathrm{m}}(t)=\hat{\alpha} \hat{\beta} t \hat{\beta}-1, \quad 0<t<T $$ Equation (7.105) can be used to extrapolate the attainable intensity if the reliability growth process were to be continued with the same statistical properties for a further time span $\Delta$ after $T$, yielding $$ \hat{\mathrm{m}}(T+\Delta)=\hat{\alpha} \hat{\beta}(T+\Delta) \hat{\beta}-1, \quad \Delta>0 $$ see

Example 7.25 for a practical application. In the case of event censoring, i. e. when the test is stopped at the occurrence of the $n$th event (Type II censoring), Eq. (7.102) yields $\mathrm{L}=e^{-\mathrm{M}\left(t_{n}^{*}\right)} \prod_{i=1}^{n} \mathrm{~m}\left(t_{i}^{*}\right)$ and thus $$ \hat{\alpha}=\frac{n}{t_{n}^{* \hat{\beta}}} \quad \& \quad \hat{\beta}=\frac{n}{\sum_{i=1}^{n-1} \ln \left(t_{n}^{*} / t_{i}^{*}\right)}, \quad \text { (event censoring) } $$ i. e. by summing over $n-1$ and taking $T=t_{n}^{*}$. Interval estimation for the parameters $\alpha$ and $\beta$ is possible, see for instance [A8.1]. For goodness-of-fit-tests one can consider the property of nonhomogeneous Poisson processes that, for given (fixed) $T$ and knowing that $n$ events have been observed in $(0, T)$, i. e. for given $T \& v(T)=n$, the occurrence times $0<\tau_{1}^{*}<\ldots<\tau_{n}^{*}<T$ are distributed as if they where the order statistic of $n$ independent and identically distributed random variables with density $\mathrm{m}(t) / \mathrm{M}(T)$, on $(0, T)$ (Eq. (7.77) or (A7.205)). (A7.200)). Results for independent and identically distributed random variables, for HPP or for exponential distribution function can thus be used. #
